An 86-year-old man was found dead inside a car pulled from the Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach after witnesses said the vehicle drove through a fence and into the water. An 86-year-old man was found dead inside a car submerged in the Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach after witnesses said the vehicle drove through a fence and into the water. The incident occurred at a condo complex, where residents said they knew the driver. Police have not yet identified the man. Tire marks were visible near the scene, and the silver Honda CRV was pulled from the water as police worked for hours to investigate. Authorities said the man had gone missing the night before. Residents on Greytwig Road were later seen cleaning up the parking lot, removing mud and scrubbing away tire marks. Many described the scene as unsettling. The investigation remains active as police work to determine what led up to the crash.

Southbound lanes on Florida’s Turnpike were closed in St. Lucie County Tuesday morning after a tractor trailer fire broke out. It started around 7:54 a.m. right before Mile Marker 161, about 10 miles north of the Okeechobee Road exit. Lucie County Fire District said it reportedly started in the cab, but they arrived to find the vehicle completely engulfed. After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

Martin County parents are celebrating a victory in a long battle to improve safety around their children's school.Citrus Grove Elementary School parents say the 45 mph speed limit outside the school puts their children's safety in jeopardy. They say a recently approved school zone is the first step to making Newfield Parkway a safer place for children who walk to school.On Southwest Newfield Parkway, morning and afternoon traffic is an obstacle for young students."It scares me," parent Kendall George said. "These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus."Kendall is among the many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from Citrus Grove Elementary, so their children walk to school. Kelly Ribaudo, the PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, told WPTV she's spent the last five years asking the county to put in a school zone."We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention," Ribaudo said. "Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic."At the previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners unanimously answered their call."Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt," Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "You will absolutely get a school zone."School Principal Rose Rynca told WPTV the need is greater than ever, with enrollment growing as new communities pop up in the area."The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased," Rynca said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students.""It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.WPTV's Cassandra Garcia followed up with the county on Thursday to find out the timeline for adding a school zone on SW Newfield Parkway. In a statement they said:In the meantime, these parents are asking drivers to be cautious."Slow down if you see a school — even if there's not a school zone sign, slow down," Ribaudo said.With a school zone on the horizon, these parents said the next step is getting better street lighting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Golfers at a Veterans Day fundraiser in Hobe Sound will share the course with local veterans, as Tee It Up for the Troops brings its tournament to The Club at Lost Lake for the first time. The event is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration listed at $750 per player. Veterans paired with foursomes will play for free, according to Chris LaRocque, the nonprofit’s president and executive director. It’s very close to my heart, LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. I’m an Army Reserve major myself. He said Tee It Up for the Troops has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that include help with the transition to civilian jobs and support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries. The tournament will also support local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, LaRocque said. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being. The tournament will be held at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

Signs reading Dump Trump and Trump for Prison rose above a crowd along Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard on Saturday as music played and demonstrators gathered to voice their opposition. Some wore Resist shirts and shirts featuring comedian Stephen Colbert. In a video posted by Palm Beach Indivisibles, a demonstrator sang songs touching on political and social issues into a microphone, drawing a chorus of Free speech chants when a West Palm Beach police officer attempted to stop her. The chanting continued until the officer left. The gathering near Target was one of several No Kings events scheduled across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast, as Trump returned to Palm Beach for his first visit of the season. For those who came out, the reasons varied, but several protesters interviewed by Palm Beach Indivisibles described a desire for change. See also: President Trump departs Palm Beach for Kentucky rally after Mar-a-Lago RNC fundraiser We don't have enough time to list all the reasons, but mainly we just need to take our country back and make sure that we have love and kindness and compassion in our hearts again, one demonstrator said. Another said they were there to oust Trump. A different attendee joked that former President Barack Obama had called and asked him to show up. Saturday’s demonstrations were part of a nationwide No Kings: Vote Early day of action. Organizers said more than 3,000 events were planned across the country, with a focus on encouraging voter participation ahead of the Nov. The effort marks an added focus for the coalition, which has organized demonstrations against what it describes as an expansion of presidential power. This time, organizers are also encouraging people to check their voter registration, learn about their voting options and make a plan to cast a ballot. They describe the voter outreach as nonpartisan. Where No Kings events were scheduled locally Palm Beach County Palm Beach Gardens: 10 a.m. to noon at PGA Boulevard and Campus Drive. on Palm Beach Lakes Boulevard, east of I-95, between Executive Center Drive and Congress Avenue. Wellington: 12:30 to 1:30 p.m. on the public sidewalk in front of the Veterans Memorial. Boynton Beach: 1 to 3 p.m. at Boynton Beach Boulevard and North Congress Avenue. to noon at Boca Raton City Hall. Treasure Coast Sebastian: 10 to 11 a.m. The address was private, with details available through registration. 1 and Kanner Highway/Colorado Avenue. at the MidFlorida Event Center. Protests coincide with Trump's Palm Beach visit President Trump arrived at Donald J. Trump International Airport shortly after 8 p.m. Friday after a rally in Dalton, Georgia. He left Saturday morning for a rally in Kentucky. His visit brought additional security measures and traffic impacts to Palm Beach. South Ocean Boulevard was closed between South County Road and Southern Boulevard, according to the Town of Palm Beach, which advised drivers heading to the island to use the middle or north bridge. The demonstrations came just days before Palm Beach County’s early voting period begins Oct. Voting is scheduled to continue through Nov. 1, ahead of Election Day on Nov.

It is as dominant a college sports program as there is anywhere in the country, and it's located on the Treasure Coast.WPTV received several emails from concerned residents that the plug may soon be pulled on this diving dynasty. We're learning the Board of Trustees at Indian River State College are looking to possibly eliminate the men's and women's swimming and diving teams.WATCH BELOW: IRSC swimmers react to possible elimination of programThis past March, the men's swim and dive team captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, and the women's team claimed its 48th crown.WPTV listened to sophomore swimmer Kalla Hall, who came to the college from Australia, joining the decorated and prestigious swimming and diving team under head coach Sion Brinn.The team has produced multiple Olympians, including Brinn.Hall was first nationally at the 100-meter freestyle last year."I knew I'd wanted to be an Olympian," Hall said. "[Brinn] dropped my swim times incredibly, but just in and out of the pool, he's an all-round incredible man."But the pool could soon be drained of its energy.Hall said he is upset about the Board of Trustees proposal to eliminate the program."We feed so many of our swimmers into NCAA Division One and Division II," Hall said. "It's just phenomenal, and I just don't know why they would want to get rid of this program."Freshman diver Tessa Simms said she's worried about her teammates from abroad."We have 14 international athletes, and what are they going to do if our program gets cut?" Simms said.Hall said this program is more than just a decorated team. He said it's a family, spanning generations."How upsetting it will be to tear down this family that has been going for so long, with hundreds of people that I’ll never even meet," Hall said.Former swimmer Ella Smith started a petition on Tuesday, now with more than 7,000 signatures, and growing."What we're doing is putting out the best kind of positive that we can," Smith said. "I genuinely think that the Board of Trustees are going to realize that this is a mistake."Smith is also from Australia, getting medals in the 100-, 200- and 400-meter breaststroke and getting gold in the 50-meter.But beyond the bling, Smith said it's the team and family she found through this program that she doesn't want to see disappear."These are more than just athletes. We are people, and this creates such an extraordinary experience in life that you can hold onto forever," Smith said.WPTV reached out to Indian River State College, and we're still working on a response.The Board of Trustees will discuss the proposal on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixie Hendry Campus in Okeechobee.

Questions about who is leading Riviera Beach and the future of City Manager William E. Wilkins took center stage during a contentious city council discussion Wednesday, as some elected leaders said they were unaware of the extent of his absence following an August car crash.Wilkins has been working remotely since the crash, according to city officials. While assistant city manager staff have handled many day-to-day operations inside city hall, some council members said they only recently learned key details about Wilkins' condition and work arrangements.The debate comes as Riviera Beach continues to navigate leadership challenges following the April 2026 firing of former City Manager Jonathan Evans, with residents and officials alike calling for stability at City Hall.WATCH: Riviera Beach leaders seek answers on city manager's future, statusCouncil members question communication and leadershipDuring Wednesday's meeting at Marina Village, some council members expressed frustration over what they described as a lack of communication regarding Wilkins' status.Councilwoman Shirley D. Lanier said she had not spoken with Wilkins since August and was unaware he had been injured in a crash."I didn't know he was in a car wreck. I didn't know he was on TV and I haven't heard from him since then," Lanier said.Lanier and Councilwoman Kashamba Miller-Anderson questioned whether the city's leadership structure is sustainable if the city manager remains out of the office for an extended period."I understand he has health issues. But someone has to run the business of the city," Lanier said during the discussion.Miller-Anderson argued that city leaders need clarity on Wilkins' plans moving forward. Miller-Anderson also questioned whether Wilkins' remote work arrangement aligns with the terms of his employment agreement."Either take leave, resign, or come back. And I think that's only right and that's only fair to ask," Miller-Anderson said.Other officials say city operations continueNot everyone on the dais agreed with the criticism.Dr. Glen Spiritis, chair pro tem, said he has maintained communication with Wilkins and believes the city manager continues to oversee city operations while working remotely."I have had communications with him, and he is clearly in charge right now," Spiritis said, while also praising the assistant city manager's handling of daily operations.Supporters argued that city business remains on track despite Wilkins' recovery and remote work arrangement.Residents call for stabilitySeveral residents who spoke during or around the meeting said they were largely unaware of the circumstances surrounding Wilkins' absence.Resident Doretta Paulk said she did not know what had happened to the city manager."This is a very sad situation because I didn't even know what happened to Mr. Wilkins," Paulk said.Other residents urged city leaders to focus on moving Riviera Beach forward rather than engaging in disputes."We're here for the business of the city," resident Margaret Shepherd said. "Let's find out how we can move the city forward."What happens next?City officials are set to review potential next steps regarding Wilkins' status. It remains unclear whether any formal action will be considered by the city council.WPTV reached out to Wilkins for comment but had not received a response as of Wednesday evening.The discussion is likely to remain a topic of public interest as city leaders work to provide clarity on Riviera Beach's management structure and long-term leadership plans.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Homebuilidng company Lennar is set to become the buyer of the Boynton Beach Mall, a company spokesperson confirmed to WPTV. The company plans to develop "a vibrant mixed-use community" on the 91-acre site. a Lennar spokesperson said in a statement. The company said the development could help "alleviate Palm Beach County’s severe housing shortage." The purchase is expected to be completed by "early" 2027, according to a Lennar spokesperson. "Although planning is in the early stages and we look forward to stakeholder feedback, our vision is to take advantage of this unique opportunity with a mix of single-family attached housing opportunities, complemented by retail, commercial, open space and civic uses that will create a walkable, connected environment," the statement said. RELATED VIDEO: Boynton Beach Mall tenants told to leave by Jan. 15 as questions surround property's futureTenants of the mall — which opened more than four decades ago — recently received lease termination notices instructing them to vacate the building by mid-January, WPTV previously reported earlier this week.

By: Amanda Boettcher Posted BOCA RATON, Fla. — Congressman Jared Moskowitz said a person was arrested near his home in Boca Raton for threatening his life. In a social media post, Moskowitz said the person is in the Palm Beach County jail and he and his family are safe. A constituent of mine has just been arrested in Boca, just a few miles from my house, for threatening my life. He is currently in the Palm Beach County jail. I’m grateful to @fdlepio and local law enforcement for acting quickly to keep myself and my family safe. This is a developing story. WPTV will provide more details as they become available.

WPTV is staying on top of the future of data centers in Palm Beach County as commissioners rethink who should help develop new regulations for an industry that has already generated significant concern among residents.County commissioners on Wednesday backed away from immediately moving forward with one consultant selected by staff, instead deciding they want to consider other options before making a final selection.At the same time, commissioners agreed to bring back plans for a formal community task force, giving the public a greater role as the county considers what its future data center regulations should look like.The discussion comes less than a month after commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on Sept. 24.County staff told commissioners the clock is now running to establish regulations before that moratorium expires.The county staff had proposed hiring VHB (Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.), an engineering and planning firm, to work alongside staff on a framework designed to protect communities, establish clearer expectations and create standards the county could administer and enforce.It would cost $224,900 for VHB's services.But the proposal quickly drew questions from residents.“I have concerns today about the consultant who was chosen,” said Rachel Smith, an Acreage resident.Resident Ben Brown questioned how the firm had been selected and whether enough alternatives were considered.“I have many questions. When did you reach out to this consultant? Are you interviewing other ones?” Brown said. “They obviously work with data centers. You are putting the fox in the henhouse.”County staff said they issued a request for information and received six proposals that were incomplete. Staff initially told commissioners the proposals ranged from $200,000 for a portion of the needed support to $2 million.Later in the discussion, staff described the range as about $125,000 for an architect who would only be part of the process, requiring additional experts, to about $2.1 million.Those concerns put particular scrutiny on VHB and its existing work involving data centers.“Do you have clients that are a part of data centers?” Mayor Sara Baxter asked the consultant representative directly.“We work for clients that have data centers in Massachusetts and Virginia,” answered Curt Ostrodka a VHB representative responded. “We don't have any clients in Florida building data centers.”The firm's representative also told commissioners VHB had worked as a consultant for private clients providing civil engineering, utility studies and other technical services supporting data centers.When Commissioner Gregg Weiss asked whether the company had ever developed regulations specifically for data centers, the answer was direct.“Not for data centers," said Ostrodka.VHB maintained it could serve as an objective third party while researching how other communities are handling data centers and studying potential impacts including noise, energy and water.“We don't know the answers right now,” Ostrodka said. “We would do that collaboratively with staff, members of the public.”The company outlined a nine-month process that would also examine applicable state and federal laws and determine thresholds and regulatory mechanisms for potential impacts.Commissioner Maria Sachs was among those who wanted more information before committing to the firm.“This is one company standing here I know nothing about,” Sachs said.But county staff stressed that the push to hire a consultant isn't simply about getting another opinion. Staff told commissioners they need additional capacity and technical expertise to develop the rules.“We are asking for this assistance because we are limited in our capacity to do the work,” staff told commissioners. “We need the technical expertise to help support the staff get this done.”Commissioner Joel Flores asked what it might cost for the county to instead bring in its own people to handle the workload.Staff estimated a dedicated team could require two employees, with an average annual salary of about $125,000 each, or roughly $250,000.Flores said the need for specialized knowledge was part of the reason he supported hiring outside help.“I'm not an expert on data centers and this technology is evolving so quick,” Flores said.Flores said commissioners will ultimately decide what the county's rules look like, but expert information could help them determine what safeguards are necessary.“Having someone on our side who is going to say these are the things you want to watch out for, these are the guardrails you want to put in place, I would feel more comfortable,” Flores said.For some residents, the concern was less about whether the county hires a consultant and more about making sure it hires the right one.“For me, at least, it’s less of a money issue and more of, I want quality information, not just necessarily what people want to hear,” Wellington resident Elizabeth Pandich said. “I want to make sure we pick a consultant that is maybe in an environmental and scientific aspect of it, not someone that’s just good at moving data around.”The timeline also weighed heavily on the discussion.Staff told commissioners the moratorium lasts a year. If it expires before the county has new regulations in place, data center applications would be handled under the regulations in place at that time. County attorneys said extending the moratorium could be possible under certain circumstances, but any extension would be limited.Weiss put the urgency bluntly.“Time is of the essence. The clock is ticking,” Weiss said.What initially appeared to be a decision to move forward with VHB changed dramatically near the end of the discussion.Commissioners first voted to proceed with the consultant, with Baxter and Sachs opposed. But moments later, Commissioner Bobby Powell moved to reconsider the decision.Powell said he wanted commissioners to have choices before committing to a single company.“My motion is not to consider two consultants,” Powell said. “It would be for us to have an option to not only consider this consultant but more options. One consultant, maybe there is another person or another consultant company.”The motion to reconsider passed 3-2.Commissioners then voted 4-1 to give the county the opportunity to look at other available consultants rather than immediately settling on VHB.That doesn't necessarily mean VHB is out of consideration.“I'm sure this gentleman may win out in the end,” Sachs said. “But then at least we would know. Let's find out.”While commissioners debated which experts should advise them, there was considerably more agreement about giving residents a direct role in the process.Several speakers called for commissioners to revive the idea of a community task force, arguing that the two public outreach meetings outlined by staff would not provide enough community involvement.Baxter supported establishing a formal task force and suggested that because the regulations would apply countywide, each commissioner could appoint someone to represent their district.“This new ordinance, it would be countywide,” Commissioner Marci Woodward said earlier in the discussion. “This isn't about a specific parcel.”Baxter said the task force proposal could come back before commissioners at their Nov. 18 meeting.Smith welcomed the idea of combining expert input with residents who could be affected by whatever rules the county ultimately adopts.“I do appreciate that they are looking at expert opinions, although I do think that we have enough experts in this area who are actually affected that could be very beneficial,” Smith said.Pandich said she and others who became involved after Project Tango have already formed the National Data Impact Coalition and hope to participate.“I’m excited about the task force. A couple of friends of mine, after Project Tango, started a national data impact coalition, and we are doing that basically internally. So we are going to put our name in the hat and hopefully get a seat at the table,” Pandich said.For Smith, commissioners' decision to take another look at the consultant while moving toward giving residents a more formal role represented progress.“Yeah, I’d say it’s a victory for the residents,” Smith said. “Thank you to Sachs and Baxter for doing what they did, and Powell, who came in last minute and saved the day.”WPTV reached out to VHB to address concerns raised during the meeting about potential conflicts of interest but has not received a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. — A celebrity golf tournament in Palm Beach County brought athletes, community leaders, and supporters together for a day on the course, but the larger goal stretched far beyond golf.Par for the Culture, presented by the Higher Learning Foundation, raised support for The Lord’s Place and its efforts to expand housing and early-intervention services for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County.The need is significant.The Lord’s Place says the county has more than 500 shelter beds dedicated to people experiencing homelessness, while roughly 1,500 people currently need housing.Those existing beds are generally prioritized for people with the greatest needs, including those who have experienced homelessness for longer periods of time or face significant health and safety concerns.That can leave people who are newly unhoused waiting for help -a gap The Lord’s Place hopes to address with a new shelter model focused on early intervention.The goal is to provide intensive, short-term support before a temporary housing crisis becomes long-term homelessness.“We would really love to shorten their experience in homelessness and get them bridged back and transitioned back into the community as quickly as possible,” said Christine Frederick, CEO of The Lord’s Place.Outreach workers say intervening early can help people maintain jobs, stay in school, address health needs and preserve the support systems that can help them regain stability.Cristina Lucier with The Lord’s Place said the longer someone remains on the streets, the greater the risk of losing those connections.“The longer people spend on the streets, they may lose some of those critical social connections that will help them get back on their feet and retain stability long term,” Lucier said.For Devin Perry, that instability was once part of everyday life.“The hardest part is knowing where you’re gonna sleep at, where you’re gonna wake up at, if your stuff is gonna be there when you come back,” Perry said.Perry later entered The Lord’s Place culinary training program, secured housing and began moving toward employment.Having a place of his own has changed what he is able to think about each day.“When the weather is changing, I don’t have to worry about getting sheets or blankets or when it’s too hot, I don’t have to worry about getting fans,” Perry said. “I have some place to call my own.”That type of stability is exactly what organizers behind Par for the Culture hope to help create for more people.Founder Darren Wingate said he created the event as a way to Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

The president of the Florida State Senate says he is voting "No" on Amendment 3, just months after the State Senate approved putting the referendum on the November ballot."As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart," Albritton said in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. "Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure."WATCH BELOW: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3Albritton also stated the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission presents: "An ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced."Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.It would also cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes.Cities and counties stand to lose significant revenue and many local leaders say it will lead to budget cuts, reduced services and possibly creating other revenue streams.The referendum needs 60% approval on Election Day to become law in Florida.

The winless Miami Dolphins returned to the practice field in Miami Gardens following a bye week, with two injured rookies rejoining drills as the 0-5 squad prepares for Week 7.Rookie wide receiver Caleb Douglas, who has been out with an ankle injury since Week 2 when he was injured against the 49ers, is getting run-throughs at practice this week. His return is a positive sign for the Fins offense.WATCH BELOW: Dolphins get key players back at practice "I think it has a big impact on our offense," head coach Jeff Hafley said. "He was a big bright spot early on. Everybody was excited about him from training camp to preseason in the first couple of games that he played," Hafley said.As for when Douglas will be game-ready, Hafley said it depends on how he does during practice this week."My expectations can't be too high because we got to see him practice today. We got to see how he feels tomorrow and if he's able to go and help us out," Hafley said.Also back at practice was rookie safety Kyle Louis. Louis has been injured since Week 1 with an MCL sprain. "As excited as I am to have him back, I think I got to kind of temper that and see how he practices today and then how does he feel after he practices and getting through Thursday and Friday and then we'll see where he's at and physically, mentally and see what he can do and if he's ready to play in a game."Hafley said, like Douglas, they will evaluate Louis and determine later his availability."He's very eager. Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance & Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH TYLER HATFIELD'S REPORT BELOW: Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance & Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. The agenda itself does not provide a reason for the proposed elimination of swimming and diving or detail the financial impact of the restructuring. All of this comes after Indian River State College's men's swim and dive team in March captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, with the women's team also claiming its 48th national title.The meeting will take place at the Williamson Conference Center Auditorium on Indian River State College's Dixon Hendry Campus at 2229 NW 9th Avenue in Okeechobee.

The Supreme Court on Thursday allowed New Hampshire officials to limit when voters may use a student ID to receive a ballot, agreeing that a lower court ruling that blocked enforcement of the policy was too close to Election Day.The unsigned order was a win for New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, and the Republican National Committee, which had supported Scanlan in the fight.The court did not provide a vote count, though it did provide a brief explanation, invoking the “Purcell principle” that warns against last-minute decisions from courts that change election rules.Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a liberal, wrote a brief dissent questioning the application of the Purcell doctrine.New Hampshire voters will fill an open Senate seat in November to replace the retiring Democratic Sen. A recent CNN poll found that Democrats enjoy a 31 percentage point advantage over Republicans among younger adults.Lower federal courts allowed the state to enforce the central prohibition of a law enacted by the state legislature this spring. Under that law, student IDs on their own may no longer be used to verify a voter’s identity. But state law also includes a “safety valve” that allows voters to attempt to prove their identity through other means and the fight at the Supreme Court was about whether, in those circumstances, student IDs could be used as one factor, along with other evidence, to help officials identify people requesting a ballot.When New Hampshire officials interpreted the new state law as shutting off the ability to use student IDs even in those circumstances, a voting rights group called Coalition for Open Democracy sued. A federal district court blocked enforcement of that interpretation on October 2.New Hampshire filed an emergency appeal at the Supreme Court arguing that the Purcell opinion meant should decide the case in its favor. The RNC had warned that the lower court’s order “threatens to disrupt identity verification in New Hampshire’s looming elections.”The Supreme Court has been called on to address several high-profile election disputes heading into next month’s midterms, most notably a decision in mid-September rejecting President Donald Trump’s proposal to change how mail ballots are sent to voters across the country.The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

A Delray Beach homeowner who got a new roof this year now is finding out her insurance will not go up.Betty Haygood contacted WPTV after finding out her insurance renewal was going up $300 even though she had a new roof installed in August.Her insurer, Universal, based in South Florida, told us they were looking over Haygood's policy and gave her a new quote of $3,087, which is $90 less than what she is paying now."I’m OK with that," the 76-year-old home healthcare worker told WPTV."You have helped by bringing it to attention because so many people and neighbors and people I didn’t know reached out to me about that, because I’m not the only one going through something like this," Haygood said. Haygood says she does plan to shop around some other insurance companies, something insurance experts now recommend.Litigation reforms in Florida have led to more insurers, more competition and lower rates.But lower rates don't always mean lower premiums as inflation has made it more expensive to build and repair homes.Many insurers also focus on the age of a roof in assessing risk, and experts also advise checking with an agent first.Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth-Rindom Insurance Agency in Stuart says one step can solve issues down the road."Call an agent who can shop multiple carriers and say what would it save me if I got a new roof," Wiglesworth says.

Lucie County Fire Chief Jeff Lee is speaking out after the fire board terminated his contract Wednesday, ending his tenure after months of turmoil surrounding a hazing investigation and growing criticism of district leadership.Lee did not attend Wednesday’s heated fire board meeting, where commissioners voted to terminate him without cause.In a statement to WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey following the vote, Lee pointed to his previous comments highlighting increases in staffing, pay and benefits he fought for during his time leading the district."During the 2023–2026 period, these efforts included approximately 19% average pay-plan growth, an increase of approximately 100 uniformed personnel, and improved minimum engine staffing from two to three firefighters," the Fire District wrote in a statement October 9. "The District also expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training opportunities, equipment, and facilities to better support personnel in carrying out their responsibilities." “That’s really all I have to say,” Lee told Hussey Thursday. Lee’s termination marks the latest fallout from a controversy that began after videos surfaced showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. A third-party investigator concluded the conduct amounted to hazing.Three veteran firefighters were fired following the investigation, prompting significant public backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who argued the punishment went too far.“Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation,” one speaker told the board Wednesday.Others said the controversy had damaged confidence in the district.“We need to restore faith in this fire district,” another speaker said.Lee’s departure also follows an overwhelming union vote of no confidence in district leadership.St Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board Member, Jamie Fowler, said the decision to remove Lee was not based solely on the vote of no confidence. “At the end of the day, it’s gotten very messy,” Fowler said. “It’s not about one single decision that he’s made. It’s about bringing peace and calm and respect.”Lee had already signaled that his time as chief could be nearing an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that “the position of fire chief requires confidence” and raised the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition.Deputy Chief Paul Langel has now been appointed interim fire chief as the district searches for Lee’s permanent replacement.Langel inherits a department facing questions about morale, trust and what some speakers Wednesday described as a broader “culture problem.”“Personally, I don’t think there is a culture problem,” Langel said. “But I’m going to do the due diligence and I’m going to evaluate whether that’s visiting fire stations, one-on-one conversations with employees, group settings to get the vibe, what's going on out there, where are we at as an organization, and then once I receive all that, process it, I'll correct the course and move this district forward." The board is now confronting several major issues left unresolved by Lee’s departure.Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to conduct a search for a permanent chief inside and outside the district. "I'm sure we have a very talented pool right here, but we'll see how it plays out," said Fowler. The district and firefighters union are also expected to continue discussions over the possible reinstatement of the three firefighters fired following the hazing investigation.“I’m excited to see if we can just come back together and collectively work together,” union representative Ryan Sapp said.At the same time, the board is moving forward with an outside law firm to overhaul the district's complaint policies after a heated Sept. 30 meeting identified what board members called "a significant gap" in existing policy. Commissioner James Clasby has also called for reconsidering the terms offered in the next fire chief’s contract, as Lee’s existing contract could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance following his termination.“That’s the consequences of firing somebody with those terms,” Clasby said. "The next chief — I'm going to be fighting very hard does not get those terms, and I think that could lead to more accountability." For the four board members who supported Lee’s removal, Wednesday’s vote represented an attempt to turn the page after months of controversy.“There was a large desire to have a change in leadership,” Clasby said, “and we delivered that today.”But Lee’s departure does not end the larger fight over the district’s future. Commissioners must now determine who will permanently lead the agency, whether the terminated firefighters will return and whether new leadership can rebuild trust among firefighters and the community.

Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

A federal judge issued a ruling late Wednesday setting limits for ICE agents visiting homes of immigrants to investigate claims of voter fraud and make arrests.With early voting already underway, ICE has taken the unprecedented step of deploying agents into communities to knock on doors and follow up on data the agency has collected that suggests people at those addresses either voted or registered to vote even though they were ineligible to do so as non-U.S. citizens.ICE INC | Major ICE contractors shower Republican candidates with campaign cashThe Trump administration continues to share pictures and videos online of ICE armed agents in the field arresting noncitizens as part of its “unlawful voting initiative.”But U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín said ICE is relying on data that is unreliable, some of it coming from “unknown artificial intelligence tools.” She pointed to the U.S. government’s acknowledgement that the target list could be tainted by similar names, incomplete records or clerical errors.The ruling says ICE cannot target immigrants using a batch of data likely to have errors or question people when there is a reasonable chance they might be eligible to vote. The order applies to nine states where ICE has been focusing voting fraud enforcement efforts: California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and WisconsinICE’s initiative also likely amounts to voter intimidation in violation of the Voting Rights Act, the judge said, siding with groups who filed the lawsuit saying legal voters were too fearful to cast a ballot.“I think that DHS's actions are absolutely having an impact on the comfort level that people have voting, canvassing or otherwise participating in the political process,” said Jessica Marsden, counsel at Protect Democracy. “And the way the administration is using their social media channels to promote these arrests is what adds to the intimidating character here.”RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersIn a statement to Scripps News, DHS said it is not questioning or investigating people it believes to be U.S. citizens.“DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders,” the statement said.The judge’s restrictions for ICE field operations in the nine states are set to take effect Friday evening and last through the end of Election Day.

WPTV had the rare opportunity to go inside the St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant on Thursday.This year, the facility is celebrating 50 years of operation and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just granted licenses for 20 more. On Thursday, WPTV learned about operations inside the plant and spoke with people who keep the power on.Watch report from Tyler Hatfield:Our Tyler Hatfield listened to Alfred Phillips, a digital INC specialist."My job is to calibrate and make sure all the equipment used to work on the equipment that controls the reactor itself meets all the government standards and accuracies."Phillips said he’s been working at the plant for nearly 20 years."You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well,” .Phillips said. Alfred’s son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed his father's footsteps and works in the operations department."There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride,” Phillips said. “Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better.”WPTV learned from Carlos Santos, site vice president, how the plant generates power."The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat," Santos said.Santos said that heat comes from nuclear fission from uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the two units on site.The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which travels into a secondary closed system into a turbine, which then generates power and produces electricity for the grid.Back in August, the plant had to be manually shut down when three control rods dropped in the reactors core.Florida Power & Light told WPTV at the time that there was no danger to staff or the public, and no one lost power.But after 50 years, technology has changed how employees work. Nicholas Negron, associate innovation specialist, showed WPTV their robotic dog, Tritium."We've named them after nuclear isotopes,” Negron said. “We're utilizing the robot to go in and out of high radiation areas, increasing efficiency both around our heavy machinery and around the plant."Negron said submersibles and drones are also used to inspect equipment"Not only does that increase a lot of the time saving, but it's also substantial cost savings for potential materials,” Negron said.This power plant produces 11 percent of FP&L’s power.Phillips said he feels proud of the responsibility he has every day. "You think about all the things in life you can be doing and " this is good,” Phillips said.

The child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver has ended after prosecutors declined to file formal charges. The State Attorney’s Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document. The filing listed the charge as child abuse intentional act, but did not explain why prosecutors decided not to proceed. Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The allegations were described in an arrest affidavit. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. The video, recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m., showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club, according to the affidavit. Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat. Alpy was seen walking through the aisle and directing the student to sit down. The student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned, the affidavit said. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student’s seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student again stood up and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down. When the child did not, she pulled the bus over, left the driver’s seat and approached the student. Investigators alleged she grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. See also: More than 4.3 million toothpaste tubes recalled, including children's brands The child’s middle finger was extended toward Alpy, according to the affidavit. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student’s hand, forced it into the child’s lap and asked, Do you want me to break this finger? The student later told investigators that Alpy grabbed and bent back the child’s middle finger and said she was going to break it off. The child said they were afraid during the encounter, according to the affidavit.

Ballet Palm Beach is bringing one of literature's most iconic stories to the stage this month with its original production of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein at the Kravis Center in West Palm Beach.The production runs Oct. Playhouse and reimagines Mary Shelley's classic novel through contemporary ballet. Ballet Palm Beach describes the performance as a dramatic exploration of ambition, abandonment and identity. The company is the professional ballet company of Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast.WATCH BELOW: Ballet Palm Beach brings 'Frankenstein' to the Kravis CenterAccording to Founding Artistic and Executive Director Colleen Smith, the story begins before Frankenstein's monster ever comes to life."It's a gorgeous production about Mary Shelley and her haunting book Frankenstein," Smith said.During the broadcast, Smith explained how the famous story was born during a gathering at Lake Geneva."They were gathered together on the shores of Lake Geneva on a stormy night, and Lord Byron was reading ghost stories and said, 'You know what, guys, let's create our own ghost stories,' and she did," Smith said. "First science fiction novel ever written by an 18-year-old woman."Dancer Leah Walker said audiences can expect something different from a traditional ballet."Most classical ballets are fantasy, but ours does follow the real story of Mary Shelley and her process as she writes it," Leah said. It's a very contemporary, very artistic take."The production is recommended for ages 9 and older and features two 45-minute acts separated by a 20-minute intermission.For audiences looking for a Halloween-season experience with a local arts connection, the performance offers a fresh take on a familiar tale. The production combines historical elements from Mary Shelley's life with the themes that have made Frankenstein one of the most enduring stories ever written.Tickets and performance information are available through Ballet Palm Beach and the Kravis Center. Three seniors at Alexander W. Dreyfoos School of the Arts have created Prodigy Pro, a free artificial intelligence platform designed to help students turn their ideas into real-world ventures.Co-founders Aiden Azoy and Anthony Tan and Head of Design Mia Rubio developed the platform after attending South Florida business networking events and realizing how few students were in the room.WATCH: Dreyfoos seniors build free AI platform for student entrepreneurs“We attended networking events and we noticed, why are we the youngest people in the room?” Azoy said. “There are so many talented students in our communities where they’re able to pursue their professional careers outside of school.”The students said they wanted to give young people a way to explore their interests, develop practical ideas and participate in West Palm Beach’s growing business community.The founders attend Dreyfoos in downtown West Palm Beach, where new development and the arrival of major companies have fueled the area’s growing reputation as “Wall Street South.”“We go to Dreyfoos, and literally hundreds of feet away are these huge constructions of Related Ross, companies like ServiceNow or even Citadel moving down to South Florida,” Tan said. “We’re right at the forefront of this new business center that is becoming West Palm Beach.”Tan said the students attempted to connect with professionals at local gatherings but struggled to find opportunities intended for people their age.“We tried to go to these meetings, and a lot of the time there wouldn’t be any opportunity for us,” Tan said. “So that’s why we wanted to create our own.”Prodigy Pro was built to help students take the first steps toward developing projects and businesses.“Prodigy Pro is a free AI entrepreneurship platform that helps a student take their idea from an idea to the final product,” Tan said.Azoy said the team created the platform after noticing that many students were not taking their ideas beyond the classroom.“Prodigy Pro is a way for students to build real ventures outside of school and be able to pursue their professional interests,” Azoy said. “We noticed that not enough students are getting out there and really putting their ideas out into the world. We gave them the ability to do that.”Users enter information about an idea and the problem they hope to solve. The platform’s AI then helps organize the concept and identify potential next steps.Rubio designed the user interface and worked to make the process understandable for students who may have little or no previous business experience.“You upload your information and the idea that you really want to pursue,” Rubio said. “And the AI will help you guide and shape and really tell you what your next step is, as well as create roadmaps, reminders and just really help your venture get off the ground.”The platform divides the development process into smaller sections and tasks.“With Prodigy [Pro], we wanted to make the next step super easy and attainable,” Rubio said. “So we grouped things into different sections and made each task super easy for the user to understand, so they know what to do next with their venture.”During a demonstration, the students used concerns about a school bus route to show how a user could enter a problem and explore possible efficiencies. “You input your information, and it really gives you the next steps, what you should do, and you can ask the AI to help develop your venture,” Rubio said.The founders said making Prodigy Pro free was central to their mission. Azoy said students should have access to the same entrepreneurial tools regardless of their school or community’s resources.“It’s completely free for students, and we want to stress that because we want to basically give the message that a student in an underprivileged school or community should have the same exact resources as, you know, a student in a resourced school,” Azoy said.According to the students, Prodigy Pro has grown to more than 15,000 users in 20 countries.The team also competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a national student entrepreneurship competition.“A few months ago in May, we competed in the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, where we won $7,500 for our venture,” Tan said.Tan said the prize money was reinvested into Prodigy Pro.“A lot of it went into the development of the platform, going through the UI, the back end, also enabling the AI to be free for other students,” he said.The three founders are seniors preparing for life after high school, but they said Prodigy Pro will continue.Asked whether the platform would remain after graduation, Rubio responded, “Yes, of course. It’ll remain to be a free platform for our users.”For Azoy, the larger goal is to show young people that they do not have to wait to begin developing their professional interests.“We really think that it’s important for them to be showing up and, you know, building ventures that really matter because every student has creativity in an underprivileged or privileged school,” Azoy said.The students’ work comes as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into education, business and everyday problem-solving. By making the platform free, the Dreyfoos seniors hope more young people will be able to turn their creativity into action and create opportunities of their own.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Tuesday was a day to remember for several youngsters who had the chance to meet their sports idols thanks to Make-A-Wish. "I was so happy I started crying; it's just an amazing experience," said Yulissa Morales Melendrez, a Make-A-Wish participant.WATCH BELOW: Make-A-Wish kids get dream opportunity to meet Lionel Messi Several kids from around the country had the opportunity to meet the defending MLS Champs, Inter Miami, a moment Make-A-Wish participant Jimmy Hoover could only dream of."I was super excited. I didn't really know what to do; it was kind of all surreal to me," Hoover said.Hoover said he's been playing soccer since he was 7 years old. "I started playing and started watching (Lionel) Messi, and he became my favorite player right away," said Hoover.On Tuesday afternoon, Hoover sat in the stands at Nu Stadium, watching his idol, Messi, and Inter Miami train.It was a simple moment, yes, but a moment that nearly didn't happen."I was going in (to the hospital) for a couple of months, and they were telling me it was just a stomach ache," said Hoover.Hoover and his family didn't think much of it until one day at his friend's house."My stomach was hurting so bad, I was in agonizing pain," said Hoover.He rushed to the hospital, where doctors found out he had cancer, so for months he endured chemotherapy, and while he was fighting for his life, he didn't want to let his teammates down, so every day after treatment he'd be with his teammates."It was really difficult; I couldn't keep up with everyone; that was the hardest part," said Hoover.Dedicated to playing soccer — and again and again kicking cancer's butt — he fought effortlessly, and last July he rang the bell as his cancer went into remission."It's been great. I'm still in a little bit of shock from everything," said Hoover.That shock would soon wear off, and days ago he and his teammates hung out. He got the surprise of a lifetime: he'd be part of the Make-A-Wish Foundation's latest effort to help him and kids from around the world meet Messi and Inter Miami."It's super rewarding. It was a bit of a wait to get out here, but after everything, it's been super great," said Hoover.Kids signed on to join the team for the day, get a jersey, watch the fellas practice, and share joy and hope with the Inter Miami guys."To see this type of resilience and they're going through it at 10 years old and younger than that, if you can take something out of that — it's that you have to keep pushing because somebody always has it worse than you do," said Ian Fray, an Inter Miami defender."It's been so crazy to meet all these players and interview; it's just all been so great," said Hoover.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

On any given Tuesday or Thursday night in the fall, you can expect to see nearly 300 young athletes playing softball at Lake Charleston Park in western Palm Beach County. Two local nonprofits are giving more young athletes the chance to play the sport, with a goal of expanding softball in a way that is affordable and accessible to all.One of those programs is the VSA Lady Lions, a travel softball program whose under-14s team runs a practice packed full of every element softball has to offer — from the tee to home plate."Our normal practice starts with stretching, throwing," Coach Ed Kunzweiler said. "They do a lot of defensive drills. Then we usually do some hitting off coaches, and then we usually try to finish with some live hitting," Kunzweiler said.Coach Kunzweiler said when he started at the club, they had just two travel teams."Now we're at 8 or 9. So it's grown pretty substantially," Kunzweiler said.He said the VSA Lady Lions are the largest women's travel softball program in South Florida — and interest is still growing."I'm really proud about what we built here. It's something that has grown every season," Kunzweiler said.One of the program's star players is Ari Merklein, who plays shortstop, third base and some outfield. She admits her favorite spot on the field is shortstop."I got involved in softball because I just didn't know what sport to pick when I was little and I just couldn't get used to 1 sport. But then I joined softball and I made a lot of friends and I got really good at it and just continued doing it," Merklein said.She never looked back. Merklein said that whether it's at practice or traveling to tournaments on the weekend, her team is having fun."It's really fun. We're all like good friends with each other, so we all hang out outside of softball and inside of softball, and we're good at communicating with each other. So it's just like a lot of good teamwork," Merklein said.Just a field away are the softball newbies who are part of West Boynton Girls Fastpitch, a recreational softball program that is beginner-friendly and has around 200 participants this year."We have kids out here right now that are four or five years old, just learning to pick up a softball for the very first time,” Coach Kunzweiler said. "It's a special program."A place to start — and a place to grow. For many players, that pathway begins with recreational softball.West Boynton Girls Fastpitch provides girls across multiple age groups and experience levels an opportunity to learn the fundamentals of the game, compete locally and become part of a softball community."What's exciting to me is coming by here and seeing all four fields being used. Whether it's rec or travel, it doesn't really matter, but to me, that's what youth sports is supposed to be like, especially community local sports, and it's exciting. We're giving these kids opportunities,” Coach Kunzweiler said.From players learning the fundamentals to athletes like Merklein who want to play at the college level, softball in Lake Charleston Park is a team effort.The West Boynton Girls Fastpitch recreational program and the VSA Lady Lions travel teams are nonprofits and are offered free or at low cost — so that every young girl who picks up a bat can swing for the fences. To learn more about the VSA Lady Lions visit their website.

as Sean Armas and Billy Brewer.Investigators said the men used a black truck marked with the word "STATE TRAPPER" and bearing Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission stickers during at least one of the encounters.Investigators said the first robbery happened near Cresthaven Boulevard and Military Trail.According to PBSO, the victim was riding an e-bike when the suspects pulled alongside him in the black truck.Investigators said the men demanded a passport or other documents proving the victim was a U.S. The victim refused because he did not believe the men were legitimate law enforcement officers, according to PBSO.Investigators said the suspects then grabbed the victim's chain and drove away.Investigators said a second robbery happened near South Military Trail and Summit Boulevard.According to PBSO, one of the men got out of the truck, approached a woman and indicated he had a gun.Investigators said the suspect then grabbed the woman's gold necklace before leaving.PBSO said a third robbery happened in the 400 block of Roberts Way.Investigators said a man was riding an electric scooter when the suspects cut him off with their truck and took his scooter.According to investigators, the suspects told a witness they were law enforcement officers.PBSO told WPTV that information provided by the victims and witnesses helped investigators use license plate reader cameras to track down the truck.Deputies said they recovered some stolen property and took Armas and Brewer into custody.The case comes as the use of license plate reader cameras continues to draw debate over their role in law enforcement investigations.WPTV's Michael Hoffman recently asked Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw whether there was any scenario in which he would consider removing the cameras."No," Bradshaw said.Asked why, Bradshaw defended the technology."Because they're legal. They're a great investigative tool. We help the public with them, and it's a crime prevention tool that we use to solve cases," Bradshaw said.Investigators believe there could be additional people who encountered the two men.PBSO is asking anyone who believes they were victimized by Armas or Brewer, or who remembers an interaction with them, to contact Crime Stoppers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
