The Treasure Coast (FL) Chapter of The Links, Incorporated is celebrating 50 years of friendship and service in 2026, marking five decades of volunteerism, education, advocacy and philanthropy across the region.Chartered October 30, 1976, by 22 women, the chapter serves Indian River, Martin and St. Its approved chapter background reports more than 125,000 volunteer service hours over its history. The chapter works with schools, health providers, civic organizations and nonprofits to address local needs.The chapter organizes its work through five national program facets: Services to Youth, The Arts, National Trends and Services, International Trends and Services, and Health and Human Services.Launched in 2011, Linking Together Against Syndrome X addresses metabolic syndrome and risk factors associated with diabetes, heart disease and stroke. Activities have included free community health symposiums, Women’s Red Dress heart-health education, screenings, nutrition and oral-health education, healthy-lifestyle coaching, and Walk for Healthy Living.The chapter’s approved background reports more than 1,450 people served through its health symposium over more than 13 years.Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. According to the chapter’s 2023-2024 program report, it provided blood glucose and blood pressure screenings, waist-circumference assessments, and COVID-19 testing and education. Other community partners have contributed venues, clinicians, outreach and health education.The 2023-2024 report describes more than 3,000 people educated through the wider Syndrome X initiative over its history and reports broader educational outreach of more than 50,000 people, including public-health campaigns in collaboration with Florida Community Health Centers, Inc. In that report, 90% of surveyed respondents rated educational delivery excellent.The chapter supports student learning and career exploration through scientist-led STEAM education and interactive STEAM Day exhibits at the Indian River State College Planetarium.Its scholarship program supports graduating seniors in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties, considering academic achievement, financial need and leadership. Typical annual awards are approximately $1,000 per recipient per county, and the chapter has also supported renewable four-year scholarships for students attending historically Black colleges and universities. Based on records recently confirmed by chapter leadership, the chapter has awarded more than $150,000 in scholarships since chartering.The chapter conducts nonpartisan voter education, Link Up the Vote activities, Get Out the Vote outreach, public-policy forums and legislative advocacy. Its approved background reports a collaborative voter-mobilization reach exceeding 40,000.Working with law enforcement and advocacy organizations, the chapter also offers human-trafficking prevention education for families and young people, including Women and Girls Human Trafficking Awareness Teas and Boys and Sneaker Balls.The Arts facet contributes to cultural enrichment and arts-related educational experiences, including integration with chapter youth and wellness activities. International Trends and Services advances cross-cultural understanding and community partnerships.Community partners across the Treasure Coast have provided educational spaces, professional expertise, outreach, screening services and other support.The chapter’s 50th-anniversary Emerald Legacy Luncheon is scheduled for Sunday, Oct. at Ballantrae Golf & Yacht Club in Port St. Lucie, recognizing community partners and five decades of friendship and service.Oct. 30, marks Golden Jubilee Day, the 50th anniversary of the chapter’s charter.

Along Maine’s northern border, ties between the United States and Canada have long extended beyond trade. Families live on both sides, and businesses depend on customers crossing the border. A golf course, the Aroostook Valley Country Club, even straddles the international boundary.But Northern Mainers say President Donald Trump’s trade fight with Canada is straining those cross-border relationships and raising economic concerns in communities like Fort Fairfield, located about two miles from the international boundary.Retiree John Foster, who lives in Fort Fairfield, told Scripps News Group that his town’s location puts it in a particularly difficult position.“The economics certainly is a big deal for us,” he said Wednesday.“Most towns,” he explained, “in the U.S. have a 360-degree area that they can haul business from.”RELATED STORY | Heating oil costs test political loyalties in northern Maine“[Half] of that is all Canada,” adding, “a lot of that is not coming here.”The political fallout could also carry implications for incumbent Republican Susan Collins, who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate since 1997 and is seeking re-election in the November midterms.Foster, who is retired and has family on both sides of the border, said he has supported Collins “every time” she’s run.Now, he says he won’t vote for Collins, though he said he still considers himself a Republican.What changed?“Trump,” Foster said flatly.“The Congress is not doing their job; they're not standing up,” he added.The economic dispute has included U.S. tariffs, some up to 50%, on Canadian goods and retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada, adding to tensions between the longtime allies.Those tensions are visible plainly at the Aroostook Valley Country Club, which nearly entirely lies in Canada, but runs along the American border.On Wednesday, a parking lot on the American side of the border across from the clubhouse was empty and partially overgrown. A single small red sign reading, “No access beyond this point,” was the only indication that things have changed.Canadian retiree Leroy Turner, who stopped his golf cart to chat with the Scripps News Group Wednesday, shouted across the border that the club has seen a decline in members from Maine, “big time.”“It's gone from 150 to 175, [or] 200 down to 25 members from Maine,” he said Wednesday.Turner, who lives seven miles from the border, said making regular crossings is harder than they used to be, and Canadians along the border have changed their habits about crossing into neighboring Maine communities.“We used to cross and buy stuff because it was cheaper, you had more to choose from,” Turner said. “People aren't doing that now.”In northern Maine, it’s not clear if a change in which party controls Congress will be enough to de-escalate tensions between Washington and Ottawa.“Until your management changes, I think it's going to stay that way,” Turner said. “We used to go to Fort Fairfield, Maine, every week. Now, [we] go once in a while.”

A man was killed Thursday morning in a crash involving a semi-truck in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP).The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street.According to FHP, a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting to make a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. At the same time, a Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection.Troopers said the Freightliner entered the path of the SUV, causing the front of the Durango to collide with the left side of the semi-trailer.Both vehicles came to rest in the area of the collision.The driver of the SUV, a 60-year-old Vero Beach man, was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m., according to FHP.The driver of the Freightliner, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured.The crash remains under investigation.

Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early. Lucie Police Department has released new information in its investigation of a hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old man seriously injured earlier this month on Oct. 9.Detectives now believe the victim may have been hit by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard.According to police, one vehicle was traveling northbound while the other was traveling southbound at the time of the incident.The crash occurred at approximately 12:56 a.m and the victim, a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries.In a previous update, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, investigators developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash.Police are now working to identify both vehicles and their drivers. Investigators have released images of the vehicles and are asking for the public's help.Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area around the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

This week, I visited a place where learning and fun go hand in hand: the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast.From the moment I walked in, I could tell this wasn't your typical museum. Instead of looking at exhibits from behind a rope or glass case, kids are encouraged to jump in, get involved and learn by doing.As I explored the museum, I discovered exhibits designed to teach important life skills in creative and engaging ways. From learning about money and budgeting to exploring different careers and practicing job skills, every corner of the museum offered a new opportunity to learn something useful.WATCH: One of my favorite stops, of course, involved the weather.As a meteorologist, I was excited to check out the museum's WPTV weather simulator and hurricane simulator. It was fascinating to see how children can experience weather concepts in a hands-on environment and gain a better understanding of the science behind storms and hurricanes.What impressed me most was how interactive everything was. Kids aren't just reading signs or watching demonstrations. They're solving problems, making decisions, using their imaginations and building confidence along the way.The museum creates an environment where learning feels more like an adventure than a lesson. Whether they're exploring future careers, practicing financial skills or learning about science and weather, children are gaining valuable experiences that can help them throughout their lives.My visit was a great reminder that some of the best learning happens when you're having fun. By rolling up their sleeves, asking questions and trying new things, kids can discover skills and interests they never knew they had.If you're looking for a family-friendly destination on the Treasure Coast that combines education, creativity and fun, the Children's Museum of the Treasure Coast is definitely worth a visit.That's where I was!

After noticing worsening water quality while rowing, South Fork High School senior Bianca Bernhard founded the Martin Oyster Restoration Initiative (MORI) a student-led nonprofit that recycles oyster shells to support restoration projects in local waterways.“The water quality got really bad,” Bernhard told WPTV’s T.A. “That’s due to discharges from Lake Okeechobee, so I decided to do something with the extra free time.”The initiative, known as MORI, collects oyster shells from local restaurants. Volunteers at South Fork High School then help dry and cure the shells so they can be used in restoration projects.WATCH: Stuart student leads oyster restoration mission“I recycle a lot of shells from local restaurants,” Bernhard said. “These local shells will help create new reef structures like what I’m holding right here, and those reef structures will grow new oysters which will filter the water.”South Fork High School students and teachers have joined Bernhard’s conservation effort through the school’s marine science, construction and agriculture programs.During the WPTV segment, Jennifer Inostroza, a teacher at South Fork High School, explained that the school helps cure and dry the oyster shells so they are ready for future projects.Information provided by the Martin County School District says MORI has recruited more than 60 students and teachers and amassed approximately 1,600 pounds of oyster shell.The district says participating students can earn honor credits through South Fork High School’s Marine Sciences program.The recycled shells do not immediately return to the water. They must first be transported, dried and cured before they can be incorporated into approved restoration structures.According to Bernhard, those structures provide places where new oysters can grow. She said the oysters then help filter and clean the surrounding water.MORI is also collaborating with Docks for a Clean Lagoon, a nonprofit that installs vertical oyster gardens. According to Bernhard’s Go Blue Awards narrative, shells cured by South Fork volunteers have been used in the creation of vertical oyster gardens intended for the Indian River Lagoon.Bernhard is a finalist in the Blue Hatchling Youth category of Loggerhead Marinelife Center’s 2026 Go Blue Awards.“Bianca is one of our finalists for the Go Blue Hatchling Awards,” said Audrey Padgett, VP of Marketing, at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, told WPTV. “We’ve had nominees from all over the world. So it’s really amazing to see someone selected by this independent panel of judges here in our backyard for the work that she’s doing to improve ocean conservation and ecosystems right here.”The annual awards recognize young people, individuals, businesses and nonprofit organizations making contributions to ocean conservation.The 2026 Go Blue Awards ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. 30, at the Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach.Bernhard’s work comes as MORI prepares for its next phase. According to her Go Blue Awards narrative, she aims to expand the initiative to three additional local schools during the 2026-27 school year.She also plans to pursue oyster restoration research with the Florida Oceanographic Society and work with students to develop additional structures for restoration projects.For Bernhard, the project began with something she saw while rowing. It has since grown into a broader effort that gives students a hands-on role in responding to the environmental challenges facing their community.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

Investing in the next generation takes more than a classroom. It takes mentors, community leaders, and organizations committed to helping young people recognize their potential and prepare for the future.That mission will take center stage at the Urban League of Palm Beach County’s annual Youth Empowerment Luncheon, which brings together students, mentors, and community leaders to celebrate achievement and highlight the importance of investing in young people.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE HERE: Dr. Marcia Andrews, a Palm Beach County School Board member representing District 6, will receive the Youth Advocate and Educator Award in recognition of her decades of service to students and the community.“The Urban League is the heartbeat of any community,” Andrews said.The Urban League of Palm Beach County works with students through programs such as the National Achievers Society, which recognizes academic achievement while helping young people prepare for life after high school.Through the program, students can gain exposure to career opportunities, participate in community service, visit college campuses, and connect with mentors who can help them explore their options.Andrews said students should be encouraged to consider their future possibilities early and understand that there are multiple paths to success.“Our children can be whatever they want to be, and we want to encourage them earlier to start investigating, looking at these possibilities, meeting people in the field,” Andrews said. “You don't have to be a straight A student to go to college; we just want you to do your best.”The effort reflects the importance of collaboration among schools, families and community organizations in helping students succeed academically and prepare for college, careers or other future opportunities.Andrews has spent 51 years working in education in Palm Beach County. Her career has included serving as a teacher, assistant principal, principal, director and chief of human resources, followed by 16 years as an elected school board member.Throughout those roles, she said, her priority has remained helping students feel supported, respected, and encouraged to pursue their goals.One reminder of that impact is a letter Andrews has kept from a former student. Written in 2008, the letter thanked Andrews for listening to students and creating a school environment where they felt comfortable and valued.The student wrote that, under Andrews' leadership as principal, it felt as though the school belonged to the students.For Andrews, the letter remains a meaningful reminder of the importance of putting students first and making sure they know their voices matter.The Youth Empowerment Luncheon celebrates not only students' achievements but also the people and organizations working throughout the year to support them.Andrews said receiving the Youth Advocate and Educator Award is a recognition she shares with the students, schools and community members who contribute to that mission.“It's an award for the students. It's an award for the schools. It's an award for the community,” Andrews said.As the Urban League continues its work to connect young people with resources and opportunities, Andrews hopes students will remain positive, seek out mentors and lean on trusted adults as they navigate the challenges ahead.Her message to the next generation is simple: “Dwell on positive things by doing your best, and the best will come to you.”The annual luncheon serves as a reminder that empowering young people is an ongoing commitment — one that depends on a community willing to stand behind them as they pursue their futures.

A campaign ad in Ohio’s governor’s race is drawing criticism from Democrats and some Republicans and raising questions about how far negative campaigning should go.The ad, paid for by Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign, features Democratic nominee Amy Acton’s birth mother calling her daughter a liar.RELATED STORY | Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother calls her liar in ad, court documents say otherwiseThe ad has drawn particular attention because Acton’s mother lost custody of her when Acton was a child amid sexual abuse allegations involving the man her mother was with at the time.Republican Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina sharply criticized the ad, calling it “the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.”Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said the ad “needs to come down,” but he would not be rescinding his endorsement of Ramaswamy. Acton worked for DeWine as the state's health director during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance were also asked about the controversy but did not condemn the ad.“I know nothing about it,” Trump said. “But I hear the mother went very rogue on the daughter, doesn't have a lot of respect for the daughter.”Trump later added, “It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I don't think that has anything to do with Vivek.”RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election DayVance defended Ramaswamy’s decision to air the commercial.“Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” Vance said.Acton herself condemned the ad, telling CNN that it has "crossed everyone's boundaries." The controversy has extended beyond Ohio, prompting a broader debate about negative political advertising. There was no indication that Ramaswamy’s campaign planned to pull the ad.Republican Sen. John Husted of Ohio also criticized the decision, telling The Associated Press he would not have aired the commercial.

Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

After months of controversy, the St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire longtime Chief Jeff Lee, following an emotional meeting filled with calls for change and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released the results of a no-confidence vote in the district's top leaders. The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether Lee should be fired with or without cause. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Those who supported Lee's removal said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Commissioner Jamie Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following Lee's termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

Voters in Michigan and Kansas saw their Senate candidates square off in high-stakes debates, with control of the Senate potentially hanging in the balance.In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded sharp attacks in one of the country’s most competitive Senate races.El-Sayed sought to tie Rogers closely to President Donald Trump, repeatedly arguing that a vote for Rogers would effectively be a vote for Trump. Rogers, meanwhile, portrayed El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan.The candidates also clashed over several major policy issues.RELATED STORY | El-Sayed, Rogers debate in closely watched Michigan Senate raceEl-Sayed said he supports changes to the U.S. Supreme Court and Medicare for All. On Social Security, he has called for raising the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes.Rogers opposes Medicare for All and previously voted against the Affordable Care Act, though he has said he wants to reform the law. On Social Security, Rogers said he wants lawmakers to work together on a solution but did not outline a specific plan during the debate.The debate also featured a heated exchange over foreign policy, campaign funding and national security, with Rogers questioning El-Sayed’s positions and El-Sayed criticizing Rogers’ ties to Trump.Meanwhile, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton also faced off in Kansas, a state that has become more competitive than many observers expected earlier in the election cycle.RELATED STORY | All eyes on Maine as critical Senate race draws closerHamilton sought to distance himself from national Democratic leadership, saying he would not support Sen. Chuck Schumer as majority leader if elected. Marshall emphasized his relationship with Trump, arguing that he would be able to work with the president to deliver results for Kansas.The candidates also sparred over tariffs and the economy. The CBS12 News I-Team has been closely following Port St. Lucie's election cycle, as there are two headline stories playing out and the future of the city is at stake. Leadership and trash are the hot-button items. On the first day of early voting in St. Lucie County, our crew visited a polling location on Rosser Blvd. We found two tents, side by side. In them, two candidates for mayor-- with such a rift between them-- the race feels like a war. The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. See also: Martin County airport committee to review overnight flights and noise concerns Mayors serve four-year terms and wield significant influence in the mayor-council form of government. But trash collection is another issue getting people fired up: Should the city switch to twice-a-week pickup? FCC is the company that handles garbage collection in Port St. "I don't want to pay for something I don't need," said resident Rob Buske. Buske is making a point we have seldom heard while covering trash in the city. At many recent city council meetings, members of the public have hurled angry comments at city leaders, saying the trash pickup is sub-par. They’ve demanded an additional collection day. Ironic, then, that on the first day of early voting, everyone we asked for comment said they’d rather keep what they’ve got. The ballot question about trash collection isn't binding; it’s simply a way to poll the residents. The council might or might not go with whatever the majority of voters say. A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. Candidates for Mayor do not declare a party, and trash is a non-party matter. Here it's not Republicans vs. Democrats, but it’s somehow more personal, more granular, while also being big-picture. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

In less than two weeks, voters in several school districts in Florida will decide whether to renew a local $1 million property tax referendum that is directly tied to teacher pay. For band teachers like Amrutha Murthy, the suspense and concern are building."We love our students and we want to be able to provide for them, but we don't want it to come at our cost of living, says Murthy.The Park Vista High School instructor is one of nearly 900 teachers in the Palm Beach County School District who could face an average pay cut of $8,000 a year if voters choose not to renew the referendum that first passed in 2018.WATCH: Teachers in the Palm Beach County School District are relying on voters to keep jobs and paySome educators say they're worried the property tax renewal supplement will be confused with the highly controversial Amendment Three Property Tax measure. The "referendum to continue ad valorem levy for school safety, teachers and operational needs" is different. It helps to pay the salaries of music, art and physical education teachers as well as teachers of specialty programs like culinary and aviation. In addition, the Palm Beach County School District says the money is also used to help fund additional security measures and personnel and provide a behavioral health professional at every school."It's been a huge boost for teachers in Palm Beach County because it literally creates a more livable situation," says Gordan Longhofer, president of the Classroom Teachers Association.By next school year, the Palm Beach County School District says some of these teaching positions could be eliminated if the referendum fails. Veteran educators like Marie Chrisphonce could lose the maximum $10,00 annual amount because of their years of experience. She is hoping to keep her job and pay intact."It's scary because that's a lot of pay. It's very scary," says Chrisphonce.While Chrisphonce already has a second job, Murthy says with her busy band schedule, there's just no time. Teachers say they can only hope for a forte of support when voters head to the polls next month.

Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

Martin County’s Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field’s Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and noise concerns. The committee advises the county on airport noise and possible mitigation measures. The airport recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those, 258 took place during the voluntary curfew, which runs from 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate. The county also sent 20 letters to aircraft operators about nighttime activity; the report does not specify how many flights, if any, were considered violations. Residents say private jet traffic can increase when flight restrictions are imposed in Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump’s visits to Mar-a-Lago, affecting their quality of life. The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which aims to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes near the airport. The agenda does not list a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules. If you would like to review the agenda for the meeting, CLICK HERE. This is a developing story.

Palm Beach County zoning staff approved a plan that nearly triples the amount of data center space previously approved on part of the property associated with Project Tango, according to new documents obtained by WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman. 7 approval came less than three months after county commissioners voted 5-1 to reject a much larger Project Tango expansion.The new plan increases the approved data center space from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.That distinction is important because the new approval is separate from the Project Tango expansion commissioners rejected in July.In 2016, plans were approved for 206,000 square feet of data center space and 1.2 million square feet of warehouse space on the property. About 600,000 square feet remained unassigned.The site is next to what would later become the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School.A decade later, a much larger proposal came before the Palm Beach County Commission.On July 15, commissioners spent roughly 12 hours reviewing the application known as Project Tango. That proposal sought to increase the project's data center footprint to more than 1 million square feet.Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny the expansion following significant opposition from nearby residents.The county also passed a moratorium on new data center applications while officials work on new rules.For residents who had fought the expansion, the July decision was a victory. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site.New documents show that was not the end of the story.Documents obtained by Hoffman show PBA Holdings, one of two companies that own property associated with Project Tango, had submitted a separate proposal before the July commission vote.Palm Beach County staff approved that plan Oct. 7 without another vote by county commissioners or a new public hearing before the commission.The approval increases the data center space on that portion of the property from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.The additional data center space uses square footage that had been unassigned under the 2016 approval.Under the newly approved plan, the property would include:Two 288,000-square-foot data center buildingsOne 122,000-square-foot data center building1.2 million square feet of warehouse spaceA utility building and offices occupying the remaining square footageThere is another significant difference between the 2016 plan and the October approval.The latest approval contains conditions governing development of the property. Palm Beach County zoning officials confirmed in July that the original 2016 approval did not include such conditions.Under the newly approved plan, data center buildings cannot be constructed within 850 feet of the property line near Arden.Noise at neighboring homes would be capped between 50 and 60 decibels, depending on the time of day. Sound monitors would run continuously, with the county receiving access to the monitoring data.The county's water utility would commit to providing no more than 100,000 gallons of water per day for the entire site.Battery storage would also be required to comply with fire safety requirements.Residents have contacted WPTV and Hoffman questioning how the plan could be approved without another commission vote and saying they believed the county's data center moratorium would prevent further movement on the property.Palm Beach County Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez told Hoffman by phone that the proposal was submitted before the moratorium took effect.Because it was already submitted, Hernandez said, county staff were able to continue reviewing it and ultimately approve it.Hernandez declined an on-camera interview.The Oct. 7 approval is not the only application involving the Project Tango property.According to Hernandez, WPB Logistics, the second owner of part of the property, has submitted its own proposal seeking to increase data center space on its roughly 60-acre portion of the site without approval from the County Commission.That proposal could result in approximately 1.2 million square feet of additional data center space.Unlike the PBA Holdings proposal approved Oct. 7, the WPB Logistics application remains under review.Hoffman also reached out to Ernie Cox, the main project manager for Project Tango, seeking a response to concerns from residents who said they felt the latest approval happened without their knowledge or an opportunity for public input.A member of Cox's staff returned Hoffman's call Tuesday and said the team would respond to the question.Hoffman had not received that response at the time of publication.

Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause after months of controversy, hazing allegations, and a no-confidence vote. Interim Chief Paul Langel said, "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job. Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." The decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced for allegedly turning a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and using it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. One of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, said, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don’t think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department." The disciplined firefighters have called the termination retaliation for previous complaints they filed against district leadership. When asked about the possibility of the terminated firefighters regaining their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there’s always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I’ve got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." The board voted to appoint Langel as interim chief. He is a familiar face in the district, with 30 years of experience. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early.

More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast.Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street.WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie homeInvestigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens.Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention.Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens."They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother," Wees said. "If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now."Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment.Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well."They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes," Wees said.Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast."We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food," Nickelson said. However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room."They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation," Wees said. "Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time."Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population."It overwhelms the staff," Wees said. "It overwhelms our resources."Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts."These little babies can't do it for themselves," Wee said. "So, we and the community need to do it for them."Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. Whether your idea of Halloween involves collecting candy with the kids or screaming your way through a haunted house, the South Florida Fairgrounds has an event designed for you.This October, the fairgrounds once again become home to two popular seasonal attractions: Spookyville, a family-friendly Halloween celebration at Yesteryear Village, and Fright Nights, a nighttime attraction featuring haunted houses, scare zones, rides, and entertainment.Spookyville transforms historic Yesteryear Village into a Halloween destination geared toward children and families.Guests can enjoy safe trick-or-treating throughout the village, costume parades, live entertainment, food vendors, and plenty of opportunities for festive family photos. The attraction's historic buildings are decorated with pumpkins, spider webs, fall decorations, and Halloween displays.Visitors can also enjoy rides, a petting zoo, balloon artists, and special performances. Among this year's entertainers is Wizard Aloysius, who brings magic tricks and family-friendly entertainment to the event on select dates.Spookyville runs Oct. 17-18, 23-25 and 30-31.When the sun goes down, the atmosphere changes dramatically.Fright Nights returns to the South Florida Fairgrounds with four haunted attractions, roaming scare actors, carnival rides, live entertainment, food vendors, and a midway designed to test visitors' courage.The event has become a Halloween tradition for thrill-seekers across South Florida and offers an alternative to traveling to larger attractions outside the area.During a behind-the-scenes visit, WPTV's T.A. Walker got a firsthand look at what it takes to become one of the monsters responsible for scaring guests. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause."At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Board Member Jamie Fowler. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.Some show a modified bug zapper being used to shock three apprentice firefighters while on duty in 2024. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were "consensual" pranks that were done "all in good fun." “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," said Hutchinson. “We’re all still friends," added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," said one public commentator. "We need to restore faith in this fire district," said another. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure could be coming to an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that it may be time to consider a “mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition," adding "the position of fire chief requires confidence." During the meeting's discussion, fire board member and business owner Travis Leonard said that gave him reason to begin the motion to Fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," said Leonard. After terminating Lee’s contract, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief. The district also plans to hire a recruiter to conduct a search for Lee’s permanent replacement."I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we’ve been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust,” Langel said.Lee's departure comes with a high cost to the district. His severance package is expected to total about $350,000.The leadership change also comes as the firefighters union continues negotiations with the district in an effort to reinstate three veteran firefighters who were fired. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.

Lucie County Fire District Board voted to terminate longtime fire chief Jeff Lee, about two weeks after the district’s firefighters union released the results of a no-confidence vote on its top leaders. Following the decision, the district voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as Interim Chief. The agenda for the board’s 3 p.m. regular meeting includes an item listed under Chair Shannon Martin titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not say whose retirement will be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public. The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released its vote results Oct. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under the rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the union would formally present the result to the Fire Board. Gonzalez and Sabol both passed that mark. The union said 74.23% of members voted no confidence in him. Local 1377 calls upon the Board to carefully consider these results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve this county and to the public they have sworn to protect, the union said in its release. Since then, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed to the move and that it had been discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days’ notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire Dec. Wednesday’s agenda also includes the selection of a law firm and a new district attorney. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother The vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district f ired three veteran firefighters , Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others. Videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper . An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing. The firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief. They can’t investigate themselves.
