A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades.The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper.WATCH BELOW: Fight over rare coral reef reaches NOAA as public comment opensScientists say decades of shrimp trawling destroyed roughly 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place. Parts of the Oculina Bank were closed to trawling beginning in the 1990s, with protections later expanded and made permanent.Now, conservationists fear some of that progress could be reversed."I'd say it's dire. It's a dire situation," said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society. "We're desperate to get this protected."The latest battle began after a Trump administration executive order directed the nation's regional fishery councils to look for ways to reduce regulatory burdens, expand fishing opportunities and increase economic profitability.The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council subsequently considered proposals that would restore commercial shrimping access to portions of the Oculina Bank that have been protected from trawling for decades. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery.Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds."The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association, previously told WPTV.Council data reviewed by WPTV shows the rock shrimp industry has declined dramatically. The number of annual trips fell from more than 700 in the mid-1990s to fewer than 100 annually since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers also dropped from 144 in 1996 to fewer than 30 in later years.Zales has blamed the decline on factors including rising costs, imported shrimp and the loss of fishing grounds. Shrimpers have also faced increasing restrictions off Port Canaveral during space launches.Scientists and conservationists argue the potential benefit to the shrimp industry is small compared with the ecological and economic value of protecting the remaining reef.NOAA data previously reviewed by WPTV showed brown rock shrimp landings nationwide totaled about 600,000 pounds in 2023, worth roughly $1 million.Florida fishermen, by comparison, landed nearly 100 million pounds of fish worth just under $300 million that year, including species such as snapper and grouper that use the reef as habitat."We know how valuable this reef system is," Perry said.Scientists also warn that recovery from additional damage could take generations."It would take centuries to grow back even some semblance of the corals," Perry said.Supporters of reopening the area point to mapping that found no live coral, standing dead coral or coral rubble within the proposed trawling zones.But that same research warned sediment kicked up by trawling could drift into nearby living reef and smother coral. Scientists have also raised concerns that snapper and grouper could be caught as bycatch.WPTV Investigates has followed the debate as opposition grew locally and nationally.Earlier public comments to the council overwhelmingly opposed reopening the area. WPTV's review found about 120 of 150 comments opposed both proposals, while 25 supported both and five supported one proposal but not the other.A similar proposal approved by the council in 2022 ultimately failed to win federal approval, garnering thousands of opposing public comments from across the country. The latest proposal nevertheless continued moving forward.WPTV also previously reviewed financial disclosure records for members of the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council and found several disclosed financial interests tied to the fishing or seafood industries. Council officials told WPTV that conflicts of interest are governed by NOAA rules and federal law.Earlier this year, despite opposition from scientists, conservationists and members of the public, the council voted to recommend reopening as much as 24 square nautical miles to shrimp trawling — an area larger than Manhattan.The proposal has now reached the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which will decide whether to approve it.The Agency has posted the proposals to its Federal Registry, asking the public to weigh in before it votes. The fight is also drawing attention from national conservation organizations.Mike Gravitz, with the Marine Conservation Institute, said the debate comes as coral reefs worldwide already face pressure from warming waters, pollution and overfishing — and as countries around the world work toward protecting more of the planet's oceans."For gosh sakes, it's the last 10% of something that occurs nowhere else on Earth," Gravitz said.He said the United States has close to 25% of its ocean protected in an effective way, while international conservation efforts are moving in the opposite direction."It's really ironic to us that people would be talking about weakening protections for these deep-sea corals at a time when the world needs to do even more, not less," Gravitz said. "This administration is rolling back those protections, especially for the very large marine protected areas, some of which have been protected since Teddy Roosevelt was president." For Perry, the federal review represents the latest — and potentially decisive — stage of a fight that has stretched for years."They understood it, and they protected it," Perry said of previous federal protections, "but now it's being attacked again."Public comment on the proposal is open through Nov. 17 before federal officials make a final decision.Click here to submit a public comment."And we just really need to, you know, stand up and fight for it," Perry said.Multiple organizations have also launched petitions opposing the proposals.

After more than four decades as a shopping destination in Palm Beach County, the future of Boynton Beach Mall is raising questions for the businesses and shoppers who have made it part of their lives.Tenants at the mall say they recently received lease termination notices from property owner Washington Prime Group, instructing them to vacate by Jan. 15, 2027.The notices come as questions swirl about a potential sale and what could happen to the property next. However, the City of Boynton Beach tells WPTV it has not been notified of a finalized sale.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: For some business owners, the uncertainty means preparing to leave a place that has been part of their livelihood for decades. For longtime shoppers, it could mean saying goodbye to a familiar community landmark.Kevin Ng has a personal connection to Boynton Beach Mall that stretches back decades.Sarku Japan, the restaurant he operates, has been at the mall since 1992. His father took over the business in 2006, and Ng assumed responsibility in 2020.After his father's death, Ng continued running the restaurant, preserving a piece of his family's legacy.While the possibility of leaving the mall was not entirely unexpected, the termination notice made the situation more concrete."It wasn't shocking for sure, but I knew this day was going to come," Ng said.The notice informed Ng that his lease would be terminated on Jan. 15, 2027."It just said, unfortunately, your lease will be terminated Jan. 15; we just have to pack up and go," he said.Now, Ng is trying to determine what comes next for him and the family business he has worked to maintain."What's next? I'm trying to figure that out right now," he said.Boynton Beach Mall first opened on Oct. Over the years, it became a familiar destination for shopping, dining and spending time with family.Today, the property presents a different picture, with sparse parking lot activity, a quieter food court and vacant storefronts.Some shoppers say the mall could benefit from a fresh start."This mall has been a little tired for a really long time, but this would be a great location to invigorate," one man told WPTV.Another shopper said he would like to see the property return to a more vibrant retail destination.Asked what he would like to see in the space, one man responded that he would like "a mall like Palm Beach Mall or the outlet malls."A third shopper said attracting a major retailer could help address the number of empty stores."I always felt like if there was a big company in here, the stores wouldn't be so empty," he said.Still, others see value in the mall beyond its retail offerings.One longtime visitor described it as a landmark for longtime residents who continue to come back despite the changes."While the mall is still open, it's like a landmark, you know, all the old-timers still come here," the shopper said.Because the potential sale is a private property matter, city officials directed questions about a possible acquisition to Washington Prime Group.WPTV reached out to Washington Prime Group for additional information about the property's future, including the status of a potential sale and what could happen to the site. The company has not responded.For now, tenants are facing a Jan. 15, 2027, deadline, while shoppers and longtime visitors are left wondering what the next chapter will bring for a property that has been part of Boynton Beach for more than 40 years.

Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously advanced a new micromobility device ordinance Tuesday that would establish speed limits, age restrictions and enforcement rules for e-bikes, electric scooters and similar devices, citing hundreds of injuries and concerns about rider and pedestrian safety. The proposal comes as local governments across Palm Beach County continue grappling with the growing popularity of e-bikes and e-scooters, particularly among younger riders.County staff told commissioners that since January 2023, the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County has documented 613 micromobility-related injuries, with 59% involving children ages 12 to 15. Officials also reported eight micromobility-related deaths across January 2025 and September 2026. The proposed ordinance would require riders to be at least 14 years old, carry a government-issued photo ID, obey a 15 mph speed limit on bicycle paths and shared-use areas, and slow to 10 mph when within 50 feet of pedestrians. The rules would also prohibit dangerous stunts and other unsafe riding behaviors.For many residents, the idea of more regulation is welcome."They should have some regulations at least, there should be more at least to restrict kids under 18 or people with no license," said Ryan Kuhnau of Palm Beach Gardens. "They've definitely popped up out of nowhere, they're pretty common to see in every side walk and every neighborhood."Others pointed to the growing number of riders in busy areas."More regulations for sure," said former teacher Pia Kresse.College student Melanie Zayas, who said e-scooters are popular on the Florida Atlantic University campus, said some limits make sense."For people getting around town that's good, but they can get a little crazy, especially when they're there's a lot of pedestrians out on the road," Zayas said.The proposal would require riders to slow down around pedestrians, something Zayas said she has experienced firsthand."So you've come close to getting hit by an e-scooter?" asked WPTV's Joel Lopez."Yes, I have and... It's, like, coming straight at me and I'm like 'hi, watch where you're going please,'" Zayas said.Kresse said the age and identification requirements could help improve accountability."As an ex-teacher I saw too many injuries. This is a big risk for a lot of kids and I want to see it get better before it gets worse," Kresse said. "I'm excited to see the ordinances actually take place."During the commission discussion, officials emphasized that the ordinance is largely driven by injury trends among young riders.Criminal Justice Commission Executive Director staff told commissioners that approximately 60% of the documented injuries involved children between ages 12 and 15, while 39% of injured adults were between 46 and 65 years old. Commissioners also debated how enforcement would work and whether younger riders could face disproportionate scrutiny."Is there concern youth will be over-policed, disproportionately stopped because they are young?" asked Bobby Powell.County staff and law enforcement officials repeatedly stressed that the focus will be education first."The intent is education and awareness," staff told commissioners. "They are not going to start writing and ticketing these kids as soon as they see it."The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said initial enforcement efforts would focus on outreach, safety campaigns and distributing helmets, particularly at schools where e-bike use is common. Officials said they secured grant funding to provide helmets and plan to launch a countywide awareness campaign directed at both children and parents."A lot of the parents don't understand that these items can be jailbroken and they can go from 20 miles an hour to 40 miles an hour," said County Commissioner Joel Flores.Flores said he routinely sees young riders weaving through traffic and riding at unsafe speeds."In my opinion this is not to jam them up. It's a way to protect them," said Flores. Some commissioners argued that e-bikes should be treated more like motorized vehicles than traditional bicycles."These are not bicycles. They're motor vehicles and they need to be treated like motor vehicles," said Gregg Weiss. Weiss also called for statewide action, saying better crash reporting and more consistent regulations are needed because current data collection remains limited.The ordinance could have impacts beyond unincorporated Palm Beach County.County staff told commissioners that many municipalities have expressed interest in adopting similar regulations and were waiting for the county to take the lead. Officials said both Wellington and the Town of Palm Beach already have ordinances on the books, with Palm Beach's rules being stricter than the county proposal. "A majority are interested. They were waiting for Palm Beach County to adopt this," staff told commissioners. Flores added that while the discussion was taking place, he received messages from officials in multiple cities interested in seeing the ordinance move forward.The ordinance was approved on first reading by a 7-0 vote and will return for additional consideration before becoming final. WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast.Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street.WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie homeInvestigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens.Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention.Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens."They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother," Wees said. "If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now."Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment.Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well."They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes," Wees said.Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast."We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food," Nickelson said. However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room."They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation," Wees said. "Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time."Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population."It overwhelms the staff," Wees said. "It overwhelms our resources."Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts."These little babies can't do it for themselves," Wee said. "So, we and the community need to do it for them."Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

It is as dominant a college sports program as there is anywhere in the country, and it's located on the Treasure Coast.WPTV received several emails from concerned residents that the plug may soon be pulled on this diving dynasty. "[Brinn] dropped my swim times incredibly, but just in and out of the pool, he's an all-round incredible man."But the pool could soon be drained of its energy.Hall said he is upset about the Board of Trustees proposal to eliminate the program."We feed so many of our swimmers into NCAA Division One and Division II," Hall said. "I genuinely think that the Board of Trustees are going to realize that this is a mistake."Smith is also from Australia, getting medals in the 100-, 200- and 400-meter breaststroke and getting gold in the 50-meter.But beyond the bling, Smith said it's the team and family she found through this program that she doesn't want to see disappear."These are more than just athletes. We are people, and this creates such an extraordinary experience in life that you can hold onto forever," Smith said.WPTV reached out to Indian River State College, and we're still working on a response.The Board of Trustees will discuss the proposal on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixie Hendry Campus in Okeechobee.

North Palm Beach County Airport could see some of its biggest changes in decades as county leaders explore proposals to help accommodate future growth. A proposal that could bring new aviation facilities, runway improvements and emerging air mobility technology to the airport is now headed to a competitive bidding process after a lengthy debate among Palm Beach County commissioners.WATCH BELOW: Major changes considered for North County AirportThe discussion focused on a proposal from Jet Greene LLC, owned by developer Jeff Greene, to purchase 131 acres of county-owned land near the airport, develop a second private aviation facility and help fund future airport improvements. But instead of moving forward exclusively with that proposal, commissioners unanimously voted to open the opportunity to other developers and aviation companies."What Jet Green has brought to the table is a starting point," Commissioner Maria Marino said.North County Airport, also known as F45, has been the subject of improvement discussions for years. The latest proposal called for a second private jet facility featuring hangars, fueling facilities, lounges and other aviation services while also supporting efforts to expand airport operations.The proposal quickly attracted interest from other aviation companies."We just don't want the plane to take off without us," said Stephen Abrams of Ellison Partners, speaking on behalf of Sky Harbour.Sky Harbour is one of several companies that appeared before commissioners expressing interest in competing for future development opportunities at the airport.One of those voices came from LuftCar, a company focused on advanced air mobility and infrastructure for electric aircraft capable of vertical takeoff and landing."Yeah, we're welcoming a wide variety of proposals," said Taniel Koushakjian, a representative working with LuftCar.They're in favor of the county starting a search for proposals. Unlike developers pursuing traditional aviation facilities, LuftCar says its role would be to build infrastructure that supports future transportation technologies."What LuftCar, my client, would like to see is the advancement of innovative technologies and the space to operate those programs," Koushakjian said.Koushakjian said North County Airport is well-positioned to become a testing ground for that technology because it is smaller than President Donald J. Trump International Airport."It is a prime area for eVTOL (electric vertical take-off and landing) and innovative technologies simply because it's a smaller airport," he said.The company envisions infrastructure that could support electric aircraft that do not require traditional runways."The energy infrastructure, the platform, the storage, the fueling area, as well as the platform itself for vertical takeoff and landing," Koushakjian said when describing what such a facility would require.He also pointed to increasing congestion in the region's airspace as one reason airport leaders are exploring future growth."I hear it's very congested and some people are experiencing flight delays because of the congested airspace, and that's why they're expanding the airport because we just need more space to accommodate that growth," he said.Supporters of airport improvements have argued that expanding North County Airport could help ease pressure on Trump International Airport by creating more capacity for private aviation activity.Airport officials, however, stressed the airport is not being expanded to attract commercial airline service. Instead, they described the discussion as part of long-term planning to avoid future congestion and accommodate continued growth in private and general aviation.While aviation companies see opportunity, some nearby residents are watching the conversation closely.Roberta Sorensen, who lives near the airport and under part of the flight path, said aircraft noise is not her biggest concern."Much more worried about the road. The traffic is really bad. The planes going over don't bother me at all," Sorensen said.She's more concerned that airport growth could bring more vehicles to already busy roads."People are going to be coming out here to fly. So there'll be more traffic on the roads. The roads are bad now up here. They're just getting worse, and by the time they finish all this building they're doing out here, it's going to be terrible," she said.Sorensen also hopes nearby residents remain part of the conversation."I think maybe the neighbors should be consulted because they've lived here a long time. I haven't," she said.Commissioners ultimately chose not to move forward directly with Jet Green's proposal. Instead, they directed staff to begin developing a competitive solicitation process that would allow multiple developers and aviation companies to submit their visions for the future of North County Airport.The move keeps the conversation alive while opening the door to a broader range of proposals that could shape the airport's future for decades to come.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Less than two weeks before what could be a pivotal U.S. Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will debate Wednesday, with polling showing a deadlocked contest.El-Sayed is vying to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Rogers is hoping to become the first Republican to represent Michigan in the Senate since Spencer Abraham, who lost his reelection bid in 2000. President Donald Trump has won Michigan twice, demonstrating Republicans can compete statewide.Wednesday’s debate begins at 7 p.m. Scripps News will air a preview beginning at 6:30 p.m. The debate will also air live on Scripps News Group’s Michigan stations, WXYZ in Detroit and WXMI in Grand Rapids.The debate will be moderated by Scripps News Group Detroit Editorial Director Chuck Stokes, along with Detroit-based anchors Carolyn Clifford and Alicia Smith.A Marist poll released Wednesday showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 50% to 48%, a difference within the poll’s margin of error. Rogers, a former member of the U.S. House, has at times sought to distance himself from some of Trump’s more divisive policies.

Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa has been arrested on felony charges after state investigators accused her of using her position to improperly obtain money through a city program designed to help businesses recover from the COVID-19 pandemic.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Wednesday that Espinosa faces charges of grand theft and organized scheme to defraud.WATCH BELOW: Florida AG holds news conference on arrestDuring an afternoon news conference in Orlando, Uthmeier said the case involves Kissimmee's Business Boost 2.0 program. In a deep, dark part of the Gulf of Mexico, the number of marine animals plummeted by about 60% in the years following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion, a new study found.In a crucial part of the Gulf between the light surface and the darkest depths, where the BP-operated well failed and dumped 134 million gallons of oil, the number of fish found dropped by 63.5% from the year after the spill to 2015. Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS.And those populations haven't come close to recovering, the study found.Researchers focused on the ocean's "twilight zone," a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University.A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep. They returned to the same place with the same equipment three-and-a-half years later and found sea life was between one-third and one-quarter of what it was in 2011."We saw this big decline," Sutton said. "The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that’s the most likely cause of the decline."Researchers kept on sampling since 2015 and the low populations remained, with a slight rise in 2022 and 2023 that did not prove statistically significant or lasting, Sutton said.Sutton's team documented the population declines with three different lines of evidence: what they caught in the nets, what their acoustic sonar found and genetic studies showing the species losing genetic diversity because of inbreeding.A lot of marine life died instantly after the explosion, which killed 11 workers, and from nearly five months of leaking oil and gas. Those pollutants got stored in the eggs of survivors and subsequent generations of critters got more compromised and weaker, Sutton said.BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi said the accident “forever changed” the company: “We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again.”Both the oil and the dispersants used to clean the spill hurt fish, but in different ways, said study co-author Isabel Romero, a chemical oceanographer at the University of South Carolina. Oil is more toxic and an overall threat, but the dispersant breaks the oil into smaller droplets, increasing the exposure of animals that live in the deeper water column, she said.Dispersants caused many problems, and new studies show that in future accidents, it would be better to avoid those chemicals and instead add agents that increase oil-munching microbes, said former National Science Foundation Director Rita Colwell, a University of Maryland environmental microbiologist who headed a 10-year, $500 million BP-funded program to study spill effects.Sutton said his team couldn’t prove an exact causal link to the BP oil spill, but by eliminating the other possibilities and looking at the timing, it's logically clear that the spill caused the problem.The krill population dropped 72%. Lanternfish — odd fish with blue-green lights embedded over their bodies — are a third of what they used to be, Sutton said. The stunning but scary dragonfish — with sharp teeth, light organs and a lure attached to its head — also had big losses, he said."These are foundational species," Sutton said. "They're the things most things eat. So it's no wonder that we had wholesale changes across the community."Scientists learned much about this unexplored area of the Gulf.“One of our biggest findings from the whole thing is how connected the whole oceanic Gulf is from top to bottom because the animals move up and down,” Sutton said. “There are predators at the top that dive deep. Lots of things that are deep that come up at night. So the system is one very large pulsing system, rather than just a layered system like people might have thought beforehand.”Outside scientists were especially bothered by where the spill damaged.“We know more about space in some ways than we do about the inner ocean. Because we can’t see these regions, there is a tendency to assume everything is fine, but here we have a clear result showing that something went very wrong," Scripps Institution of Oceanography marine scientist Kaitlin Frasier said in an email.Frasier, who wasn't part of the study released Monday, published a post-spill study in 2024 looking at Gulf of Mexico whales and dolphins, finding population drops as high as 83%."It's shocking how a single failure in a drilling rig can have this vast and sustained impact over thousands of square kilometers, with little visible recovery over 13 years after the spill," said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn't part of the study. "It is important that we see this, because for the longest time these consequences were completely out of sight and out of mind."Worm and Colwell said this damage should be kept in mind as the world talks about deep-sea mining and increased oil drilling in deep waters.___The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. Just outside Boynton Beach, Bedner's Farm offers a little bit of country, a whole lot of fall fun and a reminder that autumn magic doesn't require chilly weather.At the family-owned South Florida staple tucked away in west Boynton Beach, even the goats get in on the hospitality. According to Judi Brooker, who has been sharing the farm's charm with visitors for more than a decade, they're a crowd favorite."They're so soft, and everybody loves the goats," Brooker said.I mentioned that the little kids probably love them."And by little kids, everybody under the age of 100," Brooker joked.Bedner's is one of South Florida's last family-owned markets, with a farming legacy that stretches back generations."A lot of people don't realize there is life in west Boynton off 441," Brooker said. "I know — I live here!"More than 50 years ago, Arthur and Henrietta Bedner brought their Pennsylvania farming roots to South Florida, trading harsh winters for a warmer climate and new opportunities."They came from farming families in Pennsylvania, but they'd had enough of the winter," Brooker said.The family began farming in the area in the mid-20th century before purchasing the property that would become home to the farm visitors know today. Their mission remains simple: grow fresh, flavorful produce that's affordable, too.And there's plenty growing here. The farm grows about 60 crops, including tomatoes, corn, strawberries, broccoli, kale, lettuce, cauliflower, peppers and zucchini. The farm also grows sunflowers, adding a splash of color to the agricultural landscape.October is one of the best months to visit. Fall at Bedner's means family outings, festive photo opportunities and plenty of seasonal fun."It's a day full of fun. Bring the family, cousins, aunties, grandmas — it's great," Brooker said.One of the biggest attractions is finding the perfect pumpkin."We have this beautiful greenery and all the pumpkins on top," Brooker said. "It's just a pumpkin wonderland."Pumpkins aren't the only seasonal stars. Visitors can also spot an assortment of colorful gourds, adding even more variety to the fall display — from the popping orange of the pumpkins to the golden glow of the sunflower fields.Those cheerful blooms also play an important role in the farm's ecosystem. Bedner's keeps beehives on the property, recognizing the essential role pollinators play in agriculture."We do have hives on the farm because the honeybee is the farmer's best friend," Brooker said.It's a reminder that behind the colorful fields and family-friendly attractions, there's a working farm where growing food and caring for the land go hand in hand.For a closer look at the operation, visitors can climb aboard one of the farm's tractor rides, which take you around all 80 acres of Bedner's. The ride offers more than a scenic tour. It's a glimpse into the technology and planning that keep the farm productive in South Florida's challenging climate.Tall crops help protect other plants from the wind, while drip irrigation delivers water directly where it's needed — helping keep the fields hydrated through changing weather conditions.The farm has a long agricultural history to match its modern techniques."Palm Beach County was once known as the winter produce capital of the United States," Brooker said.That legacy is still visible in the fields, where agriculture remains at the heart of the experience.Of course, no fall adventure would be complete without a corn maze — and at Bedner's, finding the exit is easier said than done. Each year brings a new maze to explore, with twists, turns and a few surprises along the way.The maze comes with its own cast of characters, including the occasional zombie and a few strategically placed scarecrows."Sometimes we have some zombie friends along the way," Brooker said.There may be a few spooky sights, but the experience is designed to be more playful than frightening. Still, the maze comes with its share of wrong turns and dead ends, but after plenty of backtracking, the exit finally comes into view.After all that walking, exploring and navigating the maze, there's only one thing left to do: cool off with a sweet treat.At Bedner's, the fall experience is about more than pumpkins and photo ops. It's about spending time outdoors, learning a little about where food comes from, and making memories with family and friends.And the best part? You can soak up all those autumn vibes without bundling up for cold weather. Because at Bedner's Farm, fall magic comes with sunshine, fresh air and just a little bit of Florida flair.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

With controls in hand and drones in the air, students at Palm Beach State College (PBSC) are learning a skill that could lead to new career opportunities.WPTV reporter Christy Waite visited the college's Belle Glade campus, where students were putting those skills into practice as part of PBSC's first drone training class.WATCH BELOW: PBSC students take flight with drone trainingThe 12-week course combines classroom instruction with hands-on flight experience and helps students work toward earning the FAA certification required for most commercial drone operations.Student Marina Medina told Waite she believes the technology has a promising future."I heard that the drone industry is taking off, and I think it is taking off," Medina said. "It's the future."The program is about more than simply learning how to control a drone. Instructor Scott Mitchell said the technology has applications across a number of industries, including one especially important to the Glades: agriculture."This program is crucial for the Glades area," Mitchell said. "Especially in agriculture, this being a huge sugar cane and sweet corn area and what we can do with mapping and surveying."While visiting the class, Waite met Alejandro Garza, a student from the Glades area who hopes to use what he is learning to help the agricultural community."I want to use my drone license to help the farmers get more yield from their crop," Garza said.Agriculture is only one potential application for the technology.Upcoming phases of the program will provide more specialized training in areas including public safety, law enforcement, fire and rescue, search and rescue, emergency response, mapping, infrastructure inspections, real estate photography and other commercial applications.Students also have access to professional-grade equipment, allowing them to train with technology they may not otherwise have access to on their own.College leaders say the goal is to help prepare students as the demand for these skills grows."Providing students with jobs in high-demand areas as the technology grows," said Andraes Alexander, executive dean of PBSC's Loxahatchee Groves campus and academic dean of the Loxahatchee Groves and Belle Glade campuses.The program is also receiving support from The Hand Foundation, which is providing scholarships to help make the training more accessible to people in the community. College leaders credited that support with helping reduce financial barriers for students interested in the program.Enrollment for the current class is closed, but another drone class is planned for the spring along with the program’s second phase. Those upcoming offerings are expected to give students additional training in drone operations, maintenance and more specialized applications.

Less than two weeks before what could be a pivotal U.S. Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will debate Wednesday, with polling showing a deadlocked contest.El-Sayed is vying to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Rogers is hoping to become the first Republican to represent Michigan in the Senate since Spencer Abraham, who lost his reelection bid in 2000. Democrats have won nine consecutive U.S. Senate races in Michigan.Although Democrats have maintained control of both of Michigan’s U.S. Senate seats, the state is considered a key battleground. President Donald Trump has won Michigan twice, demonstrating Republicans can compete statewide.Wednesday’s debate begins at 7 p.m. Scripps News will air a preview beginning at 6:30 p.m. The debate will also air live on Scripps News Group’s Michigan stations, WXYZ in Detroit and WXMI in Grand Rapids.The debate will be moderated by Scripps News Group Detroit Editorial Director Chuck Stokes, along with Detroit-based anchors Carolyn Clifford and Alicia Smith.A Marist poll released Wednesday showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 50% to 48%, a difference within the poll’s margin of error. The poll also found both candidates had high unfavorable ratings. Forty-eight percent of likely voters viewed El-Sayed unfavorably, while 52% had an unfavorable view of Rogers.RELATED STORY | Abdul El-Sayed emphasizes Muslim faith after Trump calls him a ‘jihadist’The poll also indicated many Michigan families are struggling more financially than they were a year ago. Forty-three percent of likely voters said they were worse off financially, compared with 16% who said they were better off.El-Sayed’s faith has come under attack during his campaign to become the country’s first Muslim U.S. Republicans have sought to portray the Democratic nominee as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terrorism.Last week, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and falsely called the former public health official a “jihadist.”Over the weekend, El-Sayed denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic political movement founded in Egypt in 1928.RELATED STORY | Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’Meanwhile, El-Sayed has sought to tie Rogers to many of Trump’s policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran. Rogers, a former member of the U.S. House, has at times sought to distance himself from some of Trump’s more divisive policies.

Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance & Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH THE LATEST REPORT BELOW: Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance & Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. The agenda itself does not provide a reason for the proposed elimination of swimming and diving or detail the financial impact of the restructuring. All of this comes after Indian River State College's men's swim and dive team in March captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, with the women's team also claiming its 48th national title.The meeting will take place at the Williamson Conference Center Auditorium on Indian River State College's Dixon Hendry Campus at 2229 NW 9th Avenue in Okeechobee.

Lucie County Fire District Board will discuss the future of Fire Chief Jeff Lee on Wednesday afternoon, about two weeks after the district’s firefighters union released the results of a no-confidence vote on its top leaders. The agenda for the board’s 3 p.m. regular meeting includes an item listed under Chair Shannon Martin titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not say whose retirement will be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public. The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released its vote results Oct. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under the rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the union would formally present the result to the Fire Board. Gonzalez and Sabol both passed that mark. The union said 74.23% of members voted no confidence in him. Local 1377 calls upon the Board to carefully consider these results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve this county and to the public they have sworn to protect, the union said in its release. Since then, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed to the move and that it had been discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days’ notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire Dec. Wednesday’s agenda also includes the selection of a law firm and a new district attorney. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother The vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district f ired three veteran firefighters , Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others. Videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper . An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing. The firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief. They can’t investigate themselves. That’s not proper, board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler said at an Oct. 6, Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district’s insurance representatives. CBS12 News has also obtained a 2022 recording in which Lee, Gonzalez and Sabol declined to investigate a female firefighter’s complaint of unwanted touching by a coworker. Lee has said the problem is not one he can solve himself. The board has to fix that problem, Lee said at an Aug. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. In August, a motion to suspend Lee and Sabol failed 2 to 4. In a statement after the vote, the district said it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action. It pointed to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee’s tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. He became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract. CBS12 News will be at Wednesday’s meeting and will update this story.

Tuesday was a day to remember for several youngsters who had the chance to meet their sports idols thanks to Make-A-Wish. "I was so happy I started crying; it's just an amazing experience," said Yulissa Morales Melendrez, a Make-A-Wish participant.Several kids from around the country had the opportunity to meet the defending MLS Champs, Inter Miami, a moment Make-A-Wish participant Jimmy Hoover could only dream of."I was super excited. I didn't really know what to do; it was kind of all surreal to me," Hoover said.Hoover said he's been playing soccer since he was 7 years old. "I started playing and started watching (Lionel) Messi, and he became my favorite player right away," said Hoover.On Tuesday afternoon, Hoover sat in the stands at Nu Stadium, watching his idol, Lionel Messi, and Inter Miami train.It was a simple moment, yes, but a moment that nearly didn't happen."I was going in (to the hospital) for a couple of months, and they were telling me it was just a stomach ache," said Hoover.Hoover and his family didn't think much of it until one day at his friend's house."My stomach was hurting so bad, I was in agonizing pain," said Hoover.He rushed to the hospital, where doctors found out he had cancer, so for months he endured chemotherapy, and while he was fighting for his life, he didn't want to let his teammates down, so every day after treatment he'd be with his teammates."It was really difficult; I couldn't keep up with everyone; that was the hardest part," said Hoover.Dedicated to playing soccer — and again and again kicking cancer's butt — he fought effortlessly, and last July he rang the bell as his cancer went into remission."It's been great. I'm still in a little bit of shock from everything," said Hoover.That shock would soon wear off, and days ago he and his teammates hung out. He got the surprise of a lifetime: he'd be part of the Make-A-Wish Foundation's latest effort to help him and kids from around the world meet Messi and Inter Miami."It's super rewarding. It was a bit of a wait to get out here, but after everything, it's been super great," said Hoover.Kids signed on to join the team for the day, get a jersey, watch the fellas practice, and share joy and hope with the Inter Miami guys."To see this type of resilience and they're going through it at 10 years old and younger than that, if you can take something out of that — it's that you have to keep pushing because somebody always has it worse than you do," said Ian Fray, an Inter Miami defender."It's been so crazy to meet all these players and interview; it's just all been so great," said Hoover.

Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. Amy Acton's estranged mother appeared in a new attack ad, calling her gubernatorial candidate daughter a liar. Court documents show Acton's stepfather was arrested for raping her as a child, and her biological mom lost custody.Watch the full video below:This new ad features Donna Arthur, formerly Stearns."I worked at Children and Family Service Association, building one of the first two sexual abuse programs in America... Amy has a serious problem." Arthur states in the ad. She lies about her past."RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election DayIt's an ad that's circulating on the internet but doesn't say who paid for it. It was first published by Columbus-based political blogger The Rooster.Acton is lying about her background, Arthur claims in the ad."She says she grew up living in a tent," she said. "None of that is true."Acton shouldn't be elected governor, Arthur states.Court documents tell a different storyActon hasn’t had contact with her mother since leaving the courthouse once her stepfather was charged with raping her, the candidate said. Mahoning County Court records we obtained show that Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with sexually abusing Acton, then 12 years old. The abuse went from ages 10-12, she said.Acton’s younger brother Phil Stearns said their mother lost custody, as she “stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.” Last week, Stearns spoke out about their upbringing."I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it," Stearns said. "She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me."Police did find the stepfather living in a tent when Acton was a child, court records show. After pleading not guilty, he posted bond and fled, becoming a fugitive of the state until his death in 2004. Police tried to find him for numerous years, documents state. He and Acton's mother moved to Pennsylvania, according to public records.BacklashThe ad has created mass backlash, including from sexual assault survivors who are blaming Acton's opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy.RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour"I was taken aback, and I feel that it is quite atrocious and vile, given the circumstances, and wondering myself, as a survivor of such heinous crimes, how someone who is running to be the governor of our state [could air this]" Jessica Miranda, a former Democratic lawmaker and current Hamilton County Auditor, said. It is "heinous and outrageous" to think that anyone would vote for him after this, Miranda continued.Even Republicans like Mark Pukita say it goes too far, adding that the constant attack ads over the past few months, as well as campaigning like this, lost his vote."I don't know a good mother who would ever do that to her child, so she's clearly an unfit mother," Pukita said. "Why would I take advice from an unfit mother? That would be like taking child-rearing advice from a child abuser."Ohio Department of Development Director Lydia Mihalik, one of Gov. Mike DeWine's top cabinet members, condemned the ad."I don’t have to agree with Amy Acton’s politics to believe that exploiting someone’s childhood trauma is wrong... I haven’t changed my political beliefs. I’m simply unwilling to set aside my personal values to defend a political ad. There is a difference between fighting for your principles and abandoning them to win," Mihalik said on social media.Other Republicans point out that Acton's stepfather was never convicted, and there is no disclaimer on the ad."You can accuse Ramaswamy of doing it, but there's no evidence that I know of of his campaign doing that," Republican strategist Terry Casey said. "That might be false too."Once we told Casey about the documentation we had of the court documents, he brought up how this ad and our subsequent investigation are all "TMI, too much information" and irrelevant to who would be the best governor.At first, the Ramaswamy team did not take explicit responsibility for the ad, but did say that "Ohioans deserve to know" that Acton's mother doesn't support her. “We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor," Ramaswamy's spokesperson Connie Luck said in a lengthy statement.We tried to ask follow-up questions about the ad, including how much Acton's mother was paid, as well as confirm who created it. After this story aired, Ramaswamy confirmed it was his ad.Acton has previously talked extensively about how she feels Ramaswamy has degraded her for what she has gone through."My opponent has said that I, someone who experienced child abuse and neglect, was a frequent flyer in children's services, that I'm just 'complaining about something done to me' in my childhood," Acton said, quoting Ramaswamy's previous statement.In the afternoon, Acton released a statement on her Facebook page, explaining more about her upbringing. "My birth mother did nothing to protect me. I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain," she wrote, in part.Her experiences shaped her values, compassion and her "belief that every person deserves to be safe, to be heard, and to have a fair chance at a better life," she continued. "They are why I will never stop fighting for Ohio's most vulnerable — especially the children and families who deserve the safety, dignity, opportunity, and hope that every Ohioan should have. No one in Ohio will ever be invisible to me," Acton stated.This article was originally produced by Morgan Trau for the Scripps News Group station in Cleveland.

Waves reaching up to 12 feet are pounding beaches across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast Monday, drawing experienced surfers into the water while prompting lifeguards in Jupiter to raise double red flags and prohibit swimming. From Boca Raton to Sebastian, beaches are experiencing rough surf and dangerous rip currents, with conditions expected to continue over the next several days. At Jupiter Beach Park Monday, CBS12 News watched surfers battle choppy waves, a kite surfer take advantage of the strong winds and beachgoers enjoy the sunshine from the sand. But lifeguards were taking the conditions seriously. "We're changing our flags from single red to double red, so this entire area is going to be with no swimming," said Ethan Sage, a Jupiter Ocean Rescue lifeguard. Sage said double red flags are typically needed only a few times a year, usually during major storms or unusually rough conditions. He estimated wave faces reaching 12 to 15 feet beyond the sandbars Monday, compared with 4 to 6 feet Sunday. Despite the warnings, some experienced surfers were eager to get into the water. "When it gets this big, I mean, we kind of want to go out there and let the ocean humble us a little bit," said surfer JC Southwell. Southwell said he would rather take on windy, choppy conditions than spend a day watching a flat ocean. Kite surfer Joe Goulet was also excited about the conditions, saying the wind and waves give him an opportunity to challenge himself and improve his skills. "It's a blast," Goulet said. But for other beachgoers, the waves were better enjoyed from a distance. Isis Alize brought her baby to the beach but had no plans to take her swimming. "Definitely a water baby," Alize said of her daughter. "We dipped our toes, and that was a bit scary, actually." What's causing the big waves? CBS12 News meteorologist Lauren Olesky said a nor'easter developing off the East Coast is sending large swells down the coastline. "So, we're dealing with waves breaking up to about 10 to 12 feet," Olesky said. The system developed along the same frontal boundary that brought rain to South Florida late last week and over the weekend. Olesky said high surf advisories extend across the region, with strong onshore winds contributing to the rough conditions. While the waves may be exciting for experienced surfers, Olesky warned that the high risk of rip currents makes swimming especially dangerous. "Even if you are a super strong swimmer, it can get tiring trying to fight the current if you're out there for an extended period of time," she said. Sage warned that even standing close to the water can be dangerous when powerful waves crash onto the shore. See also: 5,543 calls in 13 days: Palm Beach County's trash troubles pile up He said surfers are allowed to enter the water at their own discretion where the Jupiter restrictions are in place, but recommended that only experts consider going out. What beachgoers should know With seasonal visitors beginning to return to South Florida, Olesky encouraged everyone to check the forecast and beach warning flags before heading into the ocean. She recommended swimming only at lifeguarded beaches when conditions allow and paying attention to posted warnings. At the Jupiter beach CBS12 News visited, double red flags mean no swimming. And beachgoers hoping for calmer conditions may have to wait. Olesky said the large waves and high rip current risk are expected to continue over the next several days, giving experienced surfers more opportunities to catch waves while keeping lifeguards on high alert.

A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award to recognize her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies.

Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

Palm Beach County zoning staff approved a plan that nearly triples the amount of data center space previously approved on part of the property associated with Project Tango, according to new documents obtained by WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman. 7 approval came less than three months after county commissioners voted 5-1 to reject a much larger Project Tango expansion.The new plan increases the approved data center space from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.That distinction is important because the new approval is separate from the Project Tango expansion commissioners rejected in July.In 2016, plans were approved for 206,000 square feet of data center space and 1.2 million square feet of warehouse space on the property. About 600,000 square feet remained unassigned.The site is next to what would later become the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School.A decade later, a much larger proposal came before the Palm Beach County Commission.On July 15, commissioners spent roughly 12 hours reviewing the application known as Project Tango. That proposal sought to increase the project's data center footprint to more than 1 million square feet.Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny the expansion following significant opposition from nearby residents.The county also passed a moratorium on new data center applications while officials work on new rules.For residents who had fought the expansion, the July decision was a victory. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site.New documents show that was not the end of the story.Documents obtained by Hoffman show PBA Holdings, one of two companies that own property associated with Project Tango, had submitted a separate proposal before the July commission vote.Palm Beach County staff approved that plan Oct. 7 without another vote by county commissioners or a new public hearing before the commission.The approval increases the data center space on that portion of the property from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.The additional data center space uses square footage that had been unassigned under the 2016 approval.Under the newly approved plan, the property would include:Two 288,000-square-foot data center buildingsOne 122,000-square-foot data center building1.2 million square feet of warehouse spaceA utility building and offices occupying the remaining square footageThere is another significant difference between the 2016 plan and the October approval.The latest approval contains conditions governing development of the property. Palm Beach County zoning officials confirmed in July that the original 2016 approval did not include such conditions.Under the newly approved plan, data center buildings cannot be constructed within 850 feet of the property line near Arden.Noise at neighboring homes would be capped between 50 and 60 decibels, depending on the time of day. Sound monitors would run continuously, with the county receiving access to the monitoring data.The county's water utility would commit to providing no more than 100,000 gallons of water per day for the entire site.Battery storage would also be required to comply with fire safety requirements.Residents have contacted WPTV and Hoffman questioning how the plan could be approved without another commission vote and saying they believed the county's data center moratorium would prevent further movement on the property.Palm Beach County Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez told Hoffman by phone that the proposal was submitted before the moratorium took effect.Because it was already submitted, Hernandez said, county staff were able to continue reviewing it and ultimately approve it.Hernandez declined an on-camera interview.The Oct. 7 approval is not the only application involving the Project Tango property.According to Hernandez, WPB Logistics, the second owner of part of the property, has submitted its own proposal seeking to increase data center space on its roughly 60-acre portion of the site without approval from the County Commission.That proposal could result in approximately 1.2 million square feet of additional data center space.Unlike the PBA Holdings proposal approved Oct. 7, the WPB Logistics application remains under review.Hoffman also reached out to Ernie Cox, the main project manager for Project Tango, seeking a response to concerns from residents who said they felt the latest approval happened without their knowledge or an opportunity for public input.A member of Cox's staff returned Hoffman's call Tuesday and said the team would respond to the question.Hoffman had not received that response at the time of publication.

Lucie County voters will decide in November on two ballot questions aimed at addressing the county's growing population and its impact on infrastructure and services. The first question asks voters to renew the half-cent sales tax, originally approved in 2018, which is set to expire in two years. County leaders are seeking to extend the tax for another decade. This is not a new tax but would keep the total sales tax rate at 7%, with the half-cent portion funding infrastructure projects such as road improvements, sidewalks, stormwater drainage, and major projects like widening St. "Now we're seeing that impact, you know, the delayed maintenance and the increased growth we've seen picked up, we're starting to have to play catch-up with those infrastructure projects and the needs are still there," said Erick Gill, communications director for St. The second question focuses on expanding the mosquito control district to include the Tradition and southwestern areas of the county, which have grown beyond the current service boundaries. Currently, mosquito control services cover about half of the county's 600 square miles. If voters approve the expansion, affected property owners would pay about $28 more annually in taxes to fund fogging, spraying, and mosquito surveillance. Both measures will appear on the November ballot, addressing different needs as St. Lucie County continues to grow. Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach.
