The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. A weekly community gathering at Bryant Park is drawing renewed scrutiny in Lake Worth Beach as organizers question how the city is enforcing a new ordinance regulating food-sharing events in public parks.Melissa Salerno, a community member involved in the weekly gatherings, says the group continues to meet to share food and spend time together. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: But she says members have repeatedly been told by law enforcement that they are violating the city's rules, even as organizers maintain they are keeping attendance below 25 people and gathering for a picnic rather than a food distribution event.The dispute centers on how the city defines a food-sharing event, which rules apply to smaller gatherings, and why Bryant Park is excluded from the locations where these events are permitted.During a recent gathering, attendance appeared significantly lower than at previous events. Legal observers were also present after organizers invited them to monitor the gathering in case tensions escalated, equipped with body cameras and a measuring tape to comply with Florida's Halo law. Rick White, one of the legal observers, said their role was to help ensure participants' rights were respected."Just to make sure no one's civil rights are being violated, either way we're neutral; we're not here for one side or the other," White said.Salerno said organizers have attempted to follow the new ordinance by keeping participation below 25 people. She also disputes the city's characterization of the gathering as a food distribution event."According to the city, this is a food distribution event, and we are therefore in violation of the ordinance," Salerno said. "And what I tried to clarify was that this is not a food distribution event; this is a picnic."Salerno said the group wants to continue gathering without feeling intimidated or monitored."We just share each other's company and time,” she said.She also emphasized the importance of transparency and public awareness surrounding the city’s decisions."I think it's really important that the community at large knows what's going on, how their taxpayer dollars are being spent,” Salerno said.The Lake Worth Beach City Commission approved Ordinance 2026-01 on Feb. 3, 2026, tightening requirements for special events on city property, including organized food-sharing events. The measure followed complaints from downtown businesses and visitors about food-sharing gatherings at Bryant Park, including events serving people experiencing homelessness. Under the ordinance, a special event generally includes a gathering that attracts, is intended to attract, or is likely to attract 25 or more people, including staff, vendors and volunteers. The ordinance defines food-sharing events to include social-service food sharing and public events where food is provided or served at no charge in a public space.Those events are restricted to three designated locations:Memorial Park PavilionHoward Park PavilionNorthwest ParkA special-event permit application must be submitted at least 30 days in advance. The ordinance also limits the number of food-sharing event permits issued to the same person, group or organization at the same public space to 12 within a consecutive 12-month period. Additional requirements may include liability insurance, food-safety credentials for certain food preparation and service, and arrangements for cleanup. The restrictions mean that staying below 25 people does not automatically resolve every question about whether a gathering is allowed. Stuart Sword, interim director of Lake Worth Beach’s Leisure Services Department, said Bryant Park is not one of the approved locations for food-sharing events.Sword said the city selected the three designated parks partly because of their proximity to public transportation, making them accessible to people who rely on those services."Anytime there's a food-sharing event, there are significant implications to the park and also waste management,” Sword said.He said the city is trying to manage the impact of these gatherings while preserving public spaces for other uses."We identified three parks where you can do that, Northwest Ball Field, Memorial Park and Howard Park, and the reason the city picked those is 'cause they're close to public transportation," Sword said.Sword acknowledged a distinction between a picnic and a food-sharing event, adding that it's a clarification that would have to be made by the city attorney. WPTV began reporting on the proposal in June 2025, when organizers said they were serving growing numbers of people facing food insecurity amid rising housing costs and inflation. At the time, Salerno said Bryant Park was important because of its central location and access to bus routes. City leaders argued that organized events involving large numbers of people require planning, cleanup and coordination to protect public spaces and ensure other residents can use them.But advocates have argued that the requirements could create financial and logistical barriers for volunteer-led groups that rely on donations and personal contributions to provide meals.For now, the disagreement between organizers and the city remains focused on the ordinance’s application to the weekly Bryant Park gathering.Organizers say they want to continue meeting and sharing meals while complying with the rules. The city maintains that Bryant Park is not an approved location for food-sharing events and says its goal is to keep public spaces safe, clean and accessible.

Betty Haygood of Delray Beach says she is happy with her new roof after it was installed in August with help from the My Safe Florida Home program.However, what does not make her happy is her homeowners insurance renewal that's due in December.WATCH BELOW: Delray resident says insurance rose $300 after she replaced her roof"They're saying it's $300," she told us as we talked in her kitchen on Monday.At 76 years old, an increase like that doesn't come easily for Haygood, so she contacted WPTV looking for some answers."I'm upset about it because the simple fact that a person has replaced an old roof, if it doesn't stay where it is, there should be some kind of reduction," Haygood says.When it comes to homeowners insurance, setting premiums can be complicated.In many cases, rates can go down, and premiums go up, especially during periods of inflation.WPTV contacted Betty's insurance company, Universal, which is based in South Florida.They told us that her old roof was only insured at 25% value because of its age. Now, with a new roof, she has more comprehensive coverage, causing the increase.Insurance experts and state leaders tell us the insurance market in Florida is improving, with more new companies, competition and more pressure to lower rates.

The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

Florida is scheduled to execute William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, will die by lethal injection at Florida State Prison unless Gov. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

Abdul El-Sayed often talks about building a new and broad coalition of Michigan voters. A looming question in the state’s pivotal Senate race is whether he can keep the old one intact — particularly with the Black voters who are pivotal to any Democratic victory.The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has spent months working to make inroads with traditional Democratic constituencies that did not support El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, in his bitter primary battle against Rep. It only takes this much of Flint to defect,” said the Rev. Charles Williams II, pastor of the Historic King Solomon Baptist Church in Detroit, holding his fingers about an inch apart to drive home his point. “If even a sliver of people don’t turn out, you run into a huge challenge in trying to get your candidate over that line.”Holding the Democratic coalitionMichigan is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of the net four-seat gain the party needs on November 3 to win control of the Senate. If the party fails to retain the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, its path to a majority would grow much more difficult — and would run almost exclusively through much redder states than this upper Midwestern perpetual political battleground.El-Sayed defeated Stevens in the August primary by just 1 percentage point — a narrow victory fueled by his strong support among Arab American and Muslim communities, young voters and progressives in college towns.But Stevens had clear strengths, too: Black voters in and around Detroit largely aligned behind her, as did Jewish voters who have long expressed deep concerns with El-Sayed, who is Muslim and a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Poll: El Sayed holds slight edge in Michigan Senate race, but struggles with older swing votersRogers has made reaching those constituencies a central focus of his campaign in the race’s closing weeks, as he looks to assemble a coalition of voters more favorable to Republicans than in 2018, the last midterm election with President Donald Trump in office. That year, Democrats won four statewide races in Michigan, all by a range of about 7 to 9 percentage points.At a Detroit Economic Club forum on Tuesday, Rogers bragged that he has “built coalitions that really are very untraditional for a Republican candidate.”He pointed to plans to incentivize new home construction in Detroit, connect those construction efforts to high school apprenticeships, and eliminate “food deserts” in the city. He also said many Democrats have told him they fear the rising influence of democratic socialists within the party.“We’ve spent a lot of time here in Detroit, Flint, Pontiac,” he said, listing cities with large Black populations. “I think if we’re going to get our state right, we have to have everybody included in its forward progress.”In a bid to ease lingering Democratic doubts about El-Sayed, former President Barack Obama is set to visit Michigan, where he’ll attend a Saturday rally in Detroit with El-Sayed and the party’s nominee for governor, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.Other prominent Black Democrats have visited Michigan in recent weeks, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, who held a roundtable focused on Black maternal healthcare with El-Sayed. Raphael Warnock of Georgia is also set to campaign with El-Sayed, as are several members of the Congressional Black Caucus.“As much as he thinks he’s making inroads, folks are smart,” El-Sayed told CNN. “Mike Rogers is simply a rubber stamp on what Donald Trump wants. They understand exactly who Mike Rogers is.”While conversations with Black leaders and voters across Detroit show widespread support for El-Sayed, quiet concerns emerged about whether questions pertaining to the nominee’s background could dampen support. Historic tensions between Arab American and Black communities also were raised as points of anxiety.“In a close race, even a sliver of doubt about Abdul could lead to defeat,” one prominent Black leader told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss concerns frankly. “And this race feels far closer than it should.”El-Sayed mocks Rogers’ Black outreachEven as prominent Black Democratic leaders in Michigan express concern about the Senate race, El-Sayed — who spent recent days campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, a sparsely populated region where he hopes his populist pitch will chip away at the GOP’s traditionally strong margins — is downplaying and even mocking Rogers’ efforts to win over Black voters.At a campaign stop in Flint, a majority-Black city, a few hundred supporters turned out for an El-Sayed rally on Sunday afternoon. Only about a dozen members of the audience who packed into a large hotel conference room were Black, which was striking for a Democratic campaign event two weeks before the election.As he spoke to reporters afterward, El-Sayed said he saw no reason for concern.“Look, one of the hardest things about this economy is that too often folks are having to work multiple jobs and having to work on weekends,” he told CNN. “We know because of exactly the policies architected by folks like Donald Trump, that falls hardest on Black folks.”He was joined at the rally by Democratic Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, one of several Black members of Congress who have traveled to campaign alongside him.“We feel really strong about the relationship we’ve built and will continue to build,” El-Sayed said of his outreach to Black voters.When asked about the Rogers campaign opening a storefront office on Livernois Avenue in Detroit as part of its effort to win over Black voters, El-Sayed answered with a laugh.“I saw he opened a cute little office in Detroit where he brought all his friends from the suburbs to come clap him in. It was nice, yeah,” El-Sayed said. “He’s got no actual message for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.”RELATED STORY | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tours for Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed in close Senate raceMarcia Turner, who attended the Flint rally, said she was optimistic about El-Sayed, who she called “the right person at the right time.” But even her kind words underscored a history of some tension between the Black and Arab communities of Michigan.“I love that he’s running,” Turner said. “I think people are looking past his religion and seeing him as a man who wants what we want for our children and grandchildren.”Rogers steps ‘out of his space’Naura Evans, a teacher and mother of two from Sterling Heights, is a proud Black Republican. She appears in a television commercial, saying: “I voted for Barack Obama, but this year, I’m voting for Mike Rogers.”She said she grew up in a Democratic family but has become more conservative since her 2008 vote for Obama. She said she thinks schools and neighborhoods haven’t improved under Democratic rule and believes in Rogers’ plans for both.She said she feels that Democrats have taken Black voters for granted over the years, so she spends time going door-to-door in Warren, Troy and Sterling Heights, trying to persuade voters to join her in supporting Rogers.“It’s very important that we elect the right people,” Evans said. “As Blacks in our community, we show that our vote matters. We’re not just giving the vote away.”She said the Rogers campaign should get credit for opening an office in Detroit.“I’ve seen Mike Rogers definitely step out of his space and go into the Black community,” Evans said. “I think it’s practical and I think it’s also symbolic that he cares about Detroit. He could have opened an office anywhere and he chose Detroit.”She dismissed one of the biggest pieces of criticism she hears from Democrats about Rogers — that he would be a rubber stamp for Trump.“This is not a presidential election, it’s a senator’s election, and ultimately Mike Rogers will be the one making his own decisions,” Evans said. “I’m sure that his decisions will not be influenced by someone else.”‘His culture is different’Quentin Murray listened to the full slate of Democratic candidates speaking at a carpenters’ union hall on Sunday in Detroit. He said he was just beginning to learn more about El-Sayed’s candidacy but liked what he heard.“I like what he’s bringing to the table — something new, something different,” said Murray, a carpenter. “His culture is different, but when you see somebody like that, it’s good to know that we have the same interests and values.”Yet even in his praise, Murray casually brought up El-Sayed’s culture, which has been at the center of the campaign in bitter attack ads about his upbringing and beliefs.El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official whose parents immigrated to the US from Egypt, was born and raised in Michigan.At nearly every campaign stop, he briefly explains his family history and pushes back at some of the racially charged conversations about his name, which has been regularly belittled by Trump, who has taken to calling him “Mohammed Abdul El-Sayed.”Rogers has attempted to connect El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood — which El-Sayed has denounced — and cast him as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror. The GOP has pointed to old tweets from his sister describing El-Sayed’s birth mother’s activism with the Muslim Brotherhood while she was in college in the early 1970s. In a recent debate, Rogers also pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a nonprofit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism. El-Sayed was primarily raised by his father and stepmother in Michigan.“My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas. My name and my faith are not the reason you cannot afford your groceries,” El-Sayed told supporters in Flint. “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t see a doctor. I mean chances are if you’re seeing a doctor, they might actually have my name and my faith.”A progressive’s bid to win over moderatesCharity Dean, who owns a Detroit coffee shop and is president of the Michigan Black Business Alliance, said she has been pleasantly surprised by the enthusiasm for El-Sayed in her city.“Detroit is more conservative than folks would think — a lot more moderate,” Dean said. “I think his campaign has done a phenomenal job of really busting out of the box and saying, ‘Are you happy with how things are now? Are you happy with forever wars?’”Since finishing a distant second in Detroit in the August primary, Dean said, El-Sayed has listened to voters — supportive and skeptical ones alike — and has worked to build a campaign to win them over.“One of the things that’s gained him a lot of ground is his ability to respond to criticism and questions,” Dean said.While Dean said she has seen many signs that Rogers is trying to expand his outreach to Black voters, including television ads and opening an office in Detroit, she questioned whether the Republican nominee’s policies followed suit with the actions of his campaign.“Everything should be taken seriously. This is not a year where we take anything for granted,” Dean said, noting that she is carefully watching what the Rogers campaign is doing. “He seriously wants to win their vote, but he doesn’t want to make life better for Black people. That’s what really matters.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida's eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation's aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful.The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution.Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. Supreme Court.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected when a bus rolls over, including whether wearing a seat belt could create an additional danger.WATCH: AN NTSB EXPERT WEIGHS IN ON SCHOOL BUS SEAT BELTSTwo weeks after the crash, investigative reporter Katie LaGrone put that question directly to Dr. Kristin Poland, a school bus safety expert with the National Transportation Safety Board.The crash killed 16-year-old Adinaluz Prieto Oyola during the morning commute on Oct. According to investigators, the school bus carrying 37 high school students was on its way to Winter Haven High School when another cut slammed into its rear, causing the bus to collide head-on with another vehicle and flip over.Following the crash, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd was asked whether any of the dozens of students aboard were wearing seat belts at the time of impact. "Quite frankly, if you try to make everyone put a seat belt on, then we would have had 37 kids hanging from the roof by a seat belt," Judd said.His comments raise a key safety question: In a rollover crash, do seat belts protect students or potentially put them at greater risk?While Poland said the NTSB cannot yet discuss specifics of its investigation into the Polk County crash, she pointed to what the agency has learned from other school bus crashes."The real risk is when they’re violently thrown during the crash sequence about the inside of the bus, where they hit other occupants, or they could potentially hit hard points inside the school bus," Poland said.According to Poland, properly worn three-point restraints, which include both a lap and shoulder belt, provide the best protection even when a bus overturns."Those seat belts are designed so that students can still release the belts even if they're under tension, like if a student is hanging from the belt," she said.Poland acknowledged that the image of a child hanging by a seat belt after a rollover may sound frightening. But she said the greater danger comes during the crash itself, when an unrestrained student can be thrown around the bus.The NTSB has not determined whether a three-point seat belt could have changed the outcome of the Polk County crash. The school district confirmed the bus involved was only equipped with lap belts as are all the school buses in its fleet, according to a district spokesperson.A safety issue investigated for yearsFor reporter LaGrone, the questions surrounding school bus restraints aren't new. More than a decade ago, she investigated a St. Lucie County school bus crash that killed 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp, who was wearing a lap belt at the time.The NTSB investigated that crash and produced simulations demonstrating the difference between the protection provided by a lap belt and the protection provided when a shoulder belt is added.A few years later, the agency formally recommended that school districts in the U.S. upgrade school bus restraints to include both lap and shoulder belts. Florida was among the states called on to make three-point seat belts state law.What does Florida require?Currently, Florida only requires school buses to be equipped with lap belts, but students are not required to wear them.Nearly a decade after the NTSB's recommendation, Poland said some Florida school districts are moving toward three-point lap-and-shoulder belts. “We're seeing some progress with some of the school districts in Florida moving to the passenger lap shoulder belts,” she said.But our investigation found that the majority of public school buses in the state still have lap belts only.Cost is one hurdle. Still, Poland said installing the equipment is only part of improving student safety. "It's not enough just to have the lap shoulder belts on the bus, there also has to be an entire layered approach to ensure that the students are wearing the belts properly," she said. That approach also requires involvement and oversight from school districts and parents, Poland said.But Poland wants to emphasize that school buses remain the safest mode of transportation for students traveling to and from school, regardless of what kind of seat belts are on board. For Poland, seat belt use on school buses is a major step toward the agency's ultimate goal. "We think we can get to zero fatalities in school buses and that's what we're looking towards," Poland said.

Early voting begins Monday across Palm Beach County and parts of the Treasure Coast, giving voters an opportunity to cast their ballots ahead of the Nov. The start of early voting comes after a weekend of No Kings protests across South Florida, where organizers encouraged voter participation and urged residents to make a plan to vote early. The demonstrations, held Saturday in communities including West Palm Beach and Palm Beach Gardens, were part of a nationwide movement protesting President Donald Trump and his administration. This weekend’s events placed an additional focus on voter turnout ahead of the 2026 general elections. When and where can you vote early? Early voting schedules vary by county, with some polling locations opening Monday and others later in the week. There are 28 early voting locations. An additional day of early voting is available Nov. to 4 p.m., with extended hours until 6 p.m. Eligible voters can cast their ballots at any designated early voting location within the county where they are registered. Voters should bring a valid photo ID with a signature. Those without acceptable identification may still cast a provisional ballot. In Palm Beach County, voters can check polling location wait times online and use an optional appointment program to schedule their check-in time. Important election deadlines: The deadline to register to vote in the general election was Oct. Voters planning to cast a ballot by mail have until Thursday, Oct. to request that a ballot be mailed to them. Completed vote-by-mail ballots must be received by election officials no later than 7 p.m. In Palm Beach County, ballots returned to a branch office or secure ballot intake station must arrive by 5 p.m. Election Day polling locations will be open from 7 a.m. Find your early voting location: Voters can find polling locations, county-specific hours and additional election information through their local supervisor of elections: Palm Beach County : VotePalmBeach.gov St. Lucie County: StLucieVotes.gov Martin County: MartinVotes.gov Indian River County: VoteIndianRiver.gov Okeechobee County: VoteOkeechobee.gov

Court officials in Florida’s 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences.The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings.At a recent WPTV Let’s Hear It meetup in Okeechobee, Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem.WATCH:“We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them,” Bryant said.The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported.That means just one in five people showed up.Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences.“It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear,” Bryant said.Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families.Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently."If we knew that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, those other monies could then be diverted to things that we as a community would rather be spending those on," Schwab said.Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty.People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury.Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest.Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court.“I encourage everyone to do the right thing, to not ignore it. If you have an issue, make a phone call. There's a number on the summons,” Litty said. "Please do the right thing." Chief Judge Schwab said the court intends to enforce the consequences moving forward.“Failure to show up there is a consequence, and the courts are going to be enforcing those consequences going forward,” he said.Palm Beach County is part of Florida’s 15th Judicial Circuit. People who miss jury duty there may receive a follow-up notice or face contempt-of-court proceedings, which can carry a fine of up to $100 under Florida law.People who receive a jury summons should read it carefully and contact the appropriate clerk of court if they have questions or cannot attend.WPTV’s Brooke Chau reported this story as part of the station’s Let’s Hear It initiative, which connects journalists with community members and brings their concerns to local decision-makers.

Florida has secured an arrest warrant charging former Cuban leader Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the 1996 shootdown of two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes that killed four men, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday.The state case comes months after federal prosecutors indicted Castro and others over the same attack, raising questions about what the new Florida prosecution could mean alongside the existing federal case.WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman spoke with a former state attorney about the practical impact of the state charges and with a Cuban American woman whose family had a close connection to Brothers to the Rescue."It was not an accident what happened. The City of Boca Raton is preparing for a leadership transition after City Manager Mark Sohaney announced he is stepping down after roughly 13 months in the position. Court officials in Florida’s 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences.The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie, and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings.At a recent WPTV Let’s Hear It meetup in Okeechobee, Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem.WATCH:“We just ask one thing, and we don't ask you to do it often, but people just ignore them,” Bryant said.The numbers illustrate the concern. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported.That means just one in five people showed up.Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences.“It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear,” Bryant said.Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families.Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently.“If we knew that that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, that money could be diverted to things that we use in the community would rather be spending those on,” Schwab said.Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty.People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury.Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest.Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court.“I encourage everyone to do the right thing, to not ignore it. If you have an issue, make a phone call. There's a number on the summons,” Litty said. "Please do the right thing." Chief Judge Schwab said the court intends to enforce the consequences moving forward.“Failure to show up there is a consequence, and the courts are going to be enforcing those consequences going forward,” he said.Palm Beach County is part of Florida’s 15th Judicial Circuit. People who miss jury duty there may receive a follow-up notice or face contempt-of-court proceedings, which can carry a fine of up to $100 under Florida law.People who receive a jury summons should read it carefully and contact the appropriate clerk of court if they have questions or cannot attend.WPTV’s Brooke Chau reported this story as part of the station’s Let’s Hear It initiative, which connects journalists with community members and brings their concerns to local decision-makers.

More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. Lucie community members had a chance to learn more about and comment on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard during a county information session at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center Thursday. The proposal focuses on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. It would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping designed to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down. A majority of the community members spoke out against the plan, saying they don't believe the changes would improve safety. County officials say the changes are intended to improve safety, reduce crashes, and help slow traffic along the corridor. "We understand it's not popular. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents." County staff estimate the project could cost about $6.1 million dollars, but don't know where that money would come from yet. Residents who couldn’t attend the workshop can review plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award in recognition of her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Trump International Airport operations have resumed to normal after a police presence caused traffic delays Sunday afternoon while law enforcement investigated a suspicious phone call.WPTV reached out to the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office and they confirmed a bomb threat was reported Sunday. More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing.Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concernsSamples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered.Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise."It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too."We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared."Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway."When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said.The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design."We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. Behind the peach paint and scalloped edges of a familiar Palm Beach seawall is a structure that engineers say has reached the end of its useful life after more than a century of protecting the island.Now, the town is preparing for a major replacement project that will change the look of the beachfront and close the beach for about a year and a half.WATCH BELOW: Seawall replacement will close this beach for 18 monthsThe pastel-colored seawall has long blended into the scenery along a beach frequented by tourists and locals. Sandra Greenberg, who was visiting with her family from Virginia and has a condo in West Palm Beach, described it simply: "It's a great beach, love it."A tourist visiting from Costa Rica shared the sentiment, saying, "Yes, it's perfect."For people who live nearby, however, the beach can be more than a destination. It is part of their regular routine."This is where I come to, like, relax," said Bridget St. Laurent, a local and owner of Palm Beach Beauty Lab on Palm Beach. "It's my life, it's my backyard, I grew up here, and the fact I can just take a five-minute drive to the ocean means so much."St. Laurent told WPTV she tries to visit once a week, if not more.But that routine is about to be interrupted.The seawall is one line of defense from hurricanes and storm surges that, over more than a century, has protected the island from what is estimated to be $7 billion in private property, along with critical infrastructure on Palm Beach.Replacing it will require a lengthy beach closure, with the project expected to keep beachgoers away for approximately a year and a half."A year and a half? Laurent said after learning from WPTV how long the closure would last.For regular visitors, the project means they will have to find another stretch of sand until the work is complete. Other beach options include Singer Island to the north, as well as Phipps Beach and Lake Worth Beach to the south.When WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked Greenberg where she might go during the closure, she didn't have an alternative in mind."No, you're going to have to tell me where to go," she said.Still, Greenberg said she understands why the work needs to be done, even if that means temporarily losing access to a beach her family enjoys."We're going to have to do it; let's just rip that band-aid off and get it done," Greenberg said.The preparations are expected to become visible by the end of the year, when the pastel backdrop will be covered by fencing as work gets underway on the next chapter of the seawall."It's going to be a little bit of a nuisance for now, but more importantly we need to keep this community safe," Greenberg said.For St. Laurent, the construction may keep her away for a while, but it won't keep her away permanently.Asked whether she would return once the year-and-a-half project is finished, St. Laurent said, "Absolutely, I live here; this is my backyard."A wildlife deterrent will also be created, including a turtle berm, a small wall to protect sea turtles from clashing with the construction.Engineers say the new seawall will also include the iconic scalloped border.Before construction gets underway, the town is also giving the community an opportunity to learn more about what is planned. The town engineer told WPTV that a meeting will be held on Oct. at the Town Council Chambers, where the public can listen to a presentation and ask questions about the project.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situation Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home. According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing a woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. A push from a Pahokee resident at a recent county commission meeting is shining new light on a long-delayed affordable housing development that local leaders say remains badly needed across the Glades.Consuela Cunningham Benjamin traveled to West Palm Beach to urge county leaders to make it a priority to complete the Everglades Townhomes project.WATCH BELOW: Long-delayed affordable housing project back on track"Pahokee, Florida is my hometown. I was born and raised in Pahokee, Florida," Consuela told commissioners. "I joined the military, served in the Army in hopes of returning home to adequate housing."She said affordable housing remains difficult to find in the community.The Everglades Townhomes project is expected to bring 60 affordable rental units to Pahokee, but Consuela noted the development has faced years of delays."It has yet to be completed, has taken five years to complete, and still is not complete," she said. "We are an underserved community in the Pahokee area, and we should be put first."Consuela called on county and state leaders to step in and help move the project across the finish line."I'm therefore asking our county and state leaders to make completing Everglades townhouses a priority and work with the city of Pahokee on a clear recovery plan with responsible oversight and qualified development partners, identify funding, measurable milestones, and realistic completion time," she said.After hearing her concerns, commissioners directed county staff to provide an update on the project and discuss what options may be available moving forward.To find out what has caused the delays, WPTV turned to Carlos Serrano, deputy director of Palm Beach County's Department of Housing and Economic Development.According to Serrano, the Everglades Townhomes development will consist of 60 townhome-style rental units for households earning no more than 60% of the area's median income.For a household of four, that income limit is approximately $77,000 annually."There's a substantial need for affordable housing in Pahokee and throughout the Glades region of the county," Serrano said. "It's one of the areas of the county that for many years had suffered from disinvestment and deteriorating housing conditions, and 60 affordable rental housing units would go a long way towards helping meet the need in Pahokee.However, Serrano said the biggest delay came after construction was already underway when the dispute turned into a legal fight.The dispute stalled construction for over a year and a half."More recently, the developer has got a new contractor on board," Serrano said. "That new contractor has mobilized, commenced construction in August, and as we speak, construction is underway on the project again."When asked what message he had for residents waiting for the project to be completed, Serrano responded, "Hold on, it's coming," Serrano said. Construction is moving along and is projected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027."A visit to the site shows visible progress. Some of the buildings have been painted and have windows and doors installed, while work continues on other structures.Residents told WPTV they are eager to see the project finished."You want them to hurry up?" WPTV asked John Wilson."Yes, please," the resident replied.Former South Bay Vice Mayor John Wilson said the housing shortage extends beyond Pahokee."We need action, we need visibility," Wilson said.Serrano said Everglades Townhomes is only one of several affordable housing projects planned for the Glades. He pointed to the proposed One North Lake development in Pahokee, which would add 50 affordable apartment units, as well as the planned Calusa Pointe project in Belle Glade, which is expected to include approximately 160 affordable apartments."We want to meet the local housing needs there," Serrano said. "This is an area that has acute housing needs, so the county works with both its municipal partners out in the Glades area as well as private industry and financial institutions to try to pull together these deals and see some housing come out of the ground that can help serve local residents."WPTV also reached out to every commissioner with the City of Pahokee over the past three weeks seeking answers about the project. As of publication on Monday evening, none had responded.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after deputies responded to a reported domestic violence incident Saturday morning in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard, where they encountered a man in the front yard. The man went back inside after seeing law enforcement, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office . Deputies say they later contacted a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated inside, prompting a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. See also: Driver tried to ram deputy before PIT maneuver ended chase, SLCSO says During the incident, the man reportedly came outside several times and indicated he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside, deputies said. Amendment 3 aims to change the property tax structure in Florida by saving money for homeowners and cutting revenue for cities and counties. The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that state prosecutors and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) have secured an arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro, accusing him of conspiring to murder four men in the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft operated by the anti-Castro group Brothers to the Rescue.According to the Attorney General's Office, Castro has been charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with an incident in which Cuban military fighter jets shot down two unarmed Brothers to the Rescue planes over international waters.Authorities said three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-locka Airport in Miami-Dade County on Feb. After crossing the 24th parallel and flying outside Cuba's territorial waters, two of the planes were destroyed by air-to-air missiles fired by Cuban MiG fighter jets.According to the affidavit, the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba at the time and received no warning before being shot down.The warrant, obtained by the Office of Statewide Prosecution and FDLE, alleges Castro played a key role in authorizing the attack that killed four men with ties to Florida: Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr."Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy," Uthmeier said in a statement. According to a probable cause affidavit, Castro, who at the time served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president, was among the final decision-makers who authorized the operation. Investigators allege Castro issued standing orders to military leaders to shoot down aircraft associated with Brothers to the Rescue if they appeared over the sea.State investigators also allege Cuban intelligence agents operating in South Florida infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and provided flight information to the Cuban government as part of what was known as "Operation Scorpion."Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz called the warrant a "historic step toward accountability" for the four men killed in the attack, while FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein said the case demonstrates that "the passage of time does not diminish the pursuit of justice."The warrant charges Castro under Florida statutes governing conspiracy and first-degree murder. Prosecutors said the offense is a first-degree felony, and the court ordered that no bond be granted.State officials said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed.

Zito said."Pink in the Rink" Night extends beyond fundraising, it also raise awareness for cancer research ans shares the resources available for families who are impacted by challenges a cancer diagnosis brings with it. WPTV is learning that potential road improvements are coming to a busy road in Port St. Lucie County staff are sharing designs and want to hear input from neighbors about a proposed project on Prima Vista Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors weigh in on Prima Vista Boulevard changesThey plan to improve a section of the roadway from Airoso Boulevard to U.S. Highway 1 by removing the center left turn lanesDan Zrallack, county engineer, said their plan is to replace the center left-turn lanes with a raised median."The center turn lane is often referred to as a suicide lane," Zrallack said. "The more turning movements you have, the more chances you have for accidents by restricting access and putting in the median turn lanes. We can kind of control where those turning movements are and protect the drivers as well as pedestrians walking along the roadway." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, there have been 578 crashes on that section of the Prima Vista Boulevard since 2020. Zrallack said the median will make the road safer. "Statistically, the safety improves by up to like 40 percent or more," Zrallack said. But not every neighbor is sold on the improvements. Kadaysha Wilkins lives on Prima Vista Boulevard and told WPTV the median will make traveling more complicated. "Adding medians or anything else is going to cause more chaos than good," Wilkins said. "Ten to 12 years of living here, I've never seen an issue with our turning lane." Wilkins said it'll make it more difficult to take her niece and nephew to school by using the median instead of driving across the street. "A five-minute ride has turned into a 15-minute travel," Wilkins said.Wilkins said trying to come home could also be an issue."Turning into my driveway, which could have taken two seconds, is that now going to take 15 minutes?” Wilkins said. Having access to a gym is one thing. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.WATCH BELOW: Man found dead after St. Lucie County barricade situationDeputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concerns Samples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered. Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. She said flooding has occurred there for years. WPTV was there when water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she already sent messages to her customers for Saturday. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business." For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." The project may take years until completion, but Collins said she already thought about moving her business. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

For nearly 40 years, The Golden Girls have entertained audiences with humor, friendship and unforgettable characters. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach on Oct. 25, bringing Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia back together in a new story that imagines the iconic friends still living under one roof decades after the original sitcom ended.Actor Vince Kelley, who portrays Blanche Devereaux, and Adam Graber, who plays Rose Nylund, say the comedy's enduring popularity comes from its ability to connect with people from all walks of life."It's a very multifaceted answer," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties.
