WEST PALM BEACH — Oxbridge Academy is unveiling its first-ever baseball field, built with a $1.8 million anonymous donation that transformed an empty space into a full ballpark right next to the school.WPTV News got an exclusive first look at the new facility, which features fresh-cut grass, new dirt, fencing, bases, a scoreboard and shady dugouts. The new facilities kick off a new era of baseball for the Thunderwolves.The field is a significant upgrade for a team that previously had to leave campus to practice. Senior Carlo Vasquez plays third base, first base and has also pitched for the team."I think it's gonna be good, because we have the field coming. We have a lot of freshmen coming in, so it's gonna be a young program, but for the future, it's gonna be good for them,” Vasquez said.Vasquez said the move will benefit the program for years to come."We used to go drive to Dyer Park and that was where we practiced at. So it was a lot harder, but we made it work. We used to practice on the soccer field,” Vasquez said.Now, instead of commuting, the Thunderwolves will take the field right next to their school."It's going to be great. It's going to be a lot easier. It's going to be easier to get the work in,” Vasquez said.Leading the program is head coach Juan Bustabad, who brings more than 30 years of professional baseball experience to Oxbridge.Bustabad was the school's first baseball coach until 2016; he returns this year excited to coach on the new field."We've been waiting for a long time, and it's finally here and these players are going to enjoy it the whole season,” Bustabad said.Under his leadership, Bustabad said he wants to bring fundamentals and a winning culture to the baseball program."Our goal is to be successful. First of all, you know, as a coach, you always want to win, but you also want to develop,” Bustabad said.The Thunderwolves went 8-8 last year, and Bustabad said this upcoming season the team will be young, with only two seniors on the roster."The most important thing is just relax, have fun, go out there and let's see how many wins can we put together this year,” Bustabad said.Vasquez said he expects the new bleachers to fill up on game days."Honestly, just your classmates coming to the games, having more people out here and just having a good time because you're by the football field. Everyone's just going to be coming. I think it's going to be great. It's going to be really fun,” Vasquez said.On Oct. 20, Oxbridge Academy will host a ribbon-cutting and dedication ceremony for its new baseball complex. The upgraded field is set to host its first games this spring.

Thirty-three years after his uncle was murdered, Brian Kunkel is still waiting for what he considers justice."There's a whole host of emotions with this," Kunkel said. "There's a tremendous amount of anger, and now as we speak, it kind of starts to build back up again."WATCH BELOW: 'It's time': Family seeks execution 33 years after loved one murderedHis uncle, Richard Kunkel, was a 32-year-old local florist remembered by his family as outgoing, generous and full of life."Richard was a fun-loving guy," Brian Kunkel said. Very outgoing — the type of person that literally would give you the shirt off his back."In 1993, Richard Kunkel went to Roosters nightclub in West Palm Beach.Court records show Ronald Knight and two other men went to the gay bar looking for a man to lure away, rob and beat."This was all premeditated," Brian Kunkel said. "He knew what he was doing."Court records show the men befriended Kunkel and convinced him to leave with them. Knight then drove him to a secluded area, where he shot and killed him.The men robbed Kunkel, stole his car and burglarized his home."Richard begged for his life," Brian Kunkel said. "He pleaded not to be shot. He was murdered in cold blood."Two years later, Knight was charged in another killing.In May 1995, 22-year-old Brendan Meehan was lured from Heartbreakers, then a gay nightclub on Olive Avenue in West Palm Beach, taken to a secluded area and killed.Knight was convicted of both murders and sentenced to death in 1998."These people had purposes in life, and it's gone," Kunkel said.More than three decades after Richard Kunkel's murder, Knight remains on death row.Now, Kunkel is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to sign his death warrant."It's been a long and arduous process," he said. "My grandparents are gone. They've passed without closure, and I know, at least in my grandmother's case, she died of really a broken heart.""This needs to be done. It needs to be finalized," Kunkel added. His request comes as Florida carries out executions at a pace rarely seen in the state.Florida executed a record 19 people in 2025. Seventeen people have been executed so far in 2026, with two more executions scheduled.That pace has drawn concern from death penalty opponents and defense attorneys, who warn increasingly compressed timelines could put additional strain on the appeals process."I can't imagine how they're keeping up with it in a way that ensures quality," capital defense attorney Carey Haughwout said.Death penalty opponents are also questioning how the state determines who is executed and when."We don't know how people are being chosen or why," said Grace Hanna with Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.But for Kunkel, the debate over whether Florida is moving too quickly stands in stark contrast to his family's experience.They have been waiting 33 years.Kunkel says his grandparents died without seeing Knight executed. His family has spent decades without Richard."Ron Knight, sitting in a jail, he can see daylight. He eats food, gets medical attention," Kunkel said. "Richard and Brendan, they don't enjoy any of that. They're in the ground, and they're lifeless. Thirty-three years is a long time."For Kunkel, the decades have not diminished the memory of the uncle behind the court records and death sentence."His smile was electric," he said. "He was a really good man."Kunkel said a representative from the Florida Attorney General's Office recently helped expedite a clemency hearing for Knight — a step that could clear the way for Gov. Ron DeSantis to sign his death warrant.Kunkel said he is still waiting to learn the outcome.

A bomb threat near Donald J. Trump International Airport. WPTV has previously reported on security concerns and threats involving the airport since the name change, although authorities have not identified any connection between Sunday’s threat and the airport’s new name.Neighbors say heavy security is expectedResidents who live near the airport said large law enforcement operations and traffic disruptions have become familiar whenever the president visits Palm Beach County.Phil, who lives near the airport, told WPTV drivers often encounter road closures and extensive security measures during presidential visits."Any time he's coming in town, traffic is lockdown," he said. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man’s possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home. According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing an adult woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concerns Samples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered. Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. She said flooding has occurred there for years. WPTV was there when water levels rose at the intersection last week. Collins said she already sent messages to her customers for Saturday. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business." For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said. The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. "That's just not OK." The project may take years until completion, but Collins said she already thought about moving her business. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the police agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. The Florida Panthers' fifth annual "Pink in the Rink" Night returned to Amerant Bank Arena on Saturday during a home game against the Seattle Kraken, honoring those who have battled breast and cervical cancer and the medical professionals working to treat the diseases and find a cure.Bill Zito, President of Hockey Operations and General Manager of the Florida Panthers, said the cause resonates with everyone."It's all of us, literally all of us." Zito said. "It has a personal touch for everybody. I don't know the situation, but as I'm describing this to you right now, you're thinking of someone. That's the thing everybody." Zito said.Zito said everyone has been impacted by cancer in one way or another — including his own family."My wife, Julie, is a breast cancer survivor and is very active in fundraising,” Zito said. “There will be a day when cancer doesn't exist. There's lots of really virtuous, smart people ready to work. They just need funding and that's where we come in." Zito said."Pink in the Rink" Night extends beyond fundraising, it also raise awareness for cancer research ans shares the resources available for families who are impacted by challenges a cancer diagnosis brings with it. "A wonderful celebration of not just fundraising, but of awareness, empathy, and spirit. Spirit for the fight." Zito said.Before puck drop, Baptist Health Cancer Care offered their MammoVan, where people at the game could learn more from cancer care staff. The Panthers also held a Rose Moment on the ice, honoring both survivors and those actively fighting cancer.Specialty "Pink in the Rink" jerseys were up for auction, with the proceeds going toward the Promise Fund."I mean, they do everything from, I mean, they organize Ubers to get people to hospice. They find programs for people who don't have insurance. Whatever it is you need, they'll find a way for you to get treatment to get healthy." Zito said.Fans at the game also received handheld fans — a functional and symbolic item for those going through cancer treatment. The idea came from one of the Panthers staff Juliana David."In the course of treatment, frequently patients will go through hot flashes or become very warm. So it was an interesting item to provide the fan. So it's not only functional for the patient, it's functional actually living in South Florida because it's so warm. But it's also symbolic and it's a reminder of how impactful this night is and how important it is," Zito said. As game attendees wave and use there pink fans, Zito hopes it will serve as a reminder. "So every time you look at your little fan, you think someone's going through chemo, someone's going through treatment and they're using this. And so that connection It can bring every fan just a little bit of a reminder, a little bit of a reminder of why we're doing Pick at the Rink this evening." Zito said.Events like "Pink in the Rink" bring awareness and remind us just how important funding for cancer research is, a cause, like Zito says, that impacts everyone. To learn more about funding and assistance visit the Promise Fund website.

Protesters gathered in Palm Beach County as part of a nationwide “No Kings” day of action, with local organizers putting a focus on encouraging people to vote early ahead of the November midterm elections.The rally was organized locally by Speaking Up for America - Indivisible. Group leader Susan Foley said Saturday’s demonstration marked the organization’s eighth rally in two years and its fourth No Kings rally.“Today is a special day, our fourth No Kings rally,” Foley said. “This one is special because of its mission to vote early.”WATCH: Palm Beach County ‘No Kings’ rally urges early votingFoley said organizers are encouraging people to cast their ballots early rather than waiting until Election Day.“If you vote early, your vote is locked in,” Foley said.But for protesters who came out Saturday, the rally was also an opportunity to speak about issues they would like to see addressed both nationally and closer to home.WPTV's Christy Waite listened to protesters like Ann Hunter. She says she wants to see more attention paid to the financial challenges facing families.“More consideration to the middle class and people that are in desperate circumstances struggling with their food, healthcare, everyday living expenses,” Hunter said.For Cynthia Heller, a former educator, education funding is among the issues that brought her out.“I was in education, so I would like to see more money go into education,” Heller said.Protesters said events like Saturday’s also give members of the community an opportunity to come together around issues that are important to them.One protester emphasized that regardless of political affiliation, participating in the election is what matters.“I am happy to see people here, and no matter how they vote, they have to vote,” the protester said.The Republican Party of Palm Beach County also responded to Saturday’s demonstrations, pointing to Republican policies and the party’s growing voter registration advantage in Florida.In a statement, the county GOP credited Gov. Ron DeSantis’ policies with Florida’s economic performance and highlighted Amendment 3, a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot dealing with property taxes.The party also defended President Donald Trump’s approach to judicial appointments and said Republican voter registration and turnout show support for the party’s direction.“Florida has transitioned into a reliably red state, with the Republican Party of Florida maintaining an advantage of over 1.55 million registered voters over Democrats,” the statement said.State voter registration data as of Sept. 30 shows more than 5.67 million active registered Republicans compared with about 4.13 million Democrats, a difference of roughly 1.55 million voters.Amendment 3 would reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5% and make other changes involving how counties and municipalities use property tax revenue.Similar demonstrations have taken place across the region, from Palm Beach County to Vero Beach, as protesters continue to make their voices heard ahead of the November elections.

A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills.The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support.WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus"We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward," Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said.The Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause.Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti."We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar," AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said.AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys & Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy.For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection."I am a Haitian American. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow," Cesar said.The Boys & Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization.The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns.AmeriCorps members' work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys & Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service.The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments.The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys & Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers.Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs.With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys & Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program's previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A welfare check on an 88-year-old Okeechobee County veteran led to the discovery of a homicide and the arrest of the victim's grandson following an early-morning police chase in Indian River County, Sheriff Eric Flowers and Chief Deputy Michael Hazellief said Thursday during a press conference.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff, chief deputy announce arrest of wanted suspectPaul Eugene Baker, a longtime Okeechobee County resident and veteran, was found dead on his property after his daughter-in-law called for a welfare check. His grandson, 35-year-old Earl Douglas Wadlington III, was taken into custody after deputies pursued him through a Walmart parking lot at approximately 4 a.m."What started off as a simple welfare check of an 88-year-old veteran in our county has turned into a tragedy and a family tragedy," Hazellief said.Baker's daughter-in-law had not seen or heard from him in several days. She went to his residence and found the house in disarray, which investigators said was highly unusual."She hadn't seen him or talked to him in several days. She went by to check on the residence. She found the house in disarray, became concerned, and it was highly unusual for him to not be around or for the house to be in this manner," Hazellief said.Law enforcement obtained and executed a search warrant for the property. Baker was found dead on the property. Investigators said the manner and location of his death made it immediately evident that it was a homicide.Baker's only vehicle was also missing from the residence, along with other property. Investigators learned that Wadlington had recently been living with Baker.The daughter-in-law told investigators that Wadlington had a history with the criminal justice system and that no other family member would allow him to live with them. Wadlington has over 800 felonies in his criminal background, the chief deputy said."The daughter-in-law also explained to us that he had been in and out of prison, that he had challenges that nobody else in the family would allow him to live with him, but the grandfather had allowed him to stay there," Hazellief said.Because the daughter-in-law also held power of attorney for Baker, law enforcement was able to enter the missing vehicle into the ALPR system — a license plate reader network connected to partner agencies across the Treasure Coast area — as stolen. The vehicle was flagged as connected to a homicide suspect. Investigators tracked the vehicle leaving the area but chose not to issue a public alert."We didn't put anything out publicly at that time because we did not want to startle. We wanted the suspect to stay in the vehicle. Quite honestly, we wanted to keep driving," Hazellief said.WATCH BELOW: Dashcam video of chase, bodycam video of arrest in Indian River CountyInvestigators noted that while the agency was required this past month to remove Flock cameras from state roads and permitted locations per a state DOT order, cameras in other qualifying locations remained operational and allowed investigators to move forward with the case."To be specific with the language, we still have them in place in places that don't meet that criteria, and because of that, we were able to really move forward with this case," Hazellief said.Senior detective Ashley Rojas and her team led the investigation, the chief deputy said.The stolen vehicle was detected by Indian River County's Flock camera system this morning, leading investigators to the suspect's location.Indian River County Sheriff Flowers described the early-morning pursuit caught on video, in which Wadlington fled from deputies through a Walmart parking lot."One of the particular things that's interesting is it's 4 o'clock in the morning. He's running from our deputies. He's running through the Walmart parking lot. You see that our deputies were able to deploy stop sticks. The reason that he ultimately stopped and got out and ran is because his truck was going to stop working. That stolen vehicle is going to stop working," Flowers said.Sebastian Police Department also responded and assisted Indian River County deputies throughout the pursuit."Doesn't matter if the uniform is green or blue, doesn't matter what color it is. We're all going to go after the bad guys," Flowers said.Flowers praised the Flock camera system and said the county will continue using it despite public criticism."For all the naysayers and all the people who don't like flock and who don't like it, we're going to continue to use it. We're going to continue to put bad guys in jail because of it," Flowers said.Flowers noted that Indian River County cameras not covered by the state DOT order remain in operation. He said the Flock system has aided in other cases, including one involving a missing elderly woman.Wadlington was arrested on fleeing and eluding charges, deputies said, in addition to driving a stolen a vehicle. A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man’s possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said.Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home.According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside.During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot.Knowing an adult woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said.Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community.Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

A program that has worked with thousands of Martin County children is returning after a brief hiatus, with a renewed focus on helping young students strengthen their reading skills. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County is celebrating the return of its AmeriCorps program, which places volunteers directly with students to provide individualized and small-group academic support. WATCH BELOW: Literacy program returns to Martin County after hiatus “We missed it. It was an extremely important piece to our success and moving the district forward,” Martin County Schools Superintendent Michael Maine said. The Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County first introduced the federal mentorship program to the area in 2019. For six years, AmeriCorps volunteers worked with thousands of local students before federal funding shortfalls forced the program to pause. Now, program leaders have set new goals for its return. WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with AmeriCorps Program Director for Martin County Boys and Girls Club, Russell Lamberti. “We want to serve 575 students, and we want to see an increase of 65% growth, and that can be in vocabulary, fluency and grammar,” AmeriCorps Program Director Russell Lamberti said. AmeriCorps volunteers will work one-on-one and in small groups with kindergarten through fifth-grade students at four Boys Girls Club locations, with an emphasis on literacy. For AmeriCorps Volunteer Experience Specialist Abelard Cesar, the mission also has a personal connection. I learned English at 13 years old, and I had mentors that helped me grow,” Cesar said. The Boys Girls Clubs says the program delivered significant academic results during its previous six-year run. In some cases, as many as eight in 10 participating students moved their reading from Level 1 to Level 4. About the same percentage maintained or improved their English Language Arts grades, according to the organization. The organization said students also showed improvements in literacy rates, assessment scores, school attendance and behavioral patterns. AmeriCorps members’ work previously extended beyond the classroom. According to the Boys Girls Clubs, volunteers completed nearly 50 service projects in Martin County and contributed more than 60,000 hours to community cleanup efforts and other acts of service. The return comes as literacy remains a focus across the county. Earlier this year, the Martin County School District reported that local kindergarten students tied for fourth place statewide in readiness scores and literacy assessments. The AmeriCorps program is part of a broader academic effort by the Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County, which serves more than 1,000 members ages 6 to 18 in its daily programs. The organization also provides after-school academic assistance through certified teachers. Beyond its Clubs, the organization runs or manages several programs serving local children, including Reading Buddies, Character Counts!, career training using virtual reality technology, culinary programs and skilled-trades programs. With AmeriCorps volunteers returning, the Boys Girls Clubs says it hopes to build on the program’s previous results while giving more Martin County students the individual attention and support they need.

A West Palm Beach woman is facing a felony animal cruelty charge after investigators said her Yorkshire terrier was so severely malnourished that veterinarians gave the dog the lowest possible body condition score before it was euthanized.The investigation began Oct. 2 when Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control officers responded to Access Specialty Animal Hospital in Royal Palm Beach after staff reported a suspected animal cruelty case involving a 7-year-old Yorkshire terrier named King.Veterinary staff told investigators King arrived in critical condition suffering from severe emaciation, a heavy flea infestation and signs of prolonged neglect. According to the affidavit, the Yorkie was unable to breathe on his own. The veterinarian determined King's condition was the result of a chronic deterioration that developed over weeks or months rather than a sudden illness. Despite emergency lifesaving measures, including intubation and assisted ventilation, the dog's condition remained poor due to the severity of his condition. The veterinarian said the dog's emaciation as among the most severe she had encountered in her veterinary career and concluded King's suffering was most likely caused by prolonged neglect and a lack of adequate care.The affidavit states Marseille and another individual declined an advanced stabilization treatment recommended by the hospital because they could not afford the cost.Hospital staff identified Charlynn Marseille, 33, as the person who brought King to the veterinary hospital. Investigators later confirmed ownership through animal records and an interview at Marseille's West Palm Beach residence, where she acknowledged owning the dog.Investigators also referenced a 2023 complaint involving the same dog. According to the affidavit, a caller reported concerns that King had been left alone for days without food and was crying.Marseille was arrested Oct. 14 and charged with aggravated animal cruelty causing excessive pain or suffering. Lucie man was arrested Thursday night after leading St. Lucie County deputies on a high-speed chase that ended on South Hutchinson Island. The pursuit began in the 9600 block of South Ocean Boulevard when a Patrol Operations deputy attempted to stop the driver of a pickup truck for a traffic violation. Andrew Bolonka, the director of communications for the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, said the driver fled instead of stopping, making a U-turn and spinning donuts in the roadway, forcing other motorists to take evasive action. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates After briefly stopping, the driver made another U-turn, cut across lanes of traffic, and accelerated toward the deputy's patrol vehicle. "The deputy tries to stop the vehicle; all of a sudden, the vehicle lunges, takes off, accelerates, does another U-turn, and then starts allegedly heading straight toward the deputy. Which you can see in the body-worn camera, where the deputy makes an evasive maneuver and says, 'Oh, he almost hit me,'" Bolonka said. Members of the department's Special Investigations Unit and deputies in the air assisted in the pursuit. The driver continued to flee even after stop sticks were deployed. Deputies eventually executed a PIT maneuver along Seaway Drive, bringing the vehicle to a stop. Despite repeated verbal commands to exit the truck, the driver refused, prompting deputies to deploy pepper balls into the vehicle. The driver then surrendered and was taken into custody without further incident. The suspect, identified as 37-year-old Joshua Gallagher of Port St. Lucie, faces several charges, including aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription, and resisting arrest without violence. He remains in custody at the St. "When people make decisions like this, and they commit an act that puts not only the deputies and other law enforcement officers in peril, but they are also putting the general public in peril. This weekend we're expected to see more heavy rain in our area. This may be exactly the kind of weekend forecast that many people in Port St. Lucie do not want to hear. Last week, parts of the city flooded when torrential rains hit Port St. According to our Stormtrac meteorologists, the city got about four inches of rain in a 48 hour period last week. Roads turned into lakes, water levels in canals rose quickly, and some drivers took their chances and drove through standing water deep enough to possibly leave them stalled with nowhere to go. One homeowner, who has a canal directly behind his house, says he was stunned to see the extent of the flooding. It was the worst he's seen in the two years he's lived in Port St. See also: Trump expected at Mar-a-Lago as Palm Beach road closures, No Kings rallies are planned "When I came out, I was like, Oh, my God! I've never seen it like this before!" said Peter Rodriguez, who lives at the intersection of SW Todd Avenue and SW Broadview Street in Port St. How concerned is he about the possibility of another flood this weekend? "I don't think it's gonna get that high. If it starts getting that high, then I'm gonna start to pray. Not another flood," he said. Luckily floodwater did not get into his house. But the water was deep enough he says, to prevent him from driving out of his driveway. One resident says he feels the city of Port St. Lucie could be doing more to prevent such flooding. "I really think they should do something, I mean really to take care of business, you know because we pay our taxes," said Frank Camarda, a Port St. Lucie resident on SW Leisure Lane. A city spokesman says they'll have Public Works employees on standby this weekend if heavy rain comes, if they need to clear storm drains or move pumps into position to lower water levels in certain areas such as near the intersection of Savona Boulevard and SW California Boulevard. That area has been prone to flooding in the past. "They've been monitoring the canals and the retention ponds. And again, they haven't had to lower them this week which is a good sign. They're where they think they need to be. So, we're as prepared as we can be. You never know what Mother Nature is going to throw at you, but this team is doing everything it can to try to to mitigate the risks as much as possible," said Scott Samples, Strategic Communications Manager and Public Information Officer, city of Port St. He says the city of Port St. Lucie received no reports last week that floodwaters got into any homes or businesses.

A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricade situation prompted deputies to evacuate a woman and children from a St. Lucie County home, according to the sheriff’s office.The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard.Deputies initially encountered a man in the front yard who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. During that interaction, a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man’s possession and ordered him to drop it, the sheriff’s office said.Instead, the man closed the door and retreated inside, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained in the home.According to investigators, the man came outside several times and said he would surrender after making a phone call, but repeatedly went back inside.During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot.Knowing an adult woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff’s office said.Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community.Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner’s Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

More rain is expected this weekend across South Florida and the Treasure Coast, and WPTV is learning that Port St. Lucie Public Works is preparing.Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said crews spent the week clearing debris from drains and grates.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie prepares for rain, flooding concernsSamples added that water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and won't need to be lowered.Staff have also been testing their new pilot water sensors, which will send alerts to select staff if water levels rise."It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming off California and Savona boulevards, said her staff is preparing too."We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared."Collins is no stranger to flooding on California and Savona boulevards. We may have to push them off to next week," Collins said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."For long-term solutions at the intersection, the city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes raising portions of the roadway."When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," Samples said.The drainage project is still in data collection before moving on to design."We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," Collins said. Lucie say students face dangerous conditions walking to school, including busy roads without sidewalks, speeding traffic and poor lighting . The concerns have drawn renewed attention after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School freshman was struck by an SUV while walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on Wednesday, Oct. Much of that stretch of the busy road has no sidewalks. On Southwest Paar Drive near Winslow Street, a sidewalk runs along one side of the road but not the other. Neighbors say children sometimes have to walk or wait for the bus just feet from passing traffic. The roads are over congested. The roads are not safe for the kids, Port St. Lucie resident Paul Virginia said. Neighbors also worry about speeding and limited lighting, particularly for students walking before sunrise. Irene Ange, who lives near Port St. Lucie Boulevard, said her granddaughter takes back roads to walk to school to avoid speeding cars and roadwork. I’m always afraid for them because there are a lot of cars that like to beat the bus, Ange said. She said the city and school district need to work together to better protect students. They deserve to be safe to walk to school, Ange said. "The city, the school district above all, needs to work with all this and have the children's safety and everything in mind." See also: Port St. Lucie residents weigh in on proposed Prima Vista Boulevard safety changes The city’s sidewalk master plan calls for sidewalks within two miles of schools and connections to major roadways. But residents point to sidewalks that end abruptly, including one on Cashmere Boulevard, and roads where sidewalks are available on only one side. "There needs to be more sidewalks for these kids," said Abby Virginia of Port St. Her husband Paul added, "On both sides of the road." The city has additional sidewalk projects scheduled through 2028. Neighbors say safety improvements are needed sooner. "The simple solution to solve the bus issue here is put a four-way stop," Paul Virginia said. An online petition is urging residents to attend the next City Council meeting on October 26 and call for immediate action to better protect students walking to school.

A man was found dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after deputies responded to a reported domestic violence incident Saturday morning in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood. For some people, Common Ground Community Development is a place to learn music or explore the arts. For others, it's a business networking hub, a source of emotional support or even a second home. As Hunger Action Month comes to a close, Feeding South Florida is continuing to raise awareness about food insecurity affecting families and seniors across South Florida.WPTV's monthlong series visited four hunger-relief organizations throughout the region, wrapping up at Feeding Palm Beach County in Boynton Beach, where leaders highlighted the growing need for food assistance and the programs helping vulnerable residents."There are 1.7 million people all the way from Tequesta down to Key West struggling to put food on the table," said Paco Vélez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida. “Now we find ourselves in a situation where prices are soaring, not just for fuel, but also for all the goods and services, especially for food.”Vélez said rising transportation and supply costs continue to increase demand at food distribution sites and partner agencies across South Florida."So many families are coming to us, so many families are coming to our partner agencies," Vélez said.At the organization’s Community Kitchen in Boynton Beach, Susan Taves, culinary director for Feeding South Florida, demonstrated how meals are prepared for seniors throughout the region."We make nutritionally balanced meals for mostly non-ambulatory seniors, and we deliver them frozen," Taves said. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" said Ebony Preston, the mother of the shooting victim. The sheriff’s office began investigating the shooting Wednesday after it happened on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors said they heard three gunshots around 8 p.m. Sheriff's Officials say Preston was armed with a handgun with a 30-clip magazine, which was recovered at the scene of the shooting Wednesday night. And they say Preston was shot and killed by his friend, who shot him from 10 feet away with an AR15 assault rifle. Now, what I gotta do, what? I gotta, like, it's horrible," Ebony Preston said. Preston's stepfather also wants answers. That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," said Rodney Clemon, the victim's stepfather. Sheriff John Budensiek, Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day, and Preston tried to rob his friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Sheriff Budensiek said. The friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend. The second time, the friend and Jarvis Preston--who was armed with a handgun-- got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Sheriff Budensiek explained. Mary’s Medical Center in West Palm Beach and did not survive. Sheriff Budensiek says they have not determined yet if the shooting was self-defense or a murder. The victim's mother says it's devastating. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" Ebony Preston said. See also: Funding for schools in Palm Beach County on your November ballot No one has been arrested. The Sheriff says they're working carefully with the State Attorney's Office to determine if anyone will be charged in this shooting or if it was a case of stand your ground, and if the shooter acted in self-defense. He says the individual who shot Preston attempted to render aid to the victim and remained at the scene following the shooting. The name of the shooter has not been released because the matter is still under investigation.

Protesters gathered in Palm Beach County as part of a nationwide “No Kings” day of action, with local organizers putting a focus on encouraging people to vote early ahead of the November midterm elections.The rally was organized locally by Speaking Up for America - Indivisible. Group leader Susan Foley said Saturday’s demonstration marked the organization’s eighth rally in two years and its fourth No Kings rally.“Today is a special day, our fourth No Kings rally,” Foley said. “This one is special because of its mission to vote early.”WATCH: Palm Beach County ‘No Kings’ rally urges early votingFoley said organizers are encouraging people to cast their ballots early rather than waiting until Election Day.“If you vote early, your vote is locked in,” Foley said.But for protesters who came out Saturday, the rally was also an opportunity to speak about issues they would like to see addressed both nationally and closer to home.WPTV's Christy Waite listened to protesters like Ann Hunter. She says she wants to see more attention paid to the financial challenges facing families.“More consideration to the middle class and people that are in desperate circumstances struggling with their food, healthcare, everyday living expenses,” Hunter said.For Cynthia Heller, a former educator, education funding is among the issues that brought her out.“I was in education, so I would like to see more money go into education,” Heller said.Protesters said events like Saturday’s also give members of the community an opportunity to come together around issues that are important to them.One protester emphasized that regardless of political affiliation, participating in the election is what matters.“I am happy to see people here, and no matter how they vote, they have to vote,” the protester said.Similar demonstrations have taken place across the region, from Palm Beach County to Vero Beach, as protesters continue to make their voices heard ahead of the November elections.

Lucie residents are being asked in a straw poll whether they would support paying more for an additional weekly trash pickup, with the proposal adding at least $131 annually to the residential solid-waste assessment. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Right now, residents receive one garbage pickup per week. The proposed change would increase costs by about $11 per month, with service potentially starting in 2028 if the city moves forward. “This is something that is nonbinding, but it gives City Council an opportunity to get a sense of the will of the people and what they would prefer to see,” said Scott Samples, spokesperson for the city of Port St. The city emphasized that the poll is not a final decision. A "yes" vote would indicate support for the additional cost, while a "no" vote would signal opposition. However, the results will not automatically change the current trash pickup schedule. City Council controls the trash contract and service levels, meaning any changes would require council approval and an updated agreement with the current waste management provider, FCC Environmental Services. The city also noted that a second pickup would be an ongoing expense and could increase with inflation. “City Council would take this up. They would have to work with the vendor to understand what the logistics of that would be. And then, the City Council would then vote on whether or not to move forward with this,” Samples said. The poll aims to provide city leaders with insight into residents' preferences, but the final decision will rest with the City Council. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

Palm Beach County voters now have a new way to check their voter information, find voting locations and track vote-by-mail ballots ahead of the 2026 General Election.Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Wendy Sartory Link announced the launch of the free Vote Palm Beach mobile app ahead of Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3.>> SPECIAL SECTION: More election coverage, early voting locationsThe app is available through the Apple App Store and Google Play Store and is designed to give voters access to election information and services from their phones."Whether you're at home, at work, or on the go, we want to make it as easy as possible for every Palm Beach County voter to access accurate, reliable election information," Link said in a Friday news release.According to the Supervisor of Elections Office, voters can use the app to:Check their voter information and registrationFind voting locationsView election dates and deadlinesTrack a vote-by-mail ballotAccess information directly from the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections Office"With the 2026 General Election approaching, our new mobile app puts another trusted resource right in the palm of your hand," Link said. "It's all about meeting voters where they are and giving them the tools they need to vote with confidence."The Elections Office said the launch follows a recent overhaul of its website and the introduction of the Palm Beach County Voter Dashboard, which also provides access to voter information and election services.The Vote Palm Beach app is available for free through the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.Voters can find additional information at VotePalmBeach.gov or call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 561-656-6200.

A 21-year-old man was fatally shot Wednesday night in the Banner Lake neighborhood of Hobe Sound, and authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident. Martin County sheriff's deputies responded to the scene along Southeast Citrus Way, where they found Jarvis Preston with three gunshot wounds to the chest. "I know you're going to ask me, was it a stand your ground? And the answer is, I don't know right now," Sheriff John Budensiek said. Budensiek explained that Preston and the shooter were friends. Witnesses reported that Preston had been drinking heavily throughout the day and began threatening the shooter and others while armed with a gun. "He's talking, I'm going to shoot you, I'm going to hurt you. The shooter walks towards him, now they're at the edge of the road, at which point the deceased starts to pull out a handgun. The shooter pulls out his AR-15, actually it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest, and he drops right there," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the shooter called 911 and attempted life-saving efforts before Preston was flown to St. Mary’s Hospital, where he died. Preston’s grandmother, Harriet Ford Gregg, said she heard the gunshots and later saw her grandson lying on the ground. "It was Jarvis laying on the ground out there, and the police officer was reviving him," Gregg said. She shared her grief over losing Preston, who lived with her, saying his empty bedroom is now too painful to face. I'm not going in there," Gregg said. A water tank at Jaycee Park has been transformed into a colorful tribute to Florida’s native wildlife thanks to Stuart-born and raised artist Christian Stanley and his wife, Jessica. "We keep an eye on the happenings that are going on here in Fort Pierce and saw that there was an open call to artists and put together a design that we thought was a strong submission and submitted it, and we're fortunately selected to come out here and paint the tank," said Stanley, co-owner of C. The decades-old, 22-foot-tall tank that can hold a million gallons of water is owned by Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. It was once a bright shade of white; now it features colorful paintings of manatees, dolphins, turtles, fish and pelicans, along with a sunset. "The great joy that I get out of being of mural artist is taking stuff from the ocean, from the forest, whatever, and bringing it out to the streets for people to see in a much larger-than-life fashion," he said. "So, when I knew the call was interested in being kind of native Florida wildlife, I knew that we could really bring something together that would be really impactful for the community." On Tuesday, Stanley and his wife traveled from Central Florida to the Treasure Coast to apply a UV clear coat to help protect the artwork against the harsh environment of the shore. The two originally began painting the tank in August, completing the mural within a month. He said they then decided to enter their work into Tnemec Company, Inc.'s 2026 Tank of the Year, not expecting much. But became the only South Florida water tank in the running against dozens across the state and the country. "We're so excited," Stanley said. "I think this is maybe our fourth tank, but yeah, definitely the first project that I've done that's kind of close to my hometown. And we're excited to be back and be a part of it. And it's really cool to be nominated. I hope that we have what it takes to be the winner, but we'll see." Stanley said it’s an honor to have their work recognized nationally, but he takes special pride in seeing it displayed in a place he still calls home: the Treasure Coast. "It's putting Fort Pierce Utilities Authority on the map in a really positive way," said Karyl Bertram, Environmental Laboratory Coordinator at Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. "We're very proud of our drinking water here. And yeah, it's just a really nice, warm feeling to know that we're being recognized for something as beautiful as this." According to Tnemec Company, Inc., one tank will be chosen by the public's vote, while 11 will be chosen by a committee of water tank enthusiasts. The people's choice voting closes on Friday, with the tank of the year expected to be announced next week.

A shooting in the Banner Lake area of Hobe Sound on Wednesday night left one person dead, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies responded to the scene along Southeast Citrus Way and spent hours investigating. Authorities said one person was detained for questioning. Harriet Ford Greg, who said the victim was her grandson, shared that he lived with her. She recalled hearing three gunshots while she was in bed and immediately worrying about him, knowing he was out that night. When she stepped outside, she said she saw him on the ground as first responders tried to save him. " laying on the ground out there and the police officer was reviving him," Greg said. "I thought that he's not going to make it. Somebody shot him." Greg said she is trying to stay strong for her family but admitted she cannot bring herself to walk into the room where her grandson stayed, saying none of this feels real. The sheriff’s office is expected to release more information Thursday afternoon. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Residents along Brooklyn Lane in Lake Worth say their only road in and out of the neighborhood is deteriorating, raising concerns about whether emergency vehicles will be able to reach their homes."You know it's one way in, one way out, so we're in trouble," resident Gerald Hruby said.WATCH: Lake Worth neighbors fear deteriorating private road could cut off emergency accessFor neighbor Doug Rua, a former EMT and police officer, the biggest concern is public safety."I'm concerned about fire trucks being able to maneuver around it or over it, along with ambulances," Rua said. "So it’s really, it’s really a public safety issue."Residents say the problem involves a pipe underneath the road."The road is corroding away because of a hole in the pipe under the road," resident Richard Scott said. "The county won't fix it, and we've had this problem since, uh, 2019."Residents said the worsening conditions have also affected trash collection. They said garbage pickup stopped when the road became too damaged for trucks to safely navigate.WPTV has been following the neighbors’ concerns. During a recent return to Brooklyn Lane, WPTV traffic reporter Johann Hoffend saw county workers assessing the damage and performing temporary work that allowed trash pickup to resume."We reached out to WPTV earlier this month and actually last month, and they’ve really been a help to us," Rua said.But those temporary repairs are already showing signs of deterioration following recent heavy rain.The county has said it cannot repair the road because Brooklyn Lane is private.That leaves residents questioning what a permanent solution might look like and who ultimately bears responsibility for fixing the deteriorating roadway.WPTV reached out to the county about whether there are options to address the damage along Brooklyn Lane. The county said it is looking into the issue.

Lucie community members had a chance to learn more about and comment on proposed safety changes to Prima Vista Boulevard during a county information session at the MidFlorida Credit Union Event Center Thursday. The proposal focuses on the stretch between Aroso Boulevard and U.S. It would replace the center turn lane with a raised median and add landscaping designed to make the road feel narrower and encourage drivers to slow down. A majority of the community members spoke out against the plan, saying they don't believe the changes would improve safety. County officials say the changes are intended to improve safety, reduce crashes, and help slow traffic along the corridor. "We understand it's not popular. That's why we have these," said St. Lucie County engineer Dan Zrallack. "We're taking away the ease of access for people who live along this corridor. There's a lot of driveways. There's a lot of residences that have historically been able to turn directly into their driveway. It's no longer safe to do that. We have to control the traffic so that we have less accidents." County staff estimate the project could cost about $6.1 million dollars, but don't know where that money would come from yet. See also: Jupiter woman sues DoorDash, alleges delivery driver sexually assaulted her County leaders said feedback from the meeting will help shape the project. The proposal is in the early stages. Lucie County still needs to design the roadway, and identify funding sources before any work can move forward. Residents who couldn’t attend the workshop can review plans and submit comments to Christopher.arnold@stlucieco.gov.

hero.headline: 86-Year-Old Found Dead After Car Plunges Into Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach
hero.body:
An 86-year-old man was found dead inside a car pulled from the Indian River Lagoon in Vero Beach after witnesses said the vehicle drove through a fence at a condo complex and into the water. Police have not yet identified the man. Authorities said he had gone missing the night before the car was discovered.

Residents at the condo complex said they knew the driver. Tire marks were visible near the scene where the car breached the fence before entering the lagoon. Police worked for hours to pull the silver Honda CR-V from the water as the investigation got underway.

The crash left a visible mark on the community. Residents on Greytwig Road were later seen cleaning up the parking lot, removing mud and scrubbing away tire marks left behind. Several described the scene as unsettling.

Police have not released the identity of the victim and continue to investigate what led up to the crash. The case remains active as authorities work to determine the circumstances that caused the vehicle to leave the roadway and enter the lagoon.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Man, 60, Dies in Crash With Turning Semi at 66th Avenue
cards.teaser: A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday when his SUV struck a turning semi-trailer at 66th Avenue and 49th Street in Indian River County. The Florida Highway Patrol is investigating the crash as a traffic homicide.
cards.body:
A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday after the SUV he was driving collided with a semi-trailer at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street in Indian River County. According to a Florida Highway Patrol crash report, a 2026 Freightliner truck-tractor pulling a flatbed trailer was turning left from a stop sign on westbound 49th Street when it entered the path of a northbound 2006 Dodge Durango traveling on 66th Avenue. The front of the Durango struck the left side of the trailer.

The Durango driver was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead at 8:02 a.m. His next of kin had not been notified, according to the report.

The 59-year-old Jacksonville man driving the Freightliner reported no injuries.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee in 4-3 Vote
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 to terminate Fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy that included hazing allegations within the department and a no-confidence vote against his leadership. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early.

The board's decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced following allegations that they turned a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and used it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three of the firefighters involved ultimately lost their jobs. Those disciplined firefighters have called Lee's termination retaliation for complaints they had previously filed against district leadership.

Jordon Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, said the board's vote was a positive step for the department as a whole. "I think it was a step in the right direction," Hutchinson said. "I don't think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department."

The board appointed Paul Langel as interim chief following Lee's termination. Langel is a familiar face within the district, bringing 30 years of experience to the role. "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job," Langel said. "Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process." Asked about the possibility that the terminated firefighters could regain their jobs, Langel said, "I believe that there's always scenarios that would unfold and happen. I've got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics."

cards.headline: Red Flag Warning Keeps St. Lucie Beaches Under High Hazard Advisory
cards.teaser: Four to six foot surf and rip current risk prompted St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue to urge swimmers toward lifeguarded beaches like Pepper Park and Waveland Beach.
cards.body:
A red flag warning has put St. Lucie County beaches under a high hazard advisory, with waves between four and six feet crashing along the shoreline at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park on Wednesday. The dangerous surf and rip current risk prompted St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue to urge swimmers to head to lifeguarded beaches such as Pepper Park and Waveland Beach, where officials say red or double red flags will likely keep flying for the next few days.

Fort Pierce Inlet State Park was among several St. Lucie County beaches under the red flag warning, which officials tied to a low pressure system off the eastern United States coast in the mid-Atlantic. Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli described the water conditions bluntly. "The sea was angry today my friends," he said.

The rough surf made for challenging conditions for people in the water. "It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop," foil surfer Lisa Rose said. Surfer Jodi Riley said she only ventured in to her waist rather than bringing her surfboard. "I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like, I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out," Riley said.

Bertucelli said he stayed cautious despite enjoying the waves. "I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else," he said. hero.headline: Veterans Golf Free as Tee It Up for the Troops Debuts at Lost Lake in Hobe Sound

A Veterans Day golf tournament is bringing paying players together with local veterans, who will golf for free, when Tee It Up for the Troops holds its event for the first time at The Club at Lost Lake in Hobe Sound on Wednesday, Nov. 11. Chris LaRocque, president and executive director of Tee It Up for the Troops, said the cause is personal. "It's very close to my heart," LaRocque said in an ARC Florida interview. He said the nonprofit has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that help with the transition to civilian jobs and provide support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries.

The tournament will take place at The Club at Lost Lake, 8300 SE Fazio Drive in Hobe Sound. Registration and event information are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee Without Cause
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 on Thursday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy that included hazing allegations and a no-confidence vote against him. Because Lee was terminated without cause, he is entitled to compensation as his contract ends early.

The board also voted to appoint Paul Langel as interim chief. Langel has 30 years of experience in the district and is a familiar face to its firefighters. "I believe that the fire board moved forward and that was their job," Langel said. "Now my job is going to be to step in and start the healing process."

The board's decision comes two months after five firefighters were displaced over allegations that they turned a bug zapper into a makeshift taser and used it to shock coworkers. Videos appear to show the alleged hazing, and three of the firefighters ultimately lost their jobs. Those firefighters have called their termination retaliation for complaints they previously filed against district leadership. Jordon Hutchinson, one of the terminated firefighters, said of Lee's removal, "I think it was a step in the right direction. I don't think today was about us by any means. I think it was the best thing for the entire department."

Asked whether the three terminated firefighters could get their jobs back, Langel did not rule it out. "I believe that there's always scenarios that would unfold and happen," he said. "I've got to get in and get up to speed on all the specifics." Langel's comments leave open the question of reinstatement as he begins transitioning into the interim chief role.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man, 60, Dies After Semi Turns Into His Path in Indian River County
hero.body:
A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday after the SUV he was driving collided with a semi-trailer at an Indian River County intersection. The Florida Highway Patrol said a 2026 Freightliner truck-tractor pulling a flatbed trailer was turning left from a stop sign on westbound 49th Street when it entered the path of a northbound 2006 Dodge Durango traveling on 66th Avenue. The Durango driver was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead at 8:02 a.m. His next of kin had not been notified, according to the crash report.

The 59-year-old Jacksonville man driving the Freightliner reported no injuries.

hero.headline: Martin County Commission Approves School Zone for Citrus Grove Elementary
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners have unanimously approved a new school zone on Southwest Newfield Parkway outside Citrus Grove Elementary School, answering years of safety concerns from parents who say the current 45 mph speed limit puts children at risk. Many families who live in the Canopy Creek community across the street from the school walk their children to class each morning and afternoon, crossing the busy roadway.

Kelly Ribaudo, the school's PTA president and Martin County PTA Advocacy Chair, said she has spent the last five years asking the county to install a school zone. "We've had so many near misses with the kids just from people not paying attention," Ribaudo said. "Everyone has a right to a free and public education and they should be safe getting there. Our main priority should be the kids not the traffic." Parent Kendall George said the current traffic conditions frighten her. "It scares me," George said. "These cars are driving 45 miles an hour plus."

At a previous Martin County Commission meeting, commissioners sided with the parents. "Whatever the number is there is no price to someone getting hurt," Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "You will absolutely get a school zone." School Principal Rose Rynca said the need has grown as new communities bring more students to the area. "The amount of students crossing Newfield Parkway has definitely increased," Rynca said. "This speed zone is going to really really improve the safety of students." George said a school zone sign will help alert drivers. "It's letting drivers know that, hey there's a school here, there's children crossing, and we have to slow down," George said.

A timeline for when the school zone will actually go in on Southwest Newfield Parkway has not been pinned down by the county. Until then, Ribaudo is urging drivers to use caution near the school regardless of posted signage. "Slow down if you see a school, even if there's not a school zone sign, slow down," Ribaudo said. With the school zone approved, parents say their next priority is pushing the county for better street lighting along the corridor.

A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday after a semi-truck turned into the path of his SUV in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street.

Troopers said a Freightliner semi-truck was attempting a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue when it entered the path of a northbound Dodge Durango traveling in the inside lane. The Durango driver was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m. The Freightliner's driver, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation by FHP.
