hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Chief Jeff Lee Terminated; Deputy Chief Langel Named Interim
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District board voted Wednesday to terminate Fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, ending his tenure after months of turmoil over a hazing investigation and mounting criticism of district leadership. Lee did not attend the heated meeting where commissioners made the decision.

In a statement issued Thursday to a reporter, Lee pointed to improvements he said he delivered during his time leading the district. The Fire District itself noted in an October 9 statement that from 2023 to 2026 the district saw approximately 19% average pay-plan growth, an increase of about 100 uniformed personnel, and improved minimum engine staffing from two to three firefighters. The district also said it expanded employee benefits, increased retirement-health contributions, and invested in additional training, equipment and facilities. "That's really all I have to say," Lee told the reporter.

Lee's exit follows fallout from videos showing probationary firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper, conduct a third-party investigator concluded amounted to hazing. Three veteran firefighters were fired after that investigation, sparking backlash from firefighters, their families and community members who said the punishment was too harsh. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they lost their reputation," one speaker told the board Wednesday. Lee's departure also came after the firefighters union delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership, though board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner Jamie Fowler said that vote was not the sole reason for his removal. "At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy," Fowler said. "It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect." Lee had previously signaled in a letter to the board that his time as chief could be ending, writing that the position "requires confidence" and raising the possibility of a mutually agreeable retirement.

Deputy Chief Paul Langel has been appointed interim fire chief while the district searches for a permanent replacement. "Personally, I don't think there is a culture problem," Langel said, adding he plans to visit fire stations and talk with employees individually and in groups to assess morale before deciding on next steps. Commissioners plan to hire a headhunter to search for a permanent chief both inside and outside the district, according to Fowler. The district and firefighters union are expected to keep discussing possible reinstatement of the three fired firefighters, with union representative Ryan Sapp saying he is eager to see the sides "come back together." The board is also working with an outside law firm to overhaul complaint policies after a September 30 meeting identified what members called "a significant gap" in existing procedures. Commissioner James Clasby said Lee's contract terms could leave taxpayers responsible for more than $350,000 in severance, and he wants the next chief's contract written to avoid similar terms. "That's the consequences of firing somebody with those terms," Clasby said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Nuclear Plant Marks 50 Years as NRC Grants 20-Year License Extension
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant, which supplies 11 percent of Florida Power & Light's power, celebrates five decades of operation after federal regulators approved another 20 years of licensing.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Nuclear Power Plant is marking 50 years of operation this year, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has granted licenses allowing the facility to keep running for another 20 years. The plant provides 11 percent of Florida Power & Light's total power generation. News crews were given rare access inside the facility to see how it operates and to speak with the employees who keep it running.

Carlos Santos, site vice president, explained the basic process behind the plant's power generation. "The simplest way to put it is the reactor creates the heat," Santos said. That heat comes from nuclear fission involving uranium pellets stacked into rods inside the plant's two reactor units. The heat from the rods builds up and produces steam, which flows into a secondary closed system to a turbine that generates power sent out to the electrical grid.

In August, the plant was manually shut down after three control rods dropped into the reactor core. Florida Power & Light said at the time there was no danger to staff or the public and that no customers lost power as a result.

Over five decades, technology at the plant has transformed how employees do their jobs. Nicholas Negron, associate innovation specialist, demonstrated a robotic dog named Tritium, part of a fleet of robots named after nuclear isotopes. "We're utilizing the robot to go in and out of high radiation areas, increasing efficiency both around our heavy machinery and around the plant," Negron said. The plant also uses submersibles and drones to inspect equipment. "Not only does that increase a lot of the time saving, but it's also substantial cost savings for potential materials," Negron said.

Alfred Phillips, a digital INC specialist who has worked at the plant for nearly 20 years, calibrates equipment used to maintain the systems that control the reactor, ensuring everything meets government standards and accuracy requirements. "You have million-dollar homes right down the street. We're here, but yet we're still invisible because what we do, we do it well," Phillips said. His son, Alfred Sinclair Phillips, followed him into the industry and now works in the plant's operations department. "There's a pressure with it, but there's also a sense of pride," the younger Phillips said. "Knowing that my dad has worked his butt off and he's left an impact with the people here on his work to make this place better." The elder Phillips said he takes pride in the responsibility of his daily work. "You think about all the things in life you can be doing and this is good," he said.

hero.headline: Veterans Day Golf Fundraiser Comes to Hobe Sound's Lost Lake Club
hero.body:
Tee It Up for the Troops will bring its Veterans Day golf fundraiser to The Club at Lost Lake in Hobe Sound for the first time this year. The tournament is scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 11, at the club, located at 8300 SE Fazio Drive. The field is capped at 106 golfers, with registration priced at $750 per player, and local veterans paired into foursomes will play for free.

Chris LaRocque, president and executive director of Tee It Up for the Troops, said the cause is personal. "It's very close to my heart," LaRocque said in an interview with ARC Florida. "I'm an Army Reserve major myself." LaRocque said the nonprofit has deployed more than $20 million and supported more than 400,000 veterans through programs that help with the transition to civilian jobs and provide support for post-traumatic stress disorder and traumatic brain injuries.

Proceeds from the Hobe Sound tournament will also benefit local veterans programs, including PGA HOPE in South Florida, according to LaRocque. PGA HOPE introduces veterans and active-duty service members to golf as a way to support their physical, mental, social and emotional well-being.

Registration and event information for the tournament are available through Tee It Up for the Troops.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man Dies After Semi-Truck Turns Into His SUV in Indian River County
hero.body:
A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday morning after a semi-truck turned into the path of his SUV at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.

The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. when a Freightliner semi-truck attempted a left turn from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. A Dodge Durango was traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at the intersection, when the semi-truck entered its path. The front of the Durango struck the left side of the semi-trailer, and both vehicles came to rest at the scene.

The Durango driver was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m. The Freightliner driver, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation.

cards.headline: Prosecutors Drop Child Abuse Case Against Indian River County Bus Driver
cards.teaser: The State Attorney's Office declined to file charges against a Sebastian school bus driver accused of grabbing and threatening to break a student's finger. The decision closes a case that began with an August surveillance video from a school bus.
cards.body:
Prosecutors have dropped the child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver accused of grabbing a student and threatening to break the child's finger. The State Attorney's Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document.

Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance video from a school bus. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. According to an arrest affidavit, the video was recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m. and showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club.

Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat, and Alpy was seen walking through the aisle to direct the student to sit down. The affidavit said the student also appeared to repeatedly raise a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student's seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student stood up again and turned around to interact with other children. The affidavit said Alpy repeatedly told the student to sit down, and when the child did not comply, she pulled the bus over, left the driver's seat and approached the student.

Investigators alleged Alpy grabbed the child, forced the child back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. The affidavit said the child's middle finger was extended toward Alpy at the time. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student's hand, forced it into the child's lap and asked, "Do you want me to break this finger?" The student later told investigators that Alpy grabbed and bent back the child's middle finger and said she was going to break it off. The child said they were afraid during the encounter, according to the affidavit. With the no information filing, the case against Alpy is now closed.

cards.headline: Police Now Say Two Vehicles Struck Man in Port St. Lucie Hit-and-Run
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police initially believed one car struck a 63-year-old man on Oct. 9, but investigators now say a second vehicle may have also hit him, and they have released images asking for help identifying both.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police are now investigating whether two vehicles, not one, struck a 63-year-old man in a hit-and-run crash earlier this month, and they have released images of both vehicles asking for the public's help identifying them. The crash happened Oct. 9 at approximately 12:56 a.m. near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard. The victim, a Port St. Lucie resident, was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries.

In an earlier update on the investigation, police said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, they developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved.

Detectives now believe the man may have been hit by two separate vehicles, one traveling northbound and the other traveling southbound at the time of the crash. Police are working to identify both vehicles and their drivers and have released images of the vehicles to help with that effort.

Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area at the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee, Names Langel Interim Chief
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy over a hazing investigation and a scathing no-confidence vote from the firefighters' union. The board then voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement.

The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged commissioners to change the district's leadership. Taylor Baldwin pointed to dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. "Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." A resident named Katie was more critical of the board itself. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," she said.

The controversy began this summer after a hazing investigation led the district to fire three veteran firefighters and suspend two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is now pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. The dispute escalated further when IAFF Local 1377 released results of a no-confidence vote earlier this month. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated, and Lee received 314 no-confidence votes against 108 confidence votes, meaning 74.23% of participants said they no longer trusted his leadership.

Lee joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023. He was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before ultimately choosing to terminate him without cause, which triggers severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported the removal, said the decision gives the district a chance at a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." The board is moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing how it will select the district's next permanent chief. The board faced a similar decision in 2017, when it accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement after a prior union no-confidence vote and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man Killed in Crash With Semi at 66th Ave and 49th St
hero.body:
A 60-year-old Vero Beach man died Thursday after his SUV collided with a semi-truck at the intersection of 66th Avenue and 49th Street in unincorporated Indian River County, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.

The crash happened around 6:45 a.m. when a Freightliner semi-truck attempted to turn left from a stop sign at westbound 49th Street onto 66th Avenue. Troopers said the truck entered the path of a Dodge Durango traveling north in the inside lane of 66th Avenue, which had no traffic controls at that point. The front of the Durango struck the left side of the semi-trailer, and both vehicles came to rest at the scene.

The Durango driver was taken to Health First's Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 a.m. The semi-truck driver, a 59-year-old Jacksonville man, was not injured. The crash remains under investigation.

cards.headline: Prosecutors Drop Child Abuse Case Against Sebastian School Bus Driver
cards.teaser: The State Attorney's Office quietly dropped the child abuse charge against Indian River County school bus driver Tracy Marie Alpy, who was arrested in September after surveillance video showed her threatening to break a student's finger.
cards.body:
Prosecutors have dropped the child abuse case against an Indian River County school bus driver who was arrested after surveillance video showed her grabbing a student's hand and threatening to break the child's finger. The State Attorney's Office filed a no information in the case against Tracy Marie Alpy on Oct. 5, according to a court document.

Alpy, 65, of Sebastian, was arrested Sept. 10 after investigators reviewed surveillance footage from her school bus. The alleged incident happened Aug. 24 as the bus was transporting students to after-school care. According to an arrest affidavit, the video was recorded from 3:44 to 4:31 p.m. and showed the bus waiting at Liberty Magnet School for another bus to exchange children headed to the Gifford Youth Aquatic Center and the Boys & Girls Club.

Investigators said a student seated near the front of the bus repeatedly got out of the seat, and Alpy walked through the aisle directing the child to sit down. The affidavit said the student also repeatedly raised a middle finger toward Alpy when her back was turned. About 15 minutes into the video, Alpy sat on the edge of the student's seat to keep the child from getting up, investigators said. After more children boarded and the bus began moving, the student stood up again and turned around to interact with other children.

Investigators alleged Alpy grabbed the child, forced the student back into the seat and fastened the seat belt. The affidavit said the child's middle finger was extended toward Alpy at the time. Investigators said Alpy then grabbed the student's hand, forced it into the child's lap and asked, 'Do you want me to break this finger?' The student later told investigators that Alpy grabbed and bent back the child's middle finger and said she was going to break it off, and the child said they were afraid during the encounter, according to the affidavit. The case is now closed after the state's decision not to file formal charges.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee, Names Interim Leader
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy that included a hazing scandal and a firefighters' union no-confidence vote. The board also voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement.

The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged commissioners to change the district's leadership. Dozens of supporters wore yellow shirts throughout the room. Taylor Baldwin pointed to the crowd and told commissioners, "Look at everyone wearing yellow. These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." A resident identified as Katie told the board, "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve."

The controversy began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. The dispute escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377, in which 423 of the union's 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes against 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants saying they no longer had confidence in his leadership.

Lee was not present for Wednesday's meeting. He joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before voting to terminate him without cause, which triggers the severance provisions in his contract. Board member James Clasby said after the vote, "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance. We will only pay what we are legally required to." Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported the removal, said, "I feel like a weight is lifted. Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing the process for selecting the district's next permanent chief. In 2017, following a similar union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee, Names Paul Langel Interim Chief
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy over a hazing scandal and a union no-confidence vote. The board's vote triggers severance provisions in Lee's contract, though the final payout has not been set. Following the termination, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search begins for a permanent replacement.

Wednesday's meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged the board to change the district's leadership. Taylor Baldwin pointed to dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. "Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." A resident identified only as Katie told the board its members had failed the public. "You participated in this cover-up," Katie said. "You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve."

The controversy began this summer after a district hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. The dispute escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. The union said 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated, with Lee receiving 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, meaning 74.23% of participants said they no longer had confidence in his leadership.

Lee joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023. He was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before settling on termination without cause. Board member James Clasby said afterward that the severance total still needs to be determined. "We will only pay what we are legally required to," Clasby said. Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported the removal, said the district needed a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." The board is also moving to hire outside legal counsel and is discussing the process for selecting the district's next permanent chief. In 2017, the board faced a similar situation after a union no-confidence vote and accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement, paying him severance through the end of his contract.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Mayor's Race and Trash Pickup Question Head to Voters
cards.teaser: Early voting is underway in Port St. Lucie, where incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steven Giordano in a bitter race that also includes a non-binding ballot question on twice-weekly trash pickup.
cards.body:
Early voting began this week in St. Lucie County, giving residents their first chance to cast ballots in a Port St. Lucie mayoral race that has turned into one of the city's most contentious in recent memory. Incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin is running for another term and says the city should stay on its current path, pointing to infrastructure repairs, including roadwork, as evidence her administration is delivering results. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, argues that City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday residents. When asked what he would change, Giordano also focused on roadwork, saying the city needs a new traffic study.

At a polling location on Rosser Blvd on the first day of early voting, campaign tents for both candidates stood side by side, reflecting the sharp divide between them. Mayors in Port St. Lucie serve four-year terms and hold significant power under the city's mayor-council form of government, making this race a pivotal one for the city's direction. Candidates for mayor do not run under a political party label.

The ballot also includes a non-binding question asking voters whether Port St. Lucie should move to twice-a-week trash collection. FCC is the company that currently handles garbage pickup in the city, and switching to a second collection day would cost residents more than a hundred dollars a year in added fees. The question will not force any change on its own. City council members can choose to act on the results or disregard them entirely.

The trash issue has drawn heated reactions at recent city council meetings, where residents have criticized the current service as inadequate and pushed for an additional pickup day each week. Despite that frustration, residents approached about the issue on the first day of early voting said they would rather keep the current single pickup schedule. Resident Rob Buske summed up that sentiment, saying, "I don't want to pay for something I don't need." With the election less than two weeks away, Port St. Lucie voters are weighing both who should lead the city and how their trash gets picked up, two questions that have proven just as personal as they are practical.

The incumbent, Shannon Martin, is running to stay in office, and she says the city needs to stay on its current course. She points to how she has prioritized infrastructure repairs, like roadwork, as a reason to keep her in City Hall. Her opponent, Steven Giordano, says City Hall is corrupt and has lost touch with everyday people. When pressed on specific things he’d do differently-- he also wanted to talk about roadwork and says the city needs a new traffic study. cards.headline: Red Flag Warnings, 4-6 Foot Surf Keep St. Lucie Beaches on High Hazard Alert
cards.teaser: Dangerous surf and rip current risk are prompting St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue to urge swimmers toward lifeguarded beaches like Pepper Park and Waveland Beach.
cards.body:
A red flag warning was in effect this week at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park and other St. Lucie County beaches, where waves between four and six feet crashed along the shoreline Wednesday. The high hazard conditions are tied to a low pressure system sitting off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic.

St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says the rough surf makes it more important than ever for swimmers to stick to lifeguarded beaches, pointing specifically to Pepper Park and Waveland Beach. Officials say both locations will likely be flying red or double red flags over the next few days as the hazardous conditions continue.

The county warns that rip currents are possible in these conditions. Ocean Rescue advises anyone caught in a rip current not to panic and to swim parallel to the shoreline until free of the current.

The choppy water has still drawn surfers into the waves. Foil surfer Lisa Rose described the challenge of the conditions. "It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop," she said. Surfer Jodi Riley said she only went in as far as her waist. "I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like, I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out," Riley said. Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli also ventured into the water but kept his distance from the deeper surf. "I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else," Bertucelli said. Describing the sea itself, Bertucelli added, "The sea was angry today my friends."

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee Without Cause
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy that included a hazing investigation and a union no-confidence vote against his leadership. The vote came after an emotional public meeting packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged commissioners to change the district's leadership.

The controversy began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is now pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. The dispute escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377, in which 423 of the union's 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants saying they no longer had confidence in his leadership.

At Wednesday's meeting, speakers including Taylor Baldwin pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts in the room. "Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." Another resident, identified only as Katie, criticized the board's handling of the matter, telling commissioners, "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve." Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for the meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before voting to terminate him without cause, which triggers severance provisions in his contract. Board member James Clasby said the final severance amount still needs to be determined. "We will only pay what we are legally required to," Clasby said.

Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported Lee's removal, said the district needs a fresh start. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." Following the termination vote, the board voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while a search for a permanent replacement begins. The board is also moving to hire outside legal counsel and is discussing the process for selecting the district's next chief. The situation echoes 2017, when the board accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's retirement after a separate union no-confidence vote and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

Port St. Lucie Police detectives now believe two separate vehicles struck a 63-year-old man during a hit-and-run crash on Oct. 9, revising their earlier theory that only one vehicle was involved. The crash happened near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard at approximately 12:56 a.m., leaving the victim, a Port St. Lucie resident, unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries.

Investigators initially said surveillance video from a nearby business captured a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and footage, they developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash.

Port St. Lucie Police are asking anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area at the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area to contact the department at 772-871-5000.

cards.headline: Red Flag Warnings, 4-6 Foot Surf Keep St. Lucie County Beaches on High Hazard Alert
cards.teaser: Dangerous rip currents and choppy surf are prompting red flag warnings at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park and other St. Lucie County beaches, with officials urging swimmers to stick to lifeguarded shorelines for the next few days.
cards.body:
A red flag warning is cautioning swimmers about dangerous surf conditions at Fort Pierce Inlet State Park, where waves between four and six feet were crashing along the shoreline Wednesday. The park is among several beaches in St. Lucie County under a red flag high hazard warning, with conditions tied to a low pressure system off the eastern U.S. coast in the mid-Atlantic.

St. Lucie County Ocean Rescue says the rough conditions make it more important than ever for beachgoers to swim at a lifeguarded beach. Officials pointed to Pepper Park and Waveland Beach, where red or double red flags are expected to fly for the next few days. The county says rip currents are possible in these conditions, and Ocean Rescue advises anyone caught in one not to panic and to swim parallel to the shoreline until free of the current.

Fort Pierce resident Lee Bertucelli described the rough water firsthand. "The sea was angry today my friends," Bertucelli said. He said he ventured into the water but kept close to shore. "I went in, you know, not too far. The waves were fun, but again not too far, didn't want to deal with rip tides or anything else," Bertucelli said.

Other beachgoers echoed concerns about the choppy surf. Foil surfer Lisa Rose said the wind made the conditions difficult to navigate. "It was very windy and very choppy and it's really challenging because you have to negotiate all of the chop," Rose said. Surfer Jodi Riley said she only waded in partway because of the risk. "I went in, not with my surfboard, but like, to my waist and it's just, it's rough and it's just not super safe for like, I'm sort of a beginner so not safe for me, but like, some of the other surfers have definitely been out," Riley said.

hero.headline: PSL Police Now Seek Two Vehicles in Hit-and-Run That Injured Man
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police are now looking for two vehicles in connection with an Oct. 9 hit-and-run crash that left a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie man seriously injured. Detectives believe the victim may have been struck by two separate vehicles near the intersection of Northwest University Boulevard and Northwest California Boulevard, one traveling northbound and the other southbound at the time of the crash.

The crash happened at approximately 12:56 a.m. The victim was found unconscious in the roadway suffering from severe head injuries.

Police previously said surveillance video from a nearby business captured the incident and showed what investigators believed to be a white four-door sedan striking the man before leaving the scene without stopping. As detectives continued reviewing evidence and surveillance footage, they developed information indicating a second vehicle may also have been involved in the crash.

Investigators have released images of both vehicles and are asking for the public's help identifying them and their drivers. Anyone who recognizes either vehicle, was in the area at the time of the crash, witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or surveillance video from the area is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Murder of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves at Florida State Prison on Tuesday evening, 40 years after he killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday after the Florida Supreme Court had already rejected his last state appeals.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution on behalf of his agency and Raczkoski's family. Flowers said Raczkoski's brother was expected to be among the witnesses and had told him that Christmas was never the same for their family after Richard was killed. Twenty-nine people were in the execution room, including 16 spectators made up of eight men and eight women. When asked for any final words, Reaves said, "No, I do not." A doctor checked him with a stethoscope and flashlight before he was pronounced dead and the curtain dropped. The Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, a friend and his spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice.

According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the convenience store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. Raczkoski's son was born after his father's death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, telling them he had been using cocaine. According to a transcript filed by the state, he said, "I've never met a finer officer in my life."

Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant in September and denied clemency the same day. Reaves' attorneys fought the execution to the end, arguing in court filings that he was a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he had been shut out of the clemency process.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Fire Board votes to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate the contract of Fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of turmoil over a hazing investigation at Station 1A. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member Jamie Fowler said the decision was not about one single action by Lee. "At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore," Fowler said.

The termination follows a union confidence vote in which more than 74% of participating firefighters said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same about Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol. That vote came after an investigation into videos showing firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to shock three apprentice firefighters on duty in 2024, dumping water on two firefighters, and placing a dead raccoon inside a fire vehicle. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, and veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired as a result. The three have disputed that characterization, describing the incidents as consensual pranks. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias added.

The firings of Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin drew community backlash, and supporters packed the Fire Administration building Wednesday wearing shirts and holding signs on their behalf. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," one public commentator said. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby said the vote to remove Lee reflected that same sentiment. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," Clasby said. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure might be ending, writing in a letter to the board that it may be time to consider a "mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition" because "the position of fire chief requires confidence." Fire Board member Travis Leonard said that letter prompted him to make the motion to fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," Leonard said.

After the vote, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief, and the district plans to hire a recruiter to search for Lee's permanent replacement. "I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we've been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust," Langel said. Lee's severance package is expected to total about $350,000. The firefighters union continues negotiating with the district to try to reinstate the three fired veteran firefighters. Union representative Ryan Sapp called Lee's termination a "positive step forward." "I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp said. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local, glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a new district attorney after Sabol submitted her notice of retirement amid the controversy.

The meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many urged the board to change the district's leadership. Among them was Taylor Baldwin, who pointed to the dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." The decision marks the latest development in a controversy that began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others . The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union have argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated . The issue later escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants voting they no longer had confidence in his leadership. Several speakers criticized both district leadership and the board's handling of the controversy. "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve," another resident Katie told the board. Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Ultimately, the board voted to terminate him without cause, triggering the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Mayor's Race and Trash Pickup Question Head to Voters
cards.teaser: Incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steven Giordano as early voting continues, while a non-binding ballot question asks residents whether the city should switch to twice-a-week trash collection.
cards.body:
Early voting is underway in Port St. Lucie's mayoral election, pitting incumbent Shannon Martin against challenger Steven Giordano, with the election less than two weeks away. Voters are also weighing in on a non-binding ballot question asking whether the city should move to twice-a-week trash pickup.

On the first day of early voting, campaign tents for both mayoral candidates stood side by side at a polling location on Rosser Blvd. Martin is running to keep her seat and says the city should stay on its current course, pointing to infrastructure work such as roadwork as a reason voters should keep her in City Hall. Giordano says City Hall has become corrupt and lost touch with everyday residents. When asked what he would do differently, he also focused on roadwork, saying the city needs a new traffic study. Port St. Lucie's mayor serves a four-year term and holds significant influence under the city's mayor-council form of government. Candidates for mayor do not run with party affiliation.

Trash collection has also become a flashpoint in the city, which contracts with FCC for garbage service. At recent city council meetings, residents have criticized the quality of pickup and demanded an additional collection day each week. But on the first day of early voting, people interviewed at the polls said they would rather keep the current schedule. Resident Rob Buske summed up that sentiment, saying, "I don't want to pay for something I don't need." A second weekly pickup day would cost residents more than $100 a year.

The ballot question on trash service is non-binding, meaning it serves only as a poll of resident opinion. City council members are not required to act on the results regardless of how residents vote. Like the mayoral race, the trash question carries no party affiliation, leaving voters to settle both the city's leadership and its collection schedule on the same ballot.

A second pick-up day would cost residents more than a hundred bucks a year, but some are adamant it's necessary. As this story comes to air and online, the election is less than 2 weeks away. When can my garbage go to the curb? Who will be in charge of the city and what's their vision? The people are about to decide.

hero.headline: Martin County Panel to Review Witham Field Nighttime Jet Noise Data
hero.body:
Martin County's Airport Noise Advisory Committee is scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. Thursday at Witham Field's Airport Administration Building to review nighttime flight activity and discuss noise concerns raised by residents near the airport. The committee advises the county on airport noise issues and possible mitigation measures, but it does not have authority to set airport rules on its own.

Witham Field recorded 7,474 takeoffs and landings in September, including 1,224 jet operations. Of those jet operations, 258 took place during the airport's voluntary nighttime curfew, which begins at 11 p.m. The airport reported a 96.55% compliance rate with the curfew for the month.

Residents near the airport have said private jet traffic increases when the Federal Aviation Administration imposes flight restrictions over Palm Beach County during President Donald Trump's visits to Mar-a-Lago, pushing more aircraft toward Witham Field and affecting their quality of life. Thursday's meeting agenda does not include a proposal to change the voluntary curfew or a vote on airport rules, so any action on those fronts is not expected at this meeting.

The committee is also scheduled to receive an update on the Residential Sound Insulation Program, which is designed to reduce aircraft noise inside eligible homes located near the airport. The meeting comes as county officials continue to track nighttime flight patterns and respond to ongoing complaints from residents who live under the airport's flight paths. This is a developing story.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee in 4-3 Vote
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board voted 4-3 Wednesday to fire Chief Jeff Lee without cause, capping months of controversy over the department's leadership and coming less than two weeks after the firefighters' union released results of a no-confidence vote against him. The board also voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim chief while it searches for a permanent replacement.

Wednesday's meeting was packed with firefighters, union members, retirees and residents, many of whom urged the board to change the district's leadership. Taylor Baldwin pointed to dozens of supporters wearing yellow shirts throughout the room. "Look at everyone wearing yellow," Baldwin told commissioners. "These are not people who want to see the fire district fail. These are people who love this department enough to stand up and beg you to save it." Another resident, identified only as Katie, told the board, "You participated in this cover-up. You protected the lies and you profoundly failed the people you are elected to serve."

The controversy began this summer after a hazing investigation led to the firing of three veteran firefighters and the suspension of two others. The district determined the conduct amounted to hazing, while the firefighters and their union argued it was consensual horseplay. A Fort Pierce Police Department investigation found no criminal violations, and the union is now pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. The dispute escalated into a no-confidence vote organized by IAFF Local 1377, in which 423 of the union's 517 dues-paying members participated. Lee received 314 no-confidence votes and 108 confidence votes, with 74.23% of participants saying they no longer had confidence in his leadership.

Lee, who joined the department in 1997 after serving in the U.S. Navy and became the district's 14th fire chief in May 2023, was not present for Wednesday's meeting. Commissioners spent more than 30 minutes debating whether to fire him with or without cause before voting to terminate him without cause, which triggers the severance provisions in his contract. "I think we still have to come to the determination of what exactly the final total is of the severance," board member James Clasby said after the vote. "We will only pay what we are legally required to." Commissioner Jamie Fowler, who supported the removal, said the decision marks a fresh start for the district. "I feel like a weight is lifted," Fowler said. "Firing someone is never an easy decision, regardless of all the factors that come into play. So I feel like we've sort of taken a step in the right direction." The board is also moving forward with hiring outside legal counsel and discussing how it will select the district's next permanent chief. In 2017, following a similar union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Lee, Faces $350K Severance and Leadership Crisis
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Fire Board voted to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause following a hazing scandal, a move expected to cost the district about $350,000 in severance. The firing comes amid near-unanimous no-confidence votes against other top officials and an ongoing union fight to reinstate three fired firefighters.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause, a decision expected to cost the district about $350,000 in severance. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that has roiled the district for months and comes alongside near-unanimous no-confidence numbers against other top leaders.

St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member Jamie Fowler said the move was about restoring order to the district rather than any single decision by Lee. "At the end of the day, it's gotten very messy. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore," Fowler said. A union vote last week found more than 74% of participating firefighters had no confidence in Lee, while about 92% said the same about Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez and 97% said the same about District Attorney Kim Sabol. Sabol has submitted her notice of retirement amid the controversy, and the Fire Board is now searching for her replacement as well as a permanent successor to Lee.

The turmoil traces back to an investigation into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A, where a modified bug zapper was used to shock three apprentice firefighters on duty in 2024, water was dumped on two firefighters, and a dead raccoon was placed inside a fire vehicle. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, leading to the firings of veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin. The three have disputed that characterization, describing the incidents as consensual pranks. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias added. Their firings drew significant community backlash, and supporters packed the Fire Administration building Wednesday holding signs and wearing shirts backing the three men. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby said the vote reflected a clear desire for new leadership. "There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," Clasby said.

Lee had signaled his departure was possible, writing in a letter to the board that it may be time to consider a "mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition" because "the position of fire chief requires confidence." Fire Board member Travis Leonard said that letter prompted him to move for termination, comparing it to resignations he has handled in the private sector. The board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief and plans to hire a recruiter to find Lee's permanent replacement. "I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we've been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust," Langel said. The firefighters union continues to negotiate with the district to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. Union representative Ryan Sapp called Lee's termination "a positive step forward" and said he hopes the district can move toward a "level field" going forward.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Man Arrested After Indecent Exposure Reports on Seaway Bridge
cards.body:
A 27-year-old Fort Pierce man was arrested Friday after police say he exposed himself in multiple incidents involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge. Kyle Kennedy now faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation following an investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department.

Investigators reviewed previous reports of indecent exposure on the bridge and identified patterns linking the incidents, according to police. Detectives then interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups as part of the investigation. Two victims positively identified Kennedy as the suspect during those lineups, leading to his arrest.

The reports rattled some residents who regularly use the bridge. "It's just crazy to know that there's something like that going on," said Leidi Cruz of Fort Pierce. "I've never had any experience like that. We walk here regularly and we've never had any issues."

Fort Pierce Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity on the bridge or has information about the incidents to come forward. Tips can be called in to the FPPD at 772-467-6800, and anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, was executed Tuesday for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski, closing a case that stretched across four decades for the Vero Beach community and the sheriff's office. Reaves was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke.

Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed that call from a payphone outside the store. While the two spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts. They struggled over the weapon, and Reaves regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. Raczkowski died from his wounds.

Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting, but the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and his subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected his final appeal Tuesday afternoon without comment, and the Florida Supreme Court had rejected his appeals to spare his life the week before. His attorneys had challenged Florida's lethal injection method and argued that jurors who recommended his death sentence were never told the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled due to post-traumatic stress disorder from his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent Gov. Ron DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.

When asked if he had a last statement, Reaves said, "No, I do not." The injection began immediately afterward. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several deep breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the execution team warden shook his shoulders and called his name, but there was no response. A medic entered the chamber to check for signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.

Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, as the state continues to far outpace the rest of the country in executions under DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms. DeSantis has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims' families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. Florida set a state record with 19 executions last year and would tie that mark if another scheduled for next month is carried out. Jesse Guardado, 64, convicted of robbing and killing a woman in 2004, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida in November.

All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Fires Chief Jeff Lee, Names Interim Chief
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire Board voted Wednesday to terminate Fire Chief Jeff Lee's contract without cause, a move expected to cost the district about $350,000 in severance. The board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief and plans to hire a recruiter to search for Lee's permanent replacement.

The termination is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that began earlier this year after videos surfaced showing firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to shock three apprentice firefighters on duty in 2024. Other videos showed water dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, and veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired as a result, though they disputed that characterization and described the incidents as consensual pranks. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias added.

Those firings sparked backlash from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom said the punishment was too harsh. More than 74% of firefighters who took part in a union vote said they had no confidence in Lee, while about 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez and 97% said the same of District Attorney Kim Sabol. At Wednesday's meeting, supporters of the three fired firefighters packed the Fire Administration building, some holding signs or wearing shirts in their support. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," one public commentator said. Another said, "We need to restore faith in this fire district."

St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member Jamie Fowler said the situation had become too messy for Lee to remain effective. "It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore," Fowler said. Fire Board member Travis Leonard said a recent letter from Lee suggesting a "mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition" prompted him to move for termination. Fire Board member James Clasby said the vote reflected a clear desire for new leadership. Interim Chief Langel said he wants to begin healing the district and restoring trust. The firefighters union is continuing negotiations with the district to try to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin, and union representative Ryan Sapp called Lee's termination a positive step forward. The Fire Board is also searching for a new district attorney after Sabol submitted her notice of retirement amid the controversy.

hero.headline: Florida Senate President Albritton Now Opposes Amendment 3
hero.body:
Florida Senate President Ben Albritton says he will vote against Amendment 3 in November, months after the State Senate voted to place the measure on the ballot. Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption for Florida homeowners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and would cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes. The measure needs 60% voter approval on Election Day to become law.

Albritton announced his opposition in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. "As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart," Albritton said. "Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure."

Albritton pointed to the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission as a better avenue for change, calling it "an ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced."

Cities and counties across Florida stand to lose significant revenue if the amendment passes. Local leaders have warned it could force budget cuts, reduce services, and push governments to find other sources of revenue.

hero.headline: More Than 100 Rescued Cats Recovering as PSL Police Weigh Charges
hero.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens removed from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are recovering at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, where Port St. Lucie police are still deciding whether to file criminal charges against the owner. Animal Control pulled the animals from the property over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said many of the cats arrived in poor health. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," she said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. Wees said staff are struggling to sort out which kittens belong to which mothers. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was contacted by Wees and arrived on site by Thursday morning. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. She said the effort is already paying off, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said.

Port St. Lucie police continue to monitor the case as they determine whether charges will be filed against the owner. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they continue treatment and work toward foster placement and adoption.

hero.headline: Florida Executes William Reaves for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves at Florida State Prison on Tuesday, 40 years after he shot and killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court had rejected his last state appeals earlier in October. The Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors before his execution, including his brother, sister, nephew, a friend and his spiritual advisor. His final meal was crackers and juice.

Twenty-nine people were present for the execution, including 16 spectators evenly split between men and women. Reaves was strapped to the gurney face-up with multiple IVs in his left arm. When asked for any final words, he said, "No, I do not." Witnesses described his breathing growing heavy before a man in a white shirt shook his shoulder and said his name. A doctor entered the room, checked his eyes with a flashlight and listened to his heart with a stethoscope before he was pronounced dead and the curtain dropped.

According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. on Nov. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts during the encounter, and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. Raczkoski's son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, telling them he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out the verdict in 1991 after it was revealed one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death.

Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant in September and denied clemency the same day. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who had pushed DeSantis to sign the warrant, witnessed the execution on behalf of the agency. He said his goal was for the last thing he saw to be an Indian River County Sheriff's Office uniform, "knowing that justice finally came." Flowers said Raczkoski's brother was expected to be among the witnesses and had told him that Christmas was never the same for their family after Richard was killed. Reaves' attorneys had argued in court filings that he was a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for PTSD by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he had been shut out of the clemency process.

hero.headline: Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa Arrested on Fraud, Grand Theft Charges
hero.body:
Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa has been arrested and charged with grand theft and organized scheme to defraud after state investigators accused her of directing $90,000 in COVID-19 recovery grant money to businesses tied to herself and her family, despite warnings from her own staff not to apply.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the charges Wednesday during a news conference in Orlando. He said the case centers on Kissimmee's Business Boost 2.0 program, which Espinosa supported and voted to approve before later submitting applications on behalf of businesses connected to herself and relatives. "This was a program to try to help small businesses get back up on their feet after the COVID pandemic," Uthmeier said. "It was not designed to help government officials enrich themselves."

Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said his office uncovered irregularities while auditing COVID-19 grant programs run by several local governments. He said seven businesses at properties owned or managed by Espinosa's family received a combined $90,000 through the Kissimmee program, with $50,000 going to the family businesses themselves and another $40,000 going to tenants. Investigators determined Espinosa submitted the grant applications on her family's behalf and found that people within her own office had cautioned her against doing so. "We started realizing that there were people within her own office that said this is not a good idea, you should not do it," Ingoglia said. He added that Espinosa was among the first applicants when the grant window opened. Uthmeier alleged she also took part in policy decisions that made it easier to apply for and receive the money, and he said charging documents and bank records would provide further detail.

Investigators referred the case to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Florida Commission on Ethics and a special prosecutor, according to Ingoglia. FDLE Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency worked alongside investigators from the CFO's office to build the case before presenting it to prosecutors. Asked about a statement from Espinosa's attorney asserting her innocence and distinguishing between an ethics violation and a criminal offense, Uthmeier said prosecutors believe the evidence supports criminal charges, citing applications he said Espinosa signed, money she allegedly received and decisions she allegedly made regarding the program. Uthmeier said he had not spoken with Gov. Ron DeSantis since the arrest when asked whether the governor might take action regarding her position as mayor. State officials also said they intend to investigate how word of the impending arrest became public beforehand, which Uthmeier said can create safety risks for law enforcement and complicate evidence. The case is part of what Uthmeier's office described as an expanded focus on public corruption investigations across Florida. Espinosa has served as Kissimmee's mayor since November 2024. The charges remain allegations, and she is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

Ron DeSantis since Espinosa's arrest when asked whether the governor could take action concerning her position as mayor.State officials also said they plan to investigate how information about the impending arrest became public before it took place. hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Murder of Indian River County Deputy
hero.teaser: Florida put William Reaves to death 40 years after he killed Deputy Richard Raczkoski near Vero Beach, closing a case Sheriff Eric Flowers pushed to resolve.
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves by lethal injection Tuesday at 6 p.m., 40 years after he killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at Florida State Prison at 6:12 p.m. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday after the Florida Supreme Court had already rejected his last state appeals in October.

According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts, and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. Raczkoski's son was born after his father's death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, telling them he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he said, according to a transcript filed by the state.

Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 after it was revealed one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant in September and denied clemency the same day. Reaves' attorneys argued in court filings that he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, witnessed the execution. He said his goal was for the last thing he saw to be an Indian River County Sheriff's Office uniform, "knowing that justice finally came." Flowers said Raczkoski's brother was expected among the witnesses and had told him that Christmas was never the same for their family after Richard was killed. The Florida Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, a friend and a spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice. Asked for final words before the execution, Reaves said, "No, I do not."

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case: Police Still Weighing Charges
cards.teaser: More than 100 cats rescued from a Port St. Lucie hoarding situation are recovering at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, where staff describe widespread flea infestations, ear mites and respiratory illness. Police say they are still deciding whether to file criminal charges against the owner.
cards.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, and police say they are still determining whether to file criminal charges against the owner. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, described the condition of the animals when they arrived. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care while others remain at the shelter. Wees said shelter staff cannot always tell which kittens belong to which mother because the cats were all living together in the same house. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was on site within days of being contacted. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. She said the cats are showing significant improvement under the added care. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said.

Port St. Lucie police continue to monitor the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed against the owner. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as treatment continues.
