hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Weighs Chief Jeff Lee's Future After No-Confidence Vote
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District Board was scheduled to discuss Fire Chief Jeff Lee's future at its regular 3 p.m. meeting Wednesday, two weeks after the district's firefighters union released a no-confidence vote against top leadership. The board's agenda, listed under Chair Shannon Martin, includes an item titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not specify whose retirement would be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public.

The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released the vote results earlier in October. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence, a 74.23% no-confidence share. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the result would be formally presented to the board. Gonzalez and Sabol both cleared that threshold. The union said in its release that it calls on the board to carefully consider the results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve the county and the public they have sworn to protect.

Since the vote, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role, which the district said both Gonzalez and Lee agreed to and had discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days' notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire in December. Wednesday's agenda also includes selection of a law firm and a new district attorney.

The no-confidence vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district fired three veteran firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others after videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing, though the firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief, with board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler saying at an Oct. 6 meeting that the district cannot investigate itself. Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district's insurance representatives. Lee has said the board must fix the lack of a complaints policy because it is not a problem he can solve himself. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. A motion in August to suspend Lee and Sabol failed on a 2 to 4 vote. The district said after the no-confidence vote that it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action, pointing to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee's tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. military and became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. In 2017, after a similar union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then-Chief Buddy Emerson's immediate retirement and paid him severance through the end of his contract.

hero.headline: Indian River Sheriff Witnesses Execution of Deputy's 1986 Killer
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves on Tuesday night at Florida State Prison. Reaves was convicted of killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. He was quickly arrested after the crime and sentenced to death, and that sentence held through a retrial and multiple appeals.

Flowers said he deliberately positioned himself in the front row of the viewing area so Reaves would be able to see him. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I'm glad that he saw that," Flowers said. The execution lasted about 12 minutes. Reaves did not give a final statement, and his last meal was crackers and juice.

"The real kicker on top of it was that he didn't say anything; he didn't make a last statement; he didn't say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. It was the first execution Flowers had ever witnessed. He described the moment as the closing of a long chapter for his agency and for Raczkowski's family, but said it did not amount to true justice.

"It's closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," he added. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office plans to unveil a monument next month honoring its two fallen deputies.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case: Shelter Details Scale of Medical Care
hero.body:
More than 100 cats rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now undergoing extensive medical treatment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, which says the animals arrived suffering from upper respiratory infections, ear mites, fleas and open sores. Port St. Lucie Animal Control removed the cats over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. Police previously confirmed that 124 cats were taken from the home, some found dead, and that two residents were cited for hoarding and failing to provide medical care. Police are still determining whether criminal charges will be filed.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said the cats arrived in poor physical condition. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one of them was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care while other kittens remain at the shelter.

The scale of the intake has created confusion over which kittens belong to which mother. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. To manage the surge, the shelter is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters.

Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was deployed to the shelter within days of being contacted. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the cats are showing significant improvement under the added care. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as treatment continues.

hero.headline: Indian River Sheriff Witnesses Execution of Deputy's 1986 Killer
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night, closing a case that stretched back 40 years to the 1986 murder of Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. He was arrested quickly after the crime and sentenced to death, a sentence that survived a retrial and several appeals over the following decades.

Flowers said he deliberately positioned himself where Reaves could see him. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I'm glad that he saw that," Flowers said. The execution lasted about 12 minutes, and Flowers said Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn't say anything; he didn't make a last statement; he didn't say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves' last meal consisted of crackers and juice.

Flowers called it his first time witnessing an execution and said the moment brought mixed emotions. "It's closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. He also honored the deputy's memory directly. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office plans to unveil a monument next month honoring its two fallen deputies. The tribute will stand as a lasting marker of the office's losses even as Tuesday's execution brings a legal end to the four-decade case surrounding Raczkowski's death.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue Honors Madison Isler With First Heroic Heart Award
hero.teaser: Nearly two months after a Martin County woman used CPR to help save a drowning 3-year-old, Martin County Fire Rescue honored her rescue efforts and reunited her with the child she saved.
hero.body:
Madison Isler, a 20-year-old Martin County woman, was honored with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award nearly two months after she used CPR to help save 3-year-old Luna, who was found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. The award ceremony, held at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters, reunited Isler with Luna for the first time since the Aug. 23 rescue.

The rescue happened as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex and noticed something unusual in the water. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." Isler said she jumped in and pulled Luna out, and the girl was blue and motionless. She called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, drawing on training she learned years earlier from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool." A family friend who works as a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said the two continued their efforts until Luna responded. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.

At the recognition ceremony, Cianciulli presented Isler with the department's inaugural Heroic Heart Award. "Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said. According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive the award.

Isler said the recognition mattered less to her than seeing Luna alive and thriving. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said. Isler calls Luna her "unicorn baby." Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she remains grateful that Isler was nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family."

hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Reaves was convicted of killing Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. He was arrested quickly after the crime and sentenced to death, and the sentence survived a retrial and several appeals over the following decades.

Flowers said he deliberately positioned himself in the front row of the execution chamber, on the side of the room where Reaves would be able to see him. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I'm glad that he saw that," Flowers said. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice."

Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, as the first he had ever witnessed. Reaves did not deliver a final statement before his death. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn't say anything; he didn't make a last statement; he didn't say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves' last meal consisted of crackers and juice.

Flowers said the execution brought a sense of closure but not full justice for the loss of his deputy nearly four decades ago. "It's closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office plans to unveil a monument next month honoring its two fallen deputies.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves Tuesday evening, 40 years after he shot and killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison at 6:12 p.m. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals.

According to court records, Raczkoski responded to the store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. The deputy's son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, saying he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant in September.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers pushed the governor to sign the warrant and witnessed the execution.

Reaves' attorneys fought the execution to the end, arguing in court filings that he was a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. DeSantis denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Florida Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, friend and spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Crews Battle Two Structure Fires in Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District crews battled two separate structure fires Monday, one on 17th Street in Fort Pierce and another on Aragon Lane in Port St. Lucie, with firefighters displacing residents at both properties while also rescuing a cat from the Aragon Lane home during the response. The two fires were part of a busy day for the district, which handled 215 calls for service Monday, and the American Red Cross is now assisting the families affected by both incidents.

Firefighters moved quickly at both scenes, bringing the flames under control and limiting how far they spread, according to the fire district. That rapid response helped reduce the amount of damage at each property. The district has not released further details about what sparked either fire or how extensive the damage turned out to be at the two homes.

The rescue at the Aragon Lane property stood out among the day's calls, as crews pulled a cat from the burning structure during their work to contain the fire. Beyond the rescue, the district has not provided additional specifics on the condition of the residents or the pet, nor has it detailed how many people were forced out of their homes as a result of the two fires.

With residents from both the Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie properties displaced, the American Red Cross stepped in to provide support as families navigate finding temporary housing and replacing lost belongings. The fire district credited its crews with containing both incidents swiftly despite the volume of calls they were managing across the county that day. Handling 215 calls in a single day reflects the kind of workload the district regularly faces, and Monday's structure fires were just two of the many emergencies firefighters responded to as part of that total.

The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to serve as the primary emergency response agency for fire and rescue calls throughout the county, routinely managing a high volume of incidents ranging from structure fires to medical emergencies and other calls for service. Monday's events underscore the kind of rapid-response work crews carry out on a daily basis, often juggling multiple serious incidents at once while still working to protect both residents and their pets. The district has not indicated whether any firefighters were injured during either response or whether investigators plan to release more information on the causes of the fires in the coming days.

hero.headline: Southeast County Line Road Bridge Closes for Year-Long $7M Rebuild in Martin County
hero.body:
A bridge on Southeast County Line Road in southern Martin County is now closed for a year-long reconstruction project expected to cost $7 million, with state and federal grants covering $6 million of that total. A road block is now in place notifying drivers to turn around, and officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route while the detour is in effect.

George May, who lives just off Southeast County Line Road, said the closure will take some adjustment for residents and commuters alike. "It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club," May said. May already drives over an hour to work each day and expects the detour to add about 20 minutes to his commute.

Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said the project involves extensive coordination because of utility work at the site. "There are a lot of utilities ther," Aveni said. "There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time." The new bridge will stand two feet higher than the current structure and will use a more resilient type of rebar designed to improve safety. Aveni said crews also plan to eliminate a sharp curve before the bridge and soften the approach, a change he said will make the area safer for pedestrians as well as drivers.

Despite the inconvenience, residents say they support the investment after watching the old bridge deteriorate. May said he had noticed large cracks underneath the structure before the closure began. Daniel Von, another area resident, said the temporary disruption is worth the upgrade. "It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that, to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area," Von said. May said his main hope now is that the county sticks to its timeline. "I'm fine with it as long as they keep the project on schedule," he said.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Murder of IRC Deputy Richard Raczkoski
hero.body:
Florida executed William Reaves by lethal injection Tuesday evening, 40 years after he shot and killed Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. at Florida State Prison. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals.

According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. The deputy's son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia, and admitted to the shooting in a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, saying he had been using cocaine. "I've never met a finer officer in my life," he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state.

A jury convicted Reaves in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant in September and denied clemency the same day. Reaves' attorneys fought the execution to the end, arguing in court filings that he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs and that the jury that sentenced him never heard details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the death warrant, planned to witness the execution in uniform. The brother told Flowers that "Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed." The Florida Department of Corrections said Reaves had five visitors Tuesday, including his brother, sister, nephew, a friend and his spiritual advisor, and that his final meal was crackers and juice.

hero.headline: William Reaves Executed for 1986 Killing of Indian River County Deputy
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. Tuesday after Florida carried out his execution by lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke, closing out a four-decade case over the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. The execution was Florida's 18th of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeal without comment Tuesday afternoon.

According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged he had placed that call from a payphone outside the store. While the two men spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts and they struggled over it. Reaves regained control of the weapon, and investigators said the deputy tried to run away before Reaves shot him four times. Raczkowski later died from his wounds.

Reaves was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court later reversed that conviction over a conflict of interest involving the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and his subsequent appeals failed. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his final appeals last week.

Reaves' attorneys had challenged Florida's three-drug lethal injection protocol, which uses a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, a method the state's courts have previously upheld against similar challenges. Defense attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled due to post-traumatic stress disorder from his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday asking him to halt the execution.

Florida Department of Corrections spokesman Jordan Kirkland said Reaves woke at 5 a.m. Tuesday and remained compliant throughout the day. His last meal was crackers and juice, and he met with four visitors, including his sister, his brother, his nephew and a friend, along with a spiritual adviser. Reaves was the eighth Florida death row inmate over age 70 executed this year. Florida set a state record with 19 executions last year, and another execution, that of Jesse Guardado, 64, convicted of robbing and killing a woman in 2004, is scheduled for November and would tie that record if carried out as planned.

hero.headline: 124 Cats, Some Dead, Removed From Port St. Lucie Home in Hoarding Case
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police recovered 124 cats, living and deceased, from a home in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street as part of a criminal hoarding investigation. Two of the three residents of the home have been cited for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, according to police.

Animal Control personnel responded to the home on October 13 after receiving concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions. Inside, they documented accumulated feces and found deceased kittens. Police said the investigation remains active and have not released details about potential future arrests.

All 124 cats have been surrendered and are now receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas, while others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care. Some of the animals were transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Police said many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed.

The case has required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

cards.headline: Humane Society of St. Lucie County Seeks Help After Port St. Lucie Cat Hoarding Case
cards.teaser: More than 120 cats and kittens were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County says the rescue has overwhelmed its staff and resources.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found inside a home in the 2500 block of Warwick Street, where investigators discovered unsanitary conditions including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens. Two of the three people living in the home were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County took in 106 of the cats and kittens, and the organization says the influx has doubled its cat population and strained its ability to care for the animals.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said the cats likely had to compete for food, leaving some underweight, and some nursing kittens may have been feeding from the wrong mother. "If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now," Wees said. She said almost all of the cats arrived with fleas and ear mites, and some had open sores requiring immediate medical treatment.

Staff and volunteers are now working to stabilize the animals. "They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes," Wees said. Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are improving quickly, pointing to their liveliness and eagerness to approach workers and take food. Still, Wees said some of the animals remain in a dangerous condition and are being treated in the shelter's sick room. "They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation," Wees said. "Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time."

Wees said the case has overwhelmed both staff and resources at the shelter. "It overwhelms the staff," Wees said. "It overwhelms our resources." The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking the community for donations, volunteers and foster homes to help with the recovery effort. "These little babies can't do it for themselves," Wees said. "So, we and the community need to do it for them." Once the cats and kittens receive the medical care they need, they will be made available for adoption.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds Brings Governor Bus Tour to Fort Pierce College Campus
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds stopped at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center in Fort Pierce, joined by Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall to rally voters ahead of election day.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate and Congressman Byron Donalds stopped in Fort Pierce on Tuesday as part of a statewide bus tour, holding a campaign event at Indian River State College's Eastman Workforce Center. Donalds was joined by his running mate for lieutenant governor, Bryan Avila, along with Congressman Brian Mast and State Senator Erin Grall, as the group worked to drive voter turnout in the final stretch before election day.

"I think for us we're just focused on making sure we drive turnout to the polls," Donalds said.

The Fort Pierce stop came in the middle of Tuesday's leg of the bus tour, which began in Melbourne and later continued to Miami. Donalds and Avila held a meet and greet in front of the campaign bus outside the Eastman Workforce Center, taking photos and talking with supporters who gathered at the stop.

"We show up, we stand outside, we take pictures with you, sign the bus, we have conversations with the voters. We've been consistently doing that for months now on the campaign trail. We're going to continue to do it every single day. I think the symbolism of the bus tour, it just helps people know that you're out here working hard for their vote and you want their support," Donalds said.

Donalds also laid out the economic message he has carried throughout the campaign, telling the Fort Pierce crowd that affordability for families and seniors remains central to his pitch to voters.

"We want our kids to achieve the Florida dream for themselves. We want to make sure it's affordable for our seniors and our working families in our state. That's what we've been laser focused on this entire time. We haven't gotten off of that," Donalds said.

hero.headline: More Than 100 Rescued Cats in Port St. Lucie Case Showing Improvement
hero.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens pulled from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are showing significant improvement as they recover at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, according to shelter officials. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. Many of the cats arrived in poor condition, and St. Lucie police are now monitoring the case to determine whether criminal charges will be filed.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said the animals came in with a range of medical problems. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one mother was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care while the rest of the cats remain at the shelter. Because all the animals had been living together in the same house, staff have struggled to sort out which kittens belong to which mothers. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said.

The Humane Society is getting help from American Humane, a national organization that assists local communities during large-scale animal intakes or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said the group mobilized quickly once Wees asked for support. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said.

Nickelsen said the intervention is paying off, with many of the cats showing clear signs of recovery. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. St. Lucie police continue to monitor the case as they decide whether to pursue criminal charges. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is asking the community for donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they recover.

William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m. Tuesday at Florida State Prison, 40 years after he fatally shot Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. The U.S. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals. He is set to die by lethal injection unless a last-minute intervention occurs.

According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. on Oct. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves' shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as Raczkoski turned away. Raczkoski's son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. hero.headline: William Reaves Set for Tuesday Execution in 1986 Killing of Indian River Deputy
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to die by lethal injection Tuesday at 6 p.m. for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski, though a pending appeal before the U.S. Supreme Court could still delay the execution. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final state appeals last week, clearing the way for the scheduled injection at Florida State Prison near Starke.

According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves had placed that call himself from a payphone outside the store. While the two men spoke, a gun fell from Reaves' shorts, and they struggled over the weapon until Reaves regained control of it. Investigators said Raczkowski tried to run before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy died from his wounds. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year later, but the Florida Supreme Court reversed that conviction because of a conflict of interest involving the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. A second jury convicted Reaves and sentenced him to death again in 1992, and his appeals since then have failed.

Reaves' attorneys challenged Florida's three-drug lethal injection protocol, which uses a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart. The Florida Supreme Court has previously upheld that method against similar legal challenges. Defense attorneys also argued that jurors who recommended the death penalty were never told the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs had rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled due to post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent Gov. Ron DeSantis a letter Monday asking him to halt the execution.

Reaves would be Florida's 18th execution of the year and the eighth this year involving a death-row prisoner over the age of 70, a trend that has drawn attention to the nation's aging death-row population. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims' families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. Florida set a state record last year with 19 executions, and another execution, that of Jesse Guardado, 64, is scheduled for November for a 2004 robbery and murder. If both scheduled executions proceed, Florida would match last year's record.

hero.headline: Southbound Turnpike Lanes Reopen After Tractor Trailer Fire in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Southbound lanes on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County have reopened after a tractor trailer fire shut them down Tuesday morning. The fire broke out around 7:54 a.m. just before Mile Marker 161, about 10 miles north of the Okeechobee Road exit.

The St. Lucie County Fire District said the fire reportedly started in the cab, but crews arrived to find the truck completely engulfed in flames. Firefighters brought the blaze under control by 8:07 a.m. The Florida Highway Patrol was also on scene. The St. Lucie County Fire District reported no injuries.

hero.headline: Tractor-Trailer Fire Shuts Down Florida's Turnpike Lanes in St. Lucie County
hero.teaser: A tractor trailer caught fire on the southbound Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County Tuesday morning, closing lanes near Mile Marker 161. Crews brought the blaze under control within about 15 minutes, and no injuries were reported.
hero.body:
A tractor trailer fire closed southbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County Tuesday morning, just before Mile Marker 161 about 10 miles north of the Okeechobee Road exit. The fire broke out around 7:54 a.m.

The St. Lucie County Fire District said the fire reportedly started in the cab of the truck. By the time crews arrived, the vehicle was completely engulfed in flames.

Firefighters brought the blaze under control by 8:07 a.m., roughly 13 minutes after it started. The Florida Highway Patrol was also on scene to assist with the response and manage traffic along the closed southbound lanes.

The St. Lucie County Fire District did not report any injuries from the fire.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue Gives First Heroic Heart Award to Pool Rescuer
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue presented its first-ever Heroic Heart Award to Madison Isler, nearly two months after the 20-year-old used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Isler, Luna and the family reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters to mark the occasion and celebrate the outcome of the August rescue.

The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. "It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl." Isler said the girl, 3-year-old Luna, was motionless at the bottom of the pool when she spotted her. "I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. "You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool." A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said the two continued their efforts until Luna responded. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.

During the recognition ceremony, Cianciulli honored Isler on behalf of the department and the community for her courage to act. According to Martin County Fire Rescue, Isler is the first person to receive the Heroic Heart Award. Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help. "It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.

For Isler, the award is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up. "What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said. Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby." Hernandez said she remains overwhelmed with gratitude toward Isler and her family. "I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said. Martin County Fire Rescue says Isler's childhood CPR training became the critical action that helped save Luna's life.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Police Arrest Man in Seaway Bridge Indecent Exposure Cases
hero.body:
Fort Pierce Police arrested Kyle Kennedy, 27, Friday after investigating multiple reports of indecent exposure involving women walking alone on the Seaway Bridge. Investigators reviewed earlier reports, identified patterns linking the incidents, interviewed victims and conducted photo lineups. Two victims positively identified Kennedy as the suspect during those lineups, leading to his arrest, police said.

Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation.

Fort Pierce resident Leidi Cruz said she regularly walks the bridge and has never had any issues. "It's just crazy to know that there's something like that going on," Cruz said.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-467-6800. Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: Martin County Woman Gets Fire Department's First Heroic Heart Award for Pool Rescue
hero.body:
Martin County fire officials have presented 20-year-old Madison Isler with the department's first-ever Heroic Heart Award after she pulled 3-year-old Luna Hernandez from the bottom of an apartment pool on Aug. 23 and performed CPR that saved the girl's life. Isler will also be recognized at an upcoming Martin County Commission meeting.

Isler said she noticed Luna motionless at the bottom of the pool while walking to retrieve a hair clip she had left on the opposite side. "I had to go get my hair clip that I left on, like, the opposite side of the pool. And as I was walking, I saw a shadow, and it kind of looked like a smudge on your sunglasses," Isler said. She jumped into the water and pulled Luna out. Finding the child blue, unresponsive, and not breathing, Isler began CPR while shouting for someone to call 911. A pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and rushed over to help.

Isler said at least 10 adults were at the pool when Luna went under, and that drownings often happen silently and quickly. She has nicknamed Luna the "unicorn baby." "Because this doesn't happen. Drownings don't end like this. When they're babies 3 years old like this, they just go under, slip right under really quick. And she's a unicorn," Isler said. "There were at least 10 adults at the swimming pool when she went down. So, it just happens right in front of you and silently quick, so for me to walk by and see it was a pretty slim chance. I call her the unicorn baby," she said.

Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented Isler with the award. "Because of the actions of one young woman who happened to be at the right place at the right time, Luna was given another chance. A chance to go home, a chance to grow up, a chance to make memories with her family. A chance to live a life that she was waiting for," Cianciulli said. "Madison is an incredible young woman." Isler's father, who works for Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, and her mother, who is retired from the department, attended the presentation. Luna's mother, Kristine Hernandez, was out of town when the incident happened. She shared photos of her daughter's smile and credited the timing of Isler's actions. "Stopping on the way to the pool to get a hair clip. There're just minor little details in the story that it's God's work that he put her when we needed her, like at the right place, at the right time," Hernandez said. "I'm just thankful for the life that Luna gets to live now," she said, adding that such accidents can happen to anyone. During a recent meeting between the two, Luna, described as shy around cameras, clung to Isler, whom she has come to see as her new best friend.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Gives Three Corners Developers Fourth Extension, Sets Dec. 8 Deadline
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council has approved a fourth extension for ClearBlue, the developer negotiating the Three Corners project, giving the company until Dec. 8 to reach an agreement on financing and lease terms or risk the city reconsidering the deal entirely.

The Three Corners project is planned for the site of the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge, with proposals calling for hotels, a marina, restaurants and walking paths. Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said he has worked on the project since 2019 and wants the city to secure favorable terms for residents. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens," Cotugno said.

Cotugno said some progress has been made on the financial side of the developer's proposal, but he made clear that the council will walk away if ClearBlue's plans do not match the city's goals. "We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens." To help close the gap, the council is appointing a liaison to work directly with the developers and bring them in for in-person discussions on the project.

Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said the company will meet with the city council on Oct. 27. He said ClearBlue had been requesting a liaison for months and welcomed the move. "It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said. "We're glad we finally have one on the books now." Salera said ClearBlue has invested more than $1 million and 21,000 hours of work into the project and remains committed to finishing it. "We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close." Cotugno said he shares that hope as long as both sides keep moving toward a resolution. "I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," he said.

hero.headline: More Than 100 Cats Rescued From Port St. Lucie Hoarding House
hero.body:
More than 100 cats and kittens are now receiving medical care and nourishment after being pulled from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie. St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over three days last week, with the first group arriving at the Humane Society of St. Lucie shelter on Tuesday.

Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Lucie, said many of the cats arrived in poor health. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," Wees said. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, and one was too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. Wees said staff are still sorting out which cats belong to which litters. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," she said.

The Humane Society is getting outside help from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane, said she was called in quickly after Wees reached out. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," Nickelsen said. Nickelsen said the extra support is already paying off, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," she said.

St. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine whether any criminal charges will be filed. The Humane Society of St. Lucie is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens as they continue treatment and work toward foster placement and adoption.

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man Sentenced to Time Served in Hotel 'Exorcism' Attack
hero.body:
A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman and throwing water on her at a Vero Beach hotel has been sentenced to nine months in jail, with credit for time already served. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. He had been held in St. Lucie County Jail since his arrest and was credited with 297 days of time served.

The case began December 23, 2025, when deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office responded to the Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. A second witness told investigators she heard a woman yelling "Stop," "Rape" and "Help Me" before seeing a man appear to drag the woman back into the room. When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, identified as Coppeto, who was visibly wet and shaken.

Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him.

Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. He was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery following the incident. With his plea and sentencing now complete, the case is closed.

Kyle Kennedy, 27, was arrested Friday after investigators reviewed previous reports and identified patterns linking the cases. Kennedy faces two counts of indecent exposure and one charge of violation of probation.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity on the bridge or has information about the incidents to call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-467-6800. Anonymous tips can also be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

cards.headline: Man Dies in Lakewood Park After Domestic Call Turns Into Barricade Standoff
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County deputies evacuated a woman and children through a side window before finding a man dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound during a Fort Pierce barricade situation. The sheriff's office says there is no ongoing threat to the community.
cards.body:
A man died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after a domestic violence call in Fort Pierce's Lakewood Park neighborhood turned into a barricaded-subject standoff Saturday morning, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard and encountered a man in the front yard, who went back inside after seeing law enforcement.

Deputies later made contact with a man and woman at the front door. A deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it, but the man shut the door and retreated inside, setting off a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still in the home. Deputies said the man came outside several times during the standoff and indicated he would surrender after making a phone call, but each time he went back inside.

During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Fearing for the safety of an adult woman and children still inside, deputies entered the home without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff's office said. Deputies then found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, along with crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office, remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. Anyone struggling with thoughts of suicide can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7, or chat online at 988lifeline.org.

hero.headline: Sheriff Eric Flowers to Witness Execution of Deputy's Killer Tuesday
hero.body:
William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection Tuesday at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski. hero.headline: Florida Secures Arrest Warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 Jet Shootdown
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that state prosecutors and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement have secured an arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro, accusing him of conspiring to murder four men in the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft operated by the anti-Castro group Brothers to the Rescue. Castro has been charged with one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in connection with the attack, in which Cuban military fighter jets destroyed two unarmed planes over international waters.

Authorities said three unarmed Cessna aircraft departed Opa-locka Airport in Miami-Dade County on a February flight in 1996. After crossing the 24th parallel and flying outside Cuba's territorial waters, two of the planes were destroyed by air-to-air missiles fired from Cuban MiG fighter jets. According to a probable cause affidavit, the aircraft were traveling away from Cuba at the time and received no warning before being shot down. The attack killed four men with ties to Florida: Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.

The warrant, obtained by the Office of Statewide Prosecution and FDLE, alleges that Castro played a key role in authorizing the attack. The affidavit states that Castro, who at the time served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces and first vice president, was among the final decision-makers who approved the operation. Investigators allege he issued standing orders to military leaders to shoot down aircraft associated with Brothers to the Rescue if the planes appeared over the sea. State investigators also allege that Cuban intelligence agents operating in South Florida infiltrated Brothers to the Rescue and fed flight information to the Cuban government as part of an operation known as "Operation Scorpion."

"Raúl Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Tests Water Sensors, Clears Drains Ahead of Weekend Rain
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Public Works crews spent the past week clearing debris from storm drains and grates as more rain is expected across the Treasure Coast this weekend. The city is also testing new pilot water-level sensors designed to send alerts to select staff when water levels rise at specific locations, according to Scott Samples, communications manager for the City of Port St. Lucie.

"It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said. He added that water levels in the city's retention ponds and canals are currently adequate and will not need to be lowered ahead of the rain.

The preparations come as chronic flooding continues to plague the intersection of California and Savona boulevards, where water levels rose last week. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near that intersection, said flooding has been a recurring problem there for years. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins said she already warned customers that Saturday grooming appointments may need to be rescheduled. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," she said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a larger drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood that would include raising portions of the roadway near the flood-prone intersection. Samples said the project would resolve the recurring flooding once finished, but the effort remains in the data collection phase and has not yet moved into design. That means a permanent fix could still be years away. Collins said the ongoing flooding has disrupted her business operations. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," she said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating Pets Play Grooming altogether, though that option comes with its own challenges. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Drug Bust: Gang Member, Two Others Charged in Fentanyl Case
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation into a reputed gang member's fentanyl and cocaine distribution has led to three arrests and the seizure of drugs, firearms and gang-related items, police said. Detectives identified Albert Johnson, 36, as an identified gang member involved in distributing fentanyl and cocaine. After building evidence linking Johnson to cocaine sales, detectives arrested him without incident and then executed a search warrant at his home on Southwest Burlington Terrace.

The search of Johnson's home led to the arrest of a juvenile, who was charged with tampering with physical evidence and cannabis-related offenses. A 19-year-old identified as Fleur was also arrested and charged with cannabis possession and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Police said the investigation resulted in the seizure of 69.5 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of fentanyl, 10 ounces of cannabis and 1 gram of MDMA. Officers also recovered three firearms, narcotics packaging equipment and gang-related items from the search.

The case underscores the scope of gang-connected drug distribution authorities say they are working to disrupt in Port St. Lucie. The seizure of fentanyl alongside cocaine, cannabis and MDMA, combined with the recovery of multiple firearms and gang-related items, reflects the breadth of narcotics activity investigators linked to Johnson before his arrest.

hero.headline: Turnpike Reopens in Martin County After Semi Jackknifes Near SE Bridge Road
hero.body:
All northbound lanes of Florida's Turnpike in Martin County reopened Friday afternoon after a jackknifed semi-truck shut down traffic and sent one person to the hospital. The crash happened shortly before noon near mile marker 125, underneath the SE Bridge Road overpass, causing heavy delays for drivers.

The Florida Highway Patrol said the truck driver lost control, causing the crash. Paramedics took one patient with minor injuries to the hospital by ground, according to Martin County Fire Rescue spokeswoman Jillian Kay.

Lanes began reopening to traffic just after 1 p.m. Friday, easing the backup that had built up along the busy corridor during the midday hours.

Kay said the Martin County Sheriff's Office and the Florida Highway Patrol also responded to the scene and will investigate the cause of the crash.

hero.headline: Northbound Turnpike Lanes Reopen in Martin County After Semi Crash
hero.body:
All northbound lanes on Florida's Turnpike have reopened in Martin County following a major crash involving a jackknifed semi-truck on Friday. The wreck was reported on Florida's Turnpike North between mile markers 122 and 125, an area that saw significant traffic disruption while crews worked to clear the scene.

Photos taken at the location showed two fire engines and Florida Highway Patrol troopers responding to the crash. The jackknifed semi had blocked all northbound lanes in the stretch, backing up traffic for drivers making their way through Martin County before crews were able to clear the roadway and restore the flow of traffic.

The cause of the crash has not been determined, and it is not yet known whether anyone was injured. Drivers in the area should still anticipate delays as the situation continues to develop and as crews finish any remaining cleanup work along the turnpike.

Further details on what caused the crash and whether there were any injuries are expected to be released by the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigation continues.

hero.headline: Man Dies in Apparent Suicide After Fort Pierce Barricade Standoff
hero.body:
A man died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound Saturday after a barricaded-subject standoff with deputies in the Lakewood Park neighborhood of Fort Pierce, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Deputies evacuated a woman and children from the home before finding the man dead, and the sheriff's office says there is no ongoing threat to the community.

Deputies responded around 10:17 a.m. to a reported domestic violence incident at a home in the 7600 block of Winter Garden Boulevard. They found a man in the front yard, but he went back inside after seeing law enforcement. Deputies later made contact with a man and woman at the front door, and a deputy spotted what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession. The deputy ordered him to drop the weapon, but he shut the door and retreated into the home, triggering a barricaded-subject situation with other occupants still inside.

Over the course of the standoff, the man came outside several times and told deputies he would surrender after making a phone call, but he repeatedly went back into the house, according to the sheriff's office. During his final retreat inside, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Concerned for the safety of an adult woman and children still in the home, deputies entered without alerting the occupants and evacuated them through a side window. They later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The sheriff's office said there is no ongoing threat to the community following the discovery. Detectives with the agency's Criminal Investigations Division, along with crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office, remained at the scene to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident. Anyone struggling with thoughts of suicide can call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24/7, or chat online at 988lifeline.org.

Authorities later made contact with a man and woman at the front door, and during that interaction a deputy saw what appeared to be a firearm in the man's possession and ordered him to drop it. Instead, the man closed the door and retreated into the home, creating a barricaded-subject situation while other people remained inside.

Investigators said the man came outside several times and told deputies he would surrender after making a phone call, but each time he went back inside. During his final retreat into the home, deputies heard what appeared to be a gunshot. Knowing an adult woman and children were still inside and could be in danger, deputies entered the residence and evacuated them through a side window, the sheriff's office said. Deputies later found the man dead from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Authorities said there is no ongoing threat to the community. Detectives, crime scene technicians and investigators from the Medical Examiner's Office are expected to remain at the scene for several hours as the investigation continues.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound Man Killed by Friend Was Trying to Rob Him, Sheriff Says
cards.teaser: Jarvis Preston, 21, died after his friend shot him with an AR15 during an alleged robbery attempt in Hobe Sound. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says no arrest has been made while investigators weigh whether the shooting was self-defense.
cards.body:
Jarvis Preston, 21, of Hobe Sound died Thursday after being shot by a close friend two days earlier, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said. New details released by Sheriff John Budensiek show the shooting followed an alleged attempted robbery, and investigators are now working with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooter acted in self-defense. No arrest has been made.

The shooting happened Wednesday night on Southeast Citrus Way, off Florida Avenue, in the Banner Lake neighborhood. Neighbors reported hearing three gunshots around 8 p.m. Sheriff Budensiek said Preston and his friend had been drinking earlier in the day and that Preston tried to rob the friend near their homes. "Multiple witnesses have now told us that he made threats to all kinds of people out on the street. He was yelling loudly, was extremely intoxicated, acting belligerent," Budensiek said.

According to the sheriff, the friend, who was armed with an AR15 assault rifle, came out of his house twice with his girlfriend during the encounter. The second time, he and Preston, who was carrying a handgun with a 30-round magazine, got into a confrontation that ended in gunfire. "The deceased (Preston) starts to pull out a handgun. Actually, it's a rifle, shoots him three times in the chest and he (Preston) drops right there," Budensiek said. The handgun was recovered at the scene. Preston was taken to St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach, where he died Thursday. Budensiek said the man who shot Preston tried to render aid and stayed at the scene afterward.

Preston's mother, Ebony Preston, said her son was not married and was the father of a small child. She said she does not know what led to the shooting and struggled to understand how it happened between two close friends. "It's just, it's dreadful, like, I can't, I can't understand what, why it expired to the way it did, because they, best friends. What escalated this to happen when it did?" she said. Preston's stepfather, Rodney Clemon, said he also could not make sense of it. "That's what I don't understand how it come about, 'cause they best friends," he said. Ebony Preston said the family is left with more questions than answers. "It's lot of unanswered questions. But my son is dead, so how do we go from there?" she said. The Sheriff's Office says it continues to work with the State Attorney's Office to determine whether the shooting was legally justified under Florida's stand your ground law or whether charges will be filed.

hero.teaser: A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation into an identified gang member led to three arrests and the seizure of fentanyl, cocaine, firearms and gang-related items.
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie Police Department narcotics investigation has resulted in three arrests after detectives received information that Albert Johnson, 36, an identified gang member, was involved in fentanyl and cocaine distribution. After gathering evidence linking Johnson to cocaine sales, detectives arrested him without incident before executing a search warrant at his home on Southwest Burlington Terrace.

The search warrant also led to the arrest of a juvenile, who was charged with tampering with physical evidence and cannabis-related offenses. A third person, 19-year-old Fleur, was arrested and charged with cannabis possession and possession of drug paraphernalia.

Police seized 69.5 grams of cocaine, 12 grams of fentanyl, 10 ounces of cannabis, 1 gram of MDMA, three firearms, narcotics packaging equipment and gang-related items during the investigation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Tests New Water Sensors as Weekend Rain Threatens Flooding
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Public Works crews are preparing for more rain expected this weekend across the Treasure Coast, with staff clearing debris from drains and grates throughout the week. Scott Samples, communications manager with the City of Port St. Lucie, said water levels in retention ponds and canals are at an adequate level and will not need to be lowered ahead of the storm.

The city is also testing new pilot water sensors designed to alert select staff when water levels rise in specific locations. "It's a way for us to respond faster to very specific locations," Samples said.

The preparations come as chronic flooding continues to threaten businesses at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards. Jennifer Collins, owner of Pets Play Grooming near the intersection, said flooding has occurred there for years and that water levels rose at the intersection again last week. "We're nervous about this storm coming up this week," Collins said. "Every time it rains, we get scared." Collins said she has already messaged customers about possibly rescheduling Saturday appointments. "We may have to reschedule their dogs. We may have to push them off to next week," she said. "Saturdays are one of our busiest days, so it does really affect us as a small business."

The city is working on a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood that includes raising portions of the roadway near the troubled intersection. Samples said the project would resolve the flooding once finished. "When this project is completed, those problems won't be problems anymore," he said. The project is still in the data collection phase before it moves into design, meaning a fix could be years away. Collins said the ongoing flooding has disrupted her ability to operate. "We can't work if it's raining, and that's in Florida," she said. "That's just not OK." She said she has considered relocating her business but is hesitant given the difficulty of such a move. "We've also talked about possibly moving, and you know that would be hard too," Collins said. "I just feel like it's not, not getting better."
